papers.title: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. The Warwan sub-basin in Jammu and Kashmir is a remote glaciated region containing several glacial lakes and has recently experienced population growth and infrastructure development. Due to inaccessibility and geomorphic masking, multiple mass movement events including avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) have remained largely unreported. This study analyzes three major avalanche events from the past two decades. The September 2005 and September 2020 avalanches originated from glaciers GL-B and GL-A within the same glacier complex, while the March 2020 rock–ice avalanche initiated from the headwall of glacier GL-F in an adjacent valley and terminated before reaching its ablation zone. Runout mapping shows that the September 2020 avalanche descended from the headwall of GL-A and impacted its proglacial lake, triggering a GLOF. In contrast, the September 2005 event terminated before reaching the glacial lake that began forming in 1999 at the terminus of GL-B. Geomorphic analysis indicates persistent sediment influx from meltwater streams of GL-D and GL-E into the lake associated with GL-A, progressively infilling the basin. Continued glacier retreat caused meltwater to accumulate behind the sediment infill, dividing the basin into two disconnected lakes. Impact from the September 2020 avalanche led to complete drainage of stored water and sediment, generating a downstream debris flow. Pre- and post-GLOF imagery reveals breaching and widening of the outflow channel and deposition of a debris fan downstream. The repeated history of mass movements and continued growth of glacial lakes raise serious hazard concerns in the Warwan sub-basin. GLOF modeling identifies Lake-B as potentially hazardous lake at the present condition posing significant downstream risk. papers.title: MPM modelling of impact-loading shallow flow-like landslides in unsaturated slopes
papers.summary: Debris avalanches (DA) pose severe hazards in urbanized piedmont areas due to their large runout and potential for progressive volume increase through bed entrainment. Impact-loading mechanisms at bedrock outcrops can trigger cascading slope failures, yet the conditions controlling whether a small initial instability arrests or evolves into a catastrophic debris avalanche remain poorly understood.,This study proposes a hydro-mechanical framework for impact-induced debris avalanche inception, integrating an energy-based interpretation of the interaction between a moving saturated mass and a downslope unsaturated deposit. An advanced Material Point Method (MPM) model is developed to simulate the coupled evolution of stresses, pore water pressures, and deformations during the impact and afterwards. The simulations reproduce the loading exerted by the incoming mass and capture the progressive response of the impacted slope. Results show that the abrupt deceleration of the impacting mass leads to rapid pore pressure buildup in the impact zone and stress redistribution in successive downslope volumes. The evolution of kinetic energy reveals progressive energy transfer from the moving mass to the impacted soil, governing whether the instability is arrested or propagates downslope.,The parametric analysis demonstrates that initial soil suction in the impacted slope is the most important parameter controlling debris avalanche inception. Cases with low initial suction exhibit sustained energy transfer, progressive volume mobilization, and debris avalanche development with large volume amplification factors. In contrast, cases with higher suction dissipate kinetic energy rapidly after impact, arresting the cascading process with limited volume growth. Variations in basal friction angle, deposit thickness, and initial mass size have secondary effects. papers.title: Multi-hazard assessment of the eastern slope of the Sistema de Famatina, La Rioja province (Argentina)
papers.summary: Abstract In the eastern sector of the Sistema de Famatina, both natural processes and anthropogenic activities pose considerable risks to the landscape and its inhabitants. This study investigates the geohazards and environmental agents that have historically affected the region, with a focus on their implications for local communities and territories. The analysis integrates case studies of documented natural events, identification of mitigation strategies, satellite imagery interpretation, landform recognition, and direct field observations. In addition, meteorological, hydrological, seismic, and demographic data were compiled to identify previously undocumented events with the potential to generate significant socio-environmental impacts. The study area is subject to a range of natural hazards, including those originated by meteorological events (e.g., intense precipitation and strong winds), fluvial processes (e.g., avulsion, gully erosion, and flooding), mass movement processes (e.g., landslides and rockfalls), and seismic activity. Our results reveal the recurrent nature of these hazards; in general, their consequences are compounded by anthropogenic pressures, including land-use changes, variations in land cover, and environmental pollution. Collectively, these factors intensify existing socio-environmental issues. This research contributes to sustainable environmental management by considering plausible future scenarios and hazard interactions. Our findings are intended to inform local and regional socio-economic development strategies and to serve as a scientific resource for policymakers and planners. Furthermore, by enhancing awareness of ongoing and recurring hazards, the study supports community resilience building and the reduction of adverse impacts at the local level.

papers.title: Time-Lapse Three-Dimensional TEM Imaging and Damage Evolution of Hydraulic Fracturing in Landslide Fracture Zones
papers.summary: Landslide fracture zones play a critical role in slope instability, yet their hydraulic fracturing processes remain difficult to monitor using conventional geophysical methods. This study proposes a time‐lapse three‐dimensional transient electromagnetic (TEM) imaging approach to characterize fracture damage evolution in the Xiaolongdong–Xiahaizi landslide, Zhaotong City, China. Repeated TEM observations, integrated with GNSS displacement monitoring and environmental measurements, were used to reconstruct dynamic resistivity fields through three‐dimensional inversion. The method achieved localization accuracies better than 1 m horizontally and 2 m vertically and detected water‐filled fractures wider than 0.3 mm. Distinct resistivity precursor anomalies, characterized by a 3%–8% increase followed by a rapid decrease, occurred 2–5 min before fracture propagation. During hydraulic fracturing, resistivity decreased from 30–50 Ω·m to 8–15 Ω·m, reflecting progressive fracture connectivity. Rainy‐season permeability coefficients reached 10⁻⁴–10⁻³ m/s, one to two orders of magnitude higher than those during the dry season. Freeze–thaw processes and rainfall infiltration jointly contributed 25%–35% of slope displacement. The proposed framework provides quantitative visualization of fracture evolution and effective geophysical constraints for landslide stability assessment and early warning.

papers.title: Role of Reforestation in Reducing Landslide Risk in Galyat, Pakistan: A Remote Sensing and GIS-Based Temporal Analysis (2011–2025)
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most common natural hazards in mountainous regions, often resulting in loss of life, damage to infrastructure, and destruction of agricultural land. Forest cover plays an important role in slope stabilization, soil erosion control, and landslide-risk reduction; however, empirical evidence regarding this relationship in specific mountainous landscapes remains limited. This study investigates the relationship between vegetation change and landslide occurrence in the Galyat region of Pakistan from 2011 to 2025. Remote sensing and Geographic Information System (GIS) techniques were used to derive the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from Landsat 5, 8, and 9 imagery for 2011, 2017, and 2025. These data were compared with a landslide inventory digitised from high?resolution Google Earth Pro imagery for the corresponding years. Mean NDVI decreased from 0.355 in 2011 to 0.181 in 2017 before increasing slightly to 0.197 in 2025. Landslide frequency decreased from 125 events in 2011 to 52 in 2017 and then increased to 76 in 2025. In contrast, total landslide-affected area increased from 55.78 ha in 2011 to 93.26 ha in 2017 and 98.38 ha in 2025. These contrasting trends indicate that vegetation condition alone does not explain changes in landslide activity in Galyat. Reforestation should therefore be considered alongside rainfall, slope characteristics, geology, and land-use change within an integrated landslide-risk reduction strategy. The study also demonstrates the usefulness of remote sensing and GIS for monitoring vegetation and landslide dynamics in data-scarce mountainous regions.

papers.title: LGSTNet: Efficient Local–Global Collaboration for Heterogeneous Remote-Sensing Landslide Segmentation
papers.summary: Purpose: Landslide segmentation from remote sensing imagery is challenged by scale variation, irregular morphology, blurred boundaries, and confusion with spectrally similar backgrounds. This study aims to develop an efficient framework that coordinates heterogeneous input regulation, local structural preservation, and hierarchical semantic modeling. Methods: LGSTNet is organized around two coupled design principles. An input-configuration-oriented local–global encoder combines input recalibration, a shallow Ghost branch, and a compact three-stage Swin Transformer. An accuracy–efficiency-oriented compressed context-fusion strategy enhances the deepest Transformer feature through compressed multi-scale, directional, and global context branches and integrates multi-level representations using a lightweight projection–fusion decoder. Results: Experiments were conducted on the Jiuzhai Valley, HR-GLDD, and Landslide4Sense datasets. On Landslide4Sense, LGSTNet achieved the best F1-score, foreground intersection over union (IoU), mean IoU (mIoU), and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) among the seven evaluated models, reaching 64.01%, 47.07%, 72.81%, and 63.39%, respectively, with 3.79 M parameters, 2.39 G FLOPs, and 63.93 frames per second. On HR-GLDD and Jiuzhai Valley, it provided competitive segmentation performance with favorable inference efficiency, although it did not outperform every baseline. A within-dataset input-configuration experiment on Landslide4Sense further showed that the F1-score of LGSTNet increased from 42.87% with RGB input to 64.01% with the full fourteen-channel input; SegFormer exhibited the same overall trend, increasing from 42.50% to 61.56%. Conclusion: LGSTNet provides a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off across the three evaluated remote-sensing configurations. The within-dataset input-configuration results provide additional evidence that the complete system can benefit from the information available in the full multi-channel input

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Evolution, Co-Sensitivity Hotspots, and Robustness of Multi-Process Composite Ecological Sensitivity in an Alpine Mountain Region: A Case Study of Aba Prefecture, China
papers.summary: Alpine mountain regions are shaped by interacting ecological processes. Using Aba Prefecture on the eastern Qinghai–Tibet Plateau as a case study, we derived sensitivity indices for desertification, soil erosion, landslide disaster, freeze–thaw erosion, and habitat quality for six selected study years between 2000 and 2024, and integrated them into a composite ecological sensitivity index (CESI) using the spatial distance index. We assessed class transitions, trajectories, multiscale clustering, co-sensitivity hotspots, county-level and elevation-stratified patterns, and robustness. The results showed that: (1) mean CESI rose slightly from 1.483 to 1.487, indicating marginally weaker sensitivity, but fell to 1.427 in 2020; (2) 75.86% of the area retained its initial class, with persistent low, stable moderate, and persistent high trajectories covering 48.65%, 9.29%, and 15.37%, respectively, while spatial clustering weakened at coarser scales; (3) persistent co-sensitivity hotspots covered 2900.93 km2, the dominant 2024 combination was desertification–soil erosion–freeze–thaw erosion, and over 97% of highly and extremely sensitive areas and hotspots occurred above 4000 m, indicating a pronounced concentration of ecological sensitivity and co-sensitivity hotspots in high-elevation areas; and (4) continuous sensitivity gradients were robust, whereas class assignments and high-sensitivity boundaries were more responsive to factor composition, aggregation, and scale. The findings can inform spatial planning, the prioritization of environmental monitoring and field assessment, and differentiated ecological management in alpine mountain regions.

papers.title: Case studies on IoT monitoring of debris flow and landslides
papers.summary: Aiming at the critical demand for real-time monitoring of slope disasters in mountainous and urbanized regions, this study develops Internet of Things (IoT)-based real-time monitoring systems to resolve the issues of data delay and fragmentation in conventional manual monitoring. Through three engineering cases conducted by the authors, we demonstrate the adaptability of IoT technology in slope disaster monitoring under different instability mechanisms (debris flows and landslides) and geological conditions (artificial-reinforced and semi-natural slopes). Specifically, in Case 1, a novel IoT monitoring system for debris flows integrated with the structural characteristics of rigid barriers is proposed. In Cases 2 and 3, multi-type monitoring sensors and equipment are deployed, including deformation sensors, rainfall gauges and video surveillance devices, to achieve accurate early warnings of rainfall-induced landslides. The novelty of this work lies in proposing a unified IoT architecture scheme applicable to different types of slope disasters. This scheme systematically integrates physico-mechanical sensing devices, a solar-battery collaborative power supply system, video monitoring equipment, data transmission methods, early warning modes, and a cloud-based processing module. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the proposed scheme is validated via successful early warning cases, and this scheme provides an effective technical framework for slope disaster prevention and control.

papers.title: Donald Trump’s Republicans suffer landslide defeat – what this means for the world
When Geology Behaves Badly, Big Fixes Are Needed: Part 1
papers.summary: The Pipestem Dam spillway, located near Jamestown, North Dakota, was undergoing a spillway rehabilitation to address the risk driving failure mode of spillway erosion starting in 2023. The design included approach channel excavation, approach channel armouring, labyrinth weir control structure, and roller compact concrete (RCC) terminal structure and stilling basin. In the spring of 2024, final excavation for the RCC terminal structure resumed. Immediately following excavation to near final grade, a landslide occurred on the right side of the terminal structure. After rigorous analysis, geologic conditions were identified which led to the landslide. The root causes for the landslide were isolated to the right side of the terminal structure excavation. Construction continued on the weir control structure and left side of the terminal structure. This paper will discuss the investigations, geologic conditions, site characterization, observations before and during construction, along with dewatering, geologic conditions, root cause, and lessons learned related to the landslide. The paper will also address the complex geologic conditions and the theory that resulted in the geologic conditions. Part 2 of this paper will discuss the repair of the landslide and other associated construction sequencing modifications to reduce downstream life safety risk.

papers.title: Design and Construction of a Retaining Wall on the Miller Creek Landslide, I-70 West Vail Pass Auxiliary Lanes Project, Eagle County, Colorado
papers.summary: In 2021, design work began for a Colorado Department of Transportation project to improve a 10-mile stretch of Interstate 70 (I-70) from the Town of Vail to the summit of Vail Pass. The project included design and construction of a 1,150-ft-long, 5-tiered soil nail wall (CP3 Wall 1) located at the toe of the Miller Creek Landslide, a large landslide complex first investigated during initial construction of I-70 in the 1970s. The primary geotechnical challenge for the design and construction of CP3 Wall 1 was maintaining stability of the wall and landslide under elevated groundwater conditions. This paper will discuss the background of the project, stability and seepage analyses conducted during the design of the CP3 Wall 1, the use of temporary and permanent horizontal drains, and geotechnical instrumentation data used to evaluate conditions during construction.

papers.title: Interpretable Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Pacitan, Indonesia Using Bayesian-Optimized XGBoost and SHAP Analysis
papers.summary: Background: Landslide susceptibility mapping is essential in areas with complex topographic and geological conditions, such as Pacitan Regency, Indonesia, to identify landslide-prone areas and assess the factors influencing landslide susceptibility. Objective: This study developed a landslide susceptibility mapping model using Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), optimized through Bayesian optimization and interpreted using the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method. Methods: The dataset consisted of 1,486 samples, comprising 743 landslide occurrence points and 743 non-landslide points. Eleven landslide conditioning factors were used as predictor variables: elevation, aspect, slope, geology, land use, profile curvature, plan curvature, distance to roads, distance to rivers, Stream Power Index (SPI), and Topographic Wetness Index (TWI). Model hyperparameter optimization was performed using Bayesian optimization with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE). Results: The optimized XGBoost model achieved an accuracy of 69.80%, a precision of 70.34%, a recall of 68.46%, an F1 score of 69.39%, and a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.7564 on the independent test set. The resulting susceptibility map classified the study area into five categories: very low, low, moderate, high, and very high susceptibility. SHAP analysis identified slope, aspect, plan curvature, geology, and distance to roads as the dominant factors influencing model predictions. Conclusion: Integrating Bayesian optimization, XGBoost, and SHAP provides an interpretable approach to landslide susceptibility mapping in Pacitan Regency. The resulting susceptibility map and feature-level explanations can support preliminary disaster risk assessment and spatial planning. However, residual classification errors and limitations associated with the use of static environmental predictors should be considered when interpreting the results.

papers.title: Quantifying spatiotemporal heterogeneity in landslide deformation using an improved graph deep learning framework for reliable displacement forecasting
Landslide Susceptibility Assessment of Lixian County, Gansu Province, China Using a Physics‐Integrated Multi‐Task Neural Network
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA) is a critical strategy for disaster prevention and mitigation. However, current machine learning‐based LSA algorithms often exhibit instability under data‐sparse conditions and suffer from a lack of physical interpretability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics‐integrated multi‐task neural network (PIMTN). The proposed framework incorporates slope‐stability information derived from the infinite slope model into a multi‐task neural network through an auxiliary learning task. The model simultaneously performs landslide susceptibility classification and learns a physics‐derived diluted probability of failure (DPOF). Through joint optimization, the auxiliary DPOF task influences the shared representation and guides susceptibility prediction towards spatial patterns consistent with physics‐derived slope‐stability information. Comparative experiments demonstrate that the PIMTN outperforms benchmark models (Precision: 0.737, F 1‐Score: 0.754, AUC: 0.817). Furthermore, quantitative analysis confirms the superiority of the proposed model and the effectiveness of knowledge transfer from the physical domain. This framework presents a novel solution for enhancing model interpretability and improving predictive robustness under limited‐inventory conditions.

papers.title: Chapter 4: Glaciogenic sediments and structures in the Port Askaig Formation on the Garvellachs and Islay
papers.summary: In this Chapter, we conduct a thorough reappraisal of evidence for glaciation in the Port Askaig Formation (PAF) based on comprehensive documentation of all exposures on the Garvellachs and parts of Islay. Diamictites and associated facies record a range of terrestrial, lacustrine and marine environments. Most massive diamictites on the Garvellachs contain structures indicating shear beneath grounded ice, including ‘stoss-lee’ clasts, strong preferred a-axis orientations, glaciotectonism of subjacent sediments, and streamlined and folded rafts, and are interpreted as subglacial traction tills and glaciotectonites. The Great Breccia on the Garvellachs and the Persabus Complex on Islay consist of folded and thrust megablocks and diamictite, interpreted as the product of proglacial glaciotectonic deformation in which permafrozen foreland materials were excavated and upthrust before being over-ridden. The PAF also contains intervals of laminated mudstones with dropstones, stratified diamictites, and interbeds of sandstone and conglomerate, interpreted as the products of subaqueous deposition in glaciolacustrine and glaciomarine environments. Glaciomarine deposition is most spectacularly recorded in the ‘Disrupted Beds’, including subaqueous fans, submarine landslides, and rain-out of ice-rafted debris. Glaciogenic facies associations exhibit systematic evolution through time, revealing the interplay of climate, glacier advance-retreat cycles and sea-level change over the course of the Sturtian panglaciation.

papers.title: Technical validation of a regional landslide forecasting system in the Eastern Himalayas
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides pose a recurrent threat in the Darjeeling–Kalimpong Himalaya, India. The Geological Survey of India developed a prototype Regional Landslide Forecasting System (RLFS) that issued daily experimental forecast bulletins during the 2020–2023 monsoon seasons. Here we present the first systematic evaluation of an Indian regional landslide early warning system using the EDuMaP framework. Performance was assessed over 2,316 block-days spanning 373 monsoon days across 11 administrative units. Of 521 landslides analysed, 96.50% of block-days recorded no or only minor activity. Aggregated validation yielded 361 correct predictions, 1,862 true negatives, 19 missed alerts, and 74 false alerts. Green and yellow grades together represented 95.60% of forecast–observation pairs, with a mean combined efficiency index of 0.86 across the nine non-overlapping forecast zones. The system’s error structure was dominated by overwarning rather than catastrophic missed events. A stakeholder-driven transition to finer administrative forecast zones improved skill scores. Because the forecasts combined an automated rainfall-threshold model with expert review, the reported skill reflects this hybrid system, not the model alone.

papers.title: Was the Nepal disaster caused by a Coulomb explosion?
papers.summary: Abstract On August 26, 2006, a huge mass of rock and glacier broke off from the parent body at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres and collapsed 1,200 metres downward. The resulting mudflow destroyed roads and bridges and flooded downstream coastal settlements along the Lende-Khola and Trishuli-Khola rivers, covering almost 100 km. Members of the intergovernmental organization "International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development" (ICIMOD), based in Kathmandu, concluded that the cause of the powerful mudflow was an avalanche of ice and rocks, not a breakout of water from a glacial lake. USGS staff reported that at the point with coordinates 28.271° N, 85.515° E, 55 km NW of Kodari̇, Nepal, a glacier collapse occurred, triggering an M5.2 earthquake and a powerful avalanche. At present (September 4, 2026), the actual cause of the disaster is unknown, but judging by similar catastrophic landslides that occurred in the past, as well as the scale of the material involved and the energy of this seismic event, it can be assumed that the cause of the landslide was a Coulomb explosion in the rock massif that served as the underlying layer for the glacier located on it. This article reveals the possible mechanism of the Coulomb explosion in the rocks and the cause of the landslide.

papers.title: Time–Cost–Quality Impact Assessment and FMEA-Based Prioritization of Geological, Environmental, and Operational Risks in Road Infrastructure Projects
papers.source: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.summary: Road infrastructure projects are exposed to geological, environmental, and operational hazards that jointly determine delivery time, cost, and quality. Risk studies and guidance often address one hazard family at a time, and hazard lists are not always converted into ranked priorities that project managers can act on. This paper presents a structured, three-stage assessment of fifteen risk factors that commonly affect road projects. First, each factor is rated for its impact on project time, cost, and quality and aggregated into a composite impact index. Second, the factors are ranked using a probability–severity matrix. Third, seven critical failure modes are prioritized using Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) with the Risk Priority Number (RPN). The results show that geological factors have the highest composite impact (mean 8.2 out of a maximum of 9), followed by operational (7.3) and environmental factors (6.5). Slope failure, earthquakes, and safety incidents are the only factors rated High on all three performance dimensions, and ten of the fifteen factors fall in the High priority tier. In the FMEA, project mismanagement (RPN 252), flooding (240), and material shortage (210) rank highest and together account for 55.5% of the total RPN. The qualitative ranking and the RPN agree on the severity of geological hazards but diverge for material supply, which illustrates the value of including detectability in prioritization. Illustrative mitigation scenarios indicate that the aggregate RPN could be reduced by roughly two-thirds if targeted controls are implemented. The ratings are judgement-based and require field validation, as discussed in the limitations

Understanding Disaster Risk and Local Response: A Study of Chhatrakot, Gulmi, Nepal
papers.source: International Journal of Advanced Business Studies
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and landslides in Nepal continue to pose a significant threat to the lives of people in the rural hills and mountains. This study focuses on the vulnerability, preparedness, and mitigation measures of natural disasters among the inhabitants of Chhatrakot-4, Gulmi. The researchers adopted a mixed-methods research design by analyzing existing policies and field observations, and engaging local actors to generate findings on the general status of natural disasters, major causes, and mitigation measures in the area. It is found that Chhatrakot-4, Gulmi, is highly vulnerable to natural disasters due to poor infrastructure, ineffective early warning systems, insufficient disaster preparedness, lack of coordination among local agencies, and other human-related factors. This study recommends that community-based disaster management coupled with strengthening of institutional coordination, improvement in infrastructure, and community education should be prioritized in order to reduce the negative impacts of natural disasters. It was also found that active community participation and local initiative, as well as collaboration between government and non-governmental organizations, can lead to improved disaster preparedness and management capacity in the area. These results suggest that disaster risk reduction requires a comprehensive response that promotes community-based initiatives as well as effective coordination at the local institutional level. The study contributes to the existing body of knowledge on climate change adaptation and disaster risk reduction by providing policy recommendations for local government, development partners, and other stakeholders to consider.

papers.title: When Geology Behaves Badly, Big Fixes Are Needed: Part 2
papers.summary: In the spring of 2024, a landslide occurred in the roller compacted concrete (RCC) terminal structure excavation for the Pipestem Dam Spillway project. This paper will build upon and present the engineering and construction solutions to address the landslide presented in Part 1. The solutions not only needed to consider worker safety during repair of the landslide and long term performance of the repair, but also protection of completed construction work, incremental downstream life safety risk in its interim condition, and minimization of cost and schedule impacts. Topics related to the repair of the landslide will include investigations, analyses, contracting approach, design, and construction of a soldier pile lagging wall with tie backs. Evaluations were performed to confirm the repair would not adversely impact the performance of the completed terminal structure and associated drainage system.

papers.title: The effect of flexural stiffness on the pipe responses to lateral ground movement
Fault Geometry and Tectonic Implications of the 2026 Jalalpur Sharif Earthquake, Pakistan
papers.summary: The moderate-magnitude (Mw 4.5) 26 May 2026 Jalalpur Sharif earthquake in northern Pakistan caused localized severe damage, one fatality, and a maximum Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) of VII. Field observations documented liquefaction-related ground deformation, transient groundwater turbidity, differential settlement, tilted utility poles, and earthquake-induced landslides in Quaternary deposits. Moment tensor inversion indicates shallow (~3 km) oblique-thrust faulting, with NE–SW strike direction (strike 217°, dip 55°, rake 46°). Gravity modeling reveals a ~20 mGal residual anomaly aligned with the Pabbi Anticline, supporting structural complexity and the presence of shallow faulting, although the causative fault cannot be uniquely resolved. Regional seismicity is concentrated at 10–15 km depth, with a peak near 12 km, indicating depth-dependent deformation within the sedimentary cover and deeper regional thrust system. Coulomb stress modeling shows negligible static stress changes (~0.001 bar) at Jalalpur Sharif from the 2019 Mw 5.8 Mirpur and 2024 Mw 5.0 Kharian earthquakes, providing little support for direct static triggering. The localized damage likely resulted from the combined effects of shallow faulting, potentially liquefiable sediments and vulnerable buildings. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating shallow seismogenic structures and local ground conditions into seismic hazard assessments across the eastern Potwar foreland.

papers.title: Suitability of Suction Stress–Based Rainfall Intensity–Duration Paradigm for Predicting Tropical Storm–Induced Multiple Slope Failures
papers.source: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract A case study analyzing three landslides in Pohang, South Korea, during tropical storm Typhoon Hinnamnor in September 2022 is conducted to assess the suitability of the recently developed suction stress–based rainfall intensity–duration (SS-ID) paradigm for predicting multiple slope instabilities. Postfailure field investigation and laboratory testing were carried out to determine field hydrologic and geotechnical settings and soil properties. This information was used to determine these slopes’ critical suction stress profiles where the effective stress reaches the failure state or the local factor of safety reaches unity. Hydromechanical numerical modeling was then conducted under various rainfall intensities to identify the slopes’ corresponding durations for slope failure and thus the rainfall intensity–duration (ID) threshold curves of the slopes. The precipitation records during and before Typhoon Hinnamnor at Pohang were used to determine rainfall episodes and slopes’ rainfall intensity–duration data. The determined rainfall intensity–duration data at the three sites for Typhoon Hinnamnor were all above the corresponding predetermined ID threshold curves, correctly and novelly predicting the occurrence of the observed landslides. Further independent physical simulations of transient two-dimensional hydromechanical processes at the three failed slopes were conducted for independent confirmation. Excellent matches in predictions of the slope failure locations and timings are demonstrated, further physically validating the suitability and effectiveness of the SS-ID paradigm for multiple slope instability prediction. Because the suction stress–based ID curves are characteristic of a given region and they can be determined a priori, the SS-ID paradigm provides a practical way to use live rainfall data to forecast multiple slope instability in a region.

papers.title: Preferential Freeze–Thaw Damage in Limestone Containing Stylolites and Calcite Veins from High-Altitude Mining Areas
papers.summary: Abstract Limestone slopes in high-altitude mining areas are subjected to strong diurnal temperature fluctuations and repeated freeze–thaw cycles, which can induce the development of internal pores and cracks and cause structural deterioration of the rock mass. However, where preferential damage occurs and how it affects the structural continuity of limestone remain unclear. To investigate how structural units, including stylolites, calcite veins, and the matrix, control the spatial distribution of freeze–thaw damage in natural limestone, this study examined limestone containing stylolites and calcite veins. The specimens were classified into sparse and dense structural-unit types according to the degree of structural-unit development. Low-field nuclear magnetic resonance T2 spectra, magnetic resonance imaging, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and P-wave velocity tests were combined to reveal the evolution of the pore structure, microscopic damage, and structural continuity under freeze–thaw cycles. The results show that the dense structural-unit specimens exhibited a more pronounced increase in long-T2 components, clustering of high-signal MRI regions, and P-wave velocity attenuation. After 30 freeze–thaw cycles, the velocity attenuation rate of the dense specimens reached 28–30%, significantly higher than that of the sparse specimens, which was 10–12%. The absolute value of the fitted porosity–velocity slope for the dense specimens was approximately 2.17 times that of the sparse specimens. SEM-EDS results indicate that the matrix and calcite vein interiors showed limited changes, although localized crack-like features developed near some vein boundaries after 30 cycles, whereas stylolites gradually evolved into widened, deepened, and rough-bounded banded damage zones, accompanied by relative Ca depletion and local enrichment of Si and Al. These findings demonstrate that freeze–thaw damage in natural limestone is not a uniform accumulati

papers.title: Three-dimensional monitoring of non-rigid ground surface deformation based on time-series multi-view collaborative tracking
papers.summary: Abstract High spatiotemporal resolution surface deformation information offers the advantage of comprehensively, precisely, and rapidly revealing surface deformation characteristics, and is key data for early identification and dynamic warning of geological disasters such as landslides and ground subsidence. However, the vast majority of monitoring methods suffer from shortcomings such as low spatiotemporal resolution, and traditional feature tracking algorithms exhibit limited reliability in long-term, non-rigid deformation scenarios. To address these issues, a surface deformation tracking method based on Time-Series Multi-View Collaborative Tracking (TS-MVCT) was constructed. The TS-MVCT framework estimates the spatial positions of the initial point cloud after deformation by establishing 2D correspondences between temporally adjacent observations within consecutive short-term intervals, followed by reliability-weighted depth fusion for 3D position estimation. To validate the effectiveness of the constructed method, an indoor simulated surface deformation experiment was conducted. The experimental results demonstrate that, compared to the M3C2 algorithm, which primarily characterizes displacement along the local surface normal, TS-MVCT effectively reduces deformation underestimation and the loss of displacement components in different spatial directions, while enabling the estimation of 3D displacement vectors at a higher density than SIFT-FT. Quantitative validation under laboratory conditions indicates that the relative deviations of the retrieved 3D displacements—measured against manually annotated reference values—are generally within 2 mm. On markerless natural surfaces, the algorithm achieves PSR and reprojection-error values within a similar numerical range to those of artificial-target regions, indicating comparable internal matching and multi-view geometric consistency under the controlled experimental conditions. In summary, the TS-MVCT framework present

papers.summary: Landslide inventory (1953-2014), Andrews Experimental Forest and Blue River Basin. This layer is a combination of data from five landslide inventory efforts that have been conducted in the area beginning in the late 1960's. Data represent landslide occurrences between 1953 and 2014. Data are in the UTM coordinate system; zone 10, NAD27. The data table that describes the characteristics of the landslides inventoried in the following: Individual layers tied to inventories by Ted Dyrness, Fred Swanson, Dan Marion, and Matt Wallenstein were appended and linked to the shape file. papers.title: PhysInSAR: Unwrapping-free ground motion from paired C- and L-band wrapped interferometric phase
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: # PhysInSAR v0.9.0 — Unwrapping-free ground motion from Sentinel-1 and NISAR PhysInSAR is a research project that rethinks how ground deformation is measured from satellite radar. Instead of unwrapping each interferogram and fusing the results of separate processing chains, it fits a single continuous, physics-informed neural model of three-dimensional ground motion directly to the wrapped interferometric phase of Sentinel-1 C-band and NISAR L-band at the same time. The two wavelengths constrain one shared description of how the ground moves, so the cycle ambiguity that limits each sensor on its own is resolved jointly rather than guessed separately. This is the first public release. The method is a research prototype, validated on a realistic synthetic benchmark and not yet applied to real NISAR acquisitions. Phase unwrapping is the weak point of InSAR time series. It fails where C-band decorrelates in vegetation, and over fast or sharply localised motion such as mining subsidence, groundwater extraction, landslides and volcanic unrest. These are often the places where reliable measurements matter most. Its errors are whole cycles: silent, spatially coherent, and carried into every product built on top of them. With NISAR now observing the same ground as Sentinel-1, two complementary wavelengths are available for the first time at global scale. C-band is precise but fragile; L-band is robust but coarse. PhysInSAR is designed to combine them where they complement each other most: in the raw phase, before any information is lost. At its core is a differentiable physics forward model that predicts each sensor's phase from its own viewing geometry, including atmospheric delay, dispersive ionosphere, orbit errors and DEM error. Predictions are compared with observations through a von Mises likelihood, a periodic noise model under which a prediction that is right modulo one cycle is right, weighted by bias-corrected coherence. Ground motion is represented as a neural fie

papers.title: Characterization of iron mining tailings for reuse in sustainable civil infrastructure
papers.summary: Iron ore production generates approximately 1.4 billion tonnes of tailings annually. Research worldwide has investigated the reuse and recycling of this material. In civil engineering applications, research has mostly focused on pavement construction and block manufacturing, both of which commonly require the addition of binders. This paper proposes the use of iron ore tailings from a large Brazilian iron ore production area as a sand substitute in general geotechnical applications, while also addressing the global scarcity of natural sand. A comprehensive geotechnical characterization was performed, including the determination of hydraulic conductivity, deformability, and shear strength at optimum compaction conditions and at 95% of maximum dry unit weight and water content deviations within ±2%. The results indicate that, without binders, the material is suitable for use as trench fill and backfill for containment structures, as a soft-soil replacement material, in geosynthetic-reinforced soil walls, and in geotextile-encased granular columns.

papers.title: A machine learning framework for predicting the unconfined compression index of nano-silica stabilized fine-grained soils using leave-one-soil-type-out validation
papers.summary: The Lesser Himalayan region presents significant challenges for infrastructure development due to weak, landslide-prone soils. This study evaluates nano-silica (NS) stabilization of three fine-grained soils and introduces the Unconfined Compression Index ( Ic ), defined as the axial strain at 50% of peak unconfined compressive strength ( qu ), as a measure of stabilized-soil deformability. Laboratory specimens were prepared with NS contents of 0–4% and cured for 3–90 days. Six machine-learning models Linear Regression, Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machine, and Lasso Regression—were trained to predict Ic from soil type, NS content, curing duration, and early-cure qu . To avoid interpolation bias inherent in random splitting of factorial data, a Leave-One-Soil-Type-Out Cross-Validation was adopted. XGB achieved the highest predictive accuracy ( R 2 = 0.961; MAE = 0.158), while multicollinearity among predictors was mitigated via regularization. The results demonstrate that Ic can be estimated from routine strength data, offering a practical tool for assessing strain compatibility in NS-stabilized Himalayan soils.

papers.title: Enhanced Shear Strength Reduction Method for Stability Analysis of High-Friction Slopes: Implementation, Verification, and Application
papers.summary: Abstract Over the last two decades, the shear strength reduction method (SRM) has emerged as a prominent alternative for slope stability analysis. However, existing studies reveal significant differences (16%–28%) between the factor of safety (FOS) achieved by the traditional SRM and the limit analysis method (LAM) for steep slopes with high friction. To address this limitation, this study proposes an enhanced shear strength reduction method (ESRM) that dynamically adjusts the dilation angle of geomaterials based on their stress states. Subsequently, the ESRM is comprehensively verified against the LAM analytical solution through extensive sensitivity analyses and a benchmark study, involving 201 sets of slope experimental groups with different geometric parameters and geomaterial parameters. The results show that the maximum error in the FOS achieved with the ESRM is only 8%, and the predicted distribution and development of the potential slip surface are also satisfactory, confirming the applicability of the ESRM for steep slopes with high friction. Simultaneously, considering that the LAM analytical solution cannot be used for engineering-level verification, the engineering-level comparison methods of the ESRM, namely, the Davis A approach and Davis B approach, are reproduced and verified within the same verification framework. Results demonstrate that only the Davis B approach achieves satisfactory accuracy. Finally, a case study of the ShaiKou landslide is conducted. The ESRM and Davis B approach achieve highly consistent FOS values of 1.259 and 1.258, respectively, along with comparable slip surface distribution and development, further evaluating the practical value of the ESRM in analyzing engineering problems involving with high-friction slopes.

papers.title: Databases of Daily and Monthly Turbidity Data from Bull Run Reservoir # 1 Turbidity Stations 59-0 and 59-1 (1965–2026), Bull Run Drainage Basin, Oregon, USA
papers.summary: Daily turbidity data from Reservoir # 1 in the Bull Run drainage basin, Oregon, were requested from the Portland Public Records Center (PPRC) to constrain estimates of elevated turbidity durations in Reservoir # 1 following 1) the 1964 flood, 2) the 972 North Fork landslide, (3) the 1996 flood, and 4) the cessation of clearcut harvesting in the Bull Run watershed. These data provide context for interpretations of gravity-cores collected in Reservoir # 1.

papers.title: Geography, geospatial analysis and artificial intelligence: between traditional methods and new spatial paradigms
papers.summary: In 1986, yes 1986, it is not a typographical error, Helen Couclelis, one of the pioneers of Geographic Information Science (GIScience) and an expert in urban and regional modelling and planning, spatial cognition, and the geography of the information society, indicated that artificial intelligence (AI) and geography were interconnected within a broad context that addressed fundamental issues of theory, epistemology, and scientific method. At the time, the still little-known logical-mathematical context of AI was explored, demonstrating substantial implications for modelling in general, prediction, the interpretation of theoretical structures, and, moreover, for our understanding of science as a process. These more abstract aspects of the 'computational revolution', of which AI is a product, could, according to the author, have far-reaching consequences for geographical research (Couclelis, 1986).Since then, AI has been profoundly transforming geography by providing advanced methods for analysing, modelling, and interpreting geospatial data. As a discipline concerned with spatial relations, places, environments and human-environment interactions, geography increasingly benefits from AI methods capable of processing large and complex spatio-temporal datasets (e.g., Big Data), generating new insights into territorial dynamics and complex geographical phenomena (Encalada-Abarca et al., 2023).AI has made significant contributions to geospatial data processing, extending existing capabilities for handling and analysing increasingly large and heterogeneous datasets (Mohamad Alshiha, 2024). Techniques based on machine learning, including deep learning, have become increasingly relevant for processing and interpreting geographic information. These methodologies enable the identification of patterns, the modelling of trends, and the development of new analytical approaches to urban, environmental, and social challenges. AI-based methodologies are now widely explored in geospa

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility probability tables and sample points from Reconstructability Analysis, Wilson-Trask-Nestucca and Siletz-Yaquina watersheds, Oregon Coast Range, USA
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Sample points and conditional landslide probability tables for the Wilson-Trask-Nestucca and Siletz-Yaquina (WTNSY) watersheds of the Oregon Coast Range, USA. The probability tables were produced with Reconstructability Analysis (RA), an information-theoretic modelling method that works directly on categorical data. The data accompany Percy et al., “Information-theoretic modeling of landslide susceptibility using mostly categorical spatial data”, submitted to Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences. The study area was stratified into volcanic and sedimentary lithologies and modelled separately. Each row of a probability table is one combination of predictor states (for example elevation bin, terrane group, landform, soil taxonomic subgroup and particle size class) with the model probability of landslide presence, P(LS=1), the predicted class, and the number of training samples (n) from which the probability was estimated. Landslide presence comes from the Statewide Landslide Information Database for Oregon (SLIDO-4.5, Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries); predictor variables come from DOGAMI geologic mapping, the USDA-NRCS Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO), NLCD 2021 land cover and terrain data. Categories below 1% of a stratum's sample count were collapsed into a single category labelled “(other/rare)”. All files are in WTNSY_landslide_RA_data_v1.0.zip, which unpacks to a single folder (README.txt is also provided separately): • volcanic_probability_table.csv and sedimentary_probability_table.csv: flat, human-readable tables covering the full state space (144 volcanic and 512 sedimentary predictor-state combinations). • landslide_probability_tables.sqlite: the same tables in normalized form (a value table for each predictor and a prediction table for each stratum, linked by integer keys), with views volcanic_readable and sedimentary_readable that rebuild readable tables for browsing; these views leave out the (other/rare) categories, so use

papers.title: Earthquake-driven influx of organic matter enhances authigenic carbonate formation in hadal trenches
papers.summary: Shallow marine carbonates are recognized as key agents in deep carbon cycling. However, the formation and burial of carbonates below the carbonate compensation depth still remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate carbonates from the > 7000 m water-depth Japan Trench hadal zone and find widespread authigenic calcium carbonate buried in these ultra-deep sediments. Stable and radiocarbon isotope depletions in the authigenic carbonates indicate an organic carbon (OC) source, likely primarily delivered by deep-sea landslides. Isotopic modeling suggests that subduction of these OC-derived carbonates can impart negative δ13C signatures to fluids released in the NE Japan subduction zone. The OC-derived carbonate flux in the Japan Trench is estimated to reach ~ 28.6 Tg C Myr–1. We propose that earthquake-driven organic matter influx into the hadal zone may have facilitated sustained carbonate production. Thus, OC-derived authigenic carbonates in hadal trenches represent an underappreciated carbon sink and a potential mechanism for transferring OC into the deep Earth. Earthquake-driven organic matter influx into hadal zones facilitates sustained organic carbon-derived carbonate production. The formation of these authigenic carbonates represents both an underappreciated carbon sink and a potential mechanism for transferring OC into the deep Earth.

papers.title: Integrated Geological and Geophysical Characterization of the 2024 Lernapat Landslide, Armenia: Slip-Surface Delineation and Stability Assessment
papers.summary: The May 2024 Lernapat landslide in northern Armenia occurred following rainfall and coincided with leakage from an irrigation pipeline. Its subsurface structure was investigated using UAV terrain analysis, four boreholes, laboratory testing, electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW), microtremor H/V (horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio) measurements, ground-penetrating radar (GPR), and limit-equilibrium modelling. Boreholes identified mechanically weakened intervals at depths of 16.4–16.7 m and 18.4–20.0 m. The borehole observations were considered together with the ERT and MASW results to constrain the probable basal deformation zone and the adopted slip-surface geometry. H/V measurements provided supplementary spectral information; their depth estimates were treated as approximate equivalent thicknesses rather than independent confirmation of the MASW interpretation. The existing slope yielded factors of safety of 0.980 under static loading and 0.496 under pseudo-static loading at Kh = 0.16. A modelled groundwater lowering of 7.0 m increased these values to 1.214 and 0.616, respectively. Within the staged embankment-construction sequence, the calculated static factors of safety ranged from 1.372 to 1.499, whereas the corresponding pseudo-static values ranged from 0.657 to 0.689. None of the investigated stabilization scenarios reached Fs = 1.00 under pseudo-static loading at Kh = 0.16. No separate calculations were performed at Kh = 0.20. These factors of safety are conditional on the adopted model; the effects of alternative basal geometries and shear-strength parameters were not quantified. The results illustrate how the integration of geological, hydrogeological, electrical, and seismic observations can provide a field-constrained basis for evaluating groundwater sensitivity and stabilization scenarios.

papers.title: A Unified Multispectral Feature Framework for Independent Recognition of Floods, Burned Areas, and Landslides
papers.summary: Multispectral disaster recognition draws on common optical measurements, but differences in feature construction, target definitions and evaluation design complicate comparisons across tasks. We present a unified feature framework that applies the same six-band interface, 78-dimensional spectral–spatial descriptor and training-side learning procedure to independently fitted flood, burned area and landslide experts. Spectral summaries, local variability and gradients describe each window; paired date and source auxiliary inputs provide task-specific extensions. Evaluation covered 88 flood patches from 11 events, 656 burned area windows in 23 source/overlap groups, and a prespecified 100-patch subset of the official Landslide4Sense test partition. The shared representation achieved F1 values of 0.8504, 0.8485 and 0.8169, respectively, under training-side classifier selection. The burned area temporal extension increased F1 to 0.8997, with gains over matched support post-event descriptors under both inner-selected and fixed Random Forest evaluation. The landslide auxiliary extension produced a larger gain under classifier selection than under fixed Random Forest, identifying an interaction between representation and classifier. Training label controls and negative class metrics distinguished learned discrimination from positive class prevalence. The framework provides a reproducible basis for testing shared optical descriptors and task-specific information under the distinct evaluation requirements of each task.

papers.title: The Agency of Nonlife: Alliances with Planetary Forces
Rethinking cascading high-mountain hazards and early warning in the Himalayas
papers.summary: Abstract Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) remain a major Himalayan hazard, but recent disasters show that destructive floods develop through several cascading pathways. Seven recent events across Nepal and the wider Himalaya show how lake outburst, avalanche, slope failure and supraglacial drainage can be amplified by sediment entrainment and debris-flow transformation, leading to similar downstream consequences. To reduce risk from such cascading hazards, we argue for a four-tier cascade-aware approach spanning from source-zone monitoring, failure detection, early warning to preparedness, planning and governance.

papers.title: Paradigms of Preparedness and Response: Crisis Management in the Gjerdrum Slide
Performance and Mechanistic Insights into an Early-Strength Eco-Friendly UHPC Grouting Material Modified with Nano-Calcium Carbonate
papers.summary: Ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) has potential as a grouting material for emergency landslide remediation due to its superior mechanical properties and dense matrix without coarse aggregates. However, its field application is restricted by the requirement for high-temperature curing, low early-age strength, and poor constructability under standard curing conditions. To enhance early-strength development under conventional standard curing conditions, nine eco-friendly UHPC mixtures incorporating steel slag micro-powder were prepared using an orthogonal experimental design. Four factors, including lithium carbonate as an early-strength admixture, nano-calcium carbonate as a reinforcing filler, steel fibers, and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) fibers, were investigated. The effects of these factors were evaluated through compressive strength, flexural strength, and flowability tests at different curing ages. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) were further employed to analyze microstructural characteristics and hydration-phase evolution. The results indicate that increasing the dosages of the four additives decreases fresh paste flowability. An appropriate dosage of lithium carbonate promotes ettringite formation and enhances early-age compressive strength, while nano-calcium carbonate improves the matrix compactness through pinning and pore-filling effects. The optimized eco-friendly steel-slag-based UHPC achieved compressive/flexural strengths of 23.4/6.4 MPa at 12 h and 45.5/13.8 MPa at 1 d under standard curing conditions. The developed UHPC exhibits potential for rapid emergency grouting applications in landslide remediation.

papers.title: Cloudburst susceptibility mapping of Pakistan using an innovative expert opinion and LLM-assisted weighted linear combination model
Method-dependent assessment of long-term soil erosion on the Loess Plateau
papers.summary: Differences between classification-based and quantitative approaches may affect interpretations of regional soil erosion patterns and long-term changes. Using Google Earth Engine, we compared the classification-based approach derived from the Standards for Classification and Gradation of Soil Erosion (SL 190-2007) with the Chinese Soil Loss Equation (CSLE) across the Loess Plateau, China, from 2000 to 2025. The comparison covered erosion intensity, spatial distribution, differences among land-use types, rainfall erosivity ranges, slope classes and fractional vegetation cover (FVC) classes, and erosion-grade transitions. Annual paired comparisons accounted for temporal autocorrelation and multiple comparisons. Soil erosion intensity showed marked spatial heterogeneity, with higher erosion grades concentrated in Qinghai, eastern Gansu, central Shaanxi, and along the Shaanxi–Shanxi border. Both approaches indicated an overall decline in erosion intensity but differed substantially in the areas assigned to individual erosion grades. Compared with SL 190-2007, CSLE mapped larger areas in the lowest and highest erosion grades, with differences of 8.57 × 10 4 and 2.33 × 10 4 km 2 , respectively. Grassland and cropland were the dominant land use types on the Loess Plateau, and intermethod differences in erosion-grade area proportions were greatest for grassland. Across all slope and FVC classes, CSLE estimated significantly lower proportions of area affected by mild or more severe erosion (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Despite broadly similar patterns of erosion mitigation during 2000-2010, CSLE identified increases in erosion grade across 11.56% of the assessed area, mainly in northern Ningxia, southern Inner Mongolia, and the Loess Hilly-Gully Region. During 2010-2025, erosion intensity declined overall, but CSLE identified increases in erosion grade across 9.01% of the assessed area, mainly in eastern Inner Mongolia, Ningxia, and northern Shaanxi.
