papers.title: Analysis of Barrier Lake Breach Flood Mitigation Under Cascade Reservoirs Operation: A Case Study of the Mogangling Event, Dadu River
papers.summary: The southeastern margin of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau is characterized by complex geological conditions and frequent disasters such as landslide-induced river blockage and subsequent barrier lake breaching. With the construction of cascade reservoirs in the basin, the potential impacts of historical barrier lakes under the current flood control system remain unclear. Reconstructing the breaching process of barrier lakes is of great guiding significance for regional flood control and disaster mitigation, risk management, and the safe operation of cascade reservoirs in the basin. In this study, the Mogangling landslide barrier lake in the Dadu River basin was selected as the research object. We constructed breach flood hydrographs for the 300 m and 600 m breach scenarios and established a one-dimensional and two-dimensional coupled hydrodynamic model of the barrier lake breach flood based on the integrated flood modeling system (IFMS). The model was used to simulate the propagation and inundation processes of the breach flood under natural propagation without reservoirs and under the joint operation of the cascade reservoirs. Spatially distributed socioeconomic data were then combined with the model to assess flood impacts and the potential disaster mitigation effect of the joint operation of the cascade reservoirs. The results show that the joint operation of the cascade reservoirs can reduce the peak discharge of the barrier lake breach flood by 30.7–97.9%, decrease the total inundated area of downstream riverside towns by 70%, and reduce the GDP losses and the affected population by 89% and 87%, respectively. In addition, artificial excavation of a spillway channel can reduce the peak discharge of the natural barrier lake breach by approximately 30%.

papers.title: Amplified transport variability in granular slope flows near the critical angle
papers.summary: Mechanical disturbances such as seismic shaking can set a granular slope in motion. Understanding the resulting transport before arrest is important for predicting topographic change, assessing landslide hazards and controlling powder flows in industrial processes. Experiments show that smaller disturbances can trigger avalanches and larger areas are mobilized as slopes approach their stability limit. Yet how much transport varies between events under the same macroscopic conditions and forcing remains unclear. Here we use numerical simulations to show that transport variability is amplified near the critical angle. We apply identical basal pulses to static granular layers with the same macroscopic conditions but different initial particle configurations. Although the mean transport increases approximately in inverse proportion to the angular distance from the critical angle, the standard deviation increases even faster and can exceed the mean. Thus, identical forcing can produce widely different transport amounts. Deterministic constitutive laws that assign a unique response to given macroscopic conditions cannot capture this variability. We introduce fluctuations into the energy balance to develop a stochastic model that captures the main features of the broadening transport distribution. These results show that assessing transport near the critical angle requires considering its distribution, not just its mean, and motivate constitutive descriptions that incorporate fluctuations.

papers.title: Unravelling information on impactful geo-hydrological hazard events with HazMiner, a multilingual text mining method developed through a global scale coverage application
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. The incidence and impacts from geo-hydrological hazards (GH) such as floods, flash floods and landslides are changing globally due to anthropogenic environmental changes and increased exposure driven by population growth. Reliable datasets on GH are essential to deepen our understanding of these hazards and their impacts. However, existing GH datasets contain data gaps leading to biased interpretations, especially in the Global South where populations are commonly the most impacted. Text mining offers new opportunities in documenting GH by automatically extracting information from large text corpora. Despite its potential, current methodologies are not adapted to improve documentation in data-scared contexts. We present HazMiner, a paragraph-based text mining method designed to document the location, timing and impact of GH through large language models across multiple languages and at various scales. Applied here globally on 6,366,905 news articles published from 2017 through 2024 in 58 languages, HazMiner extracted 21,411 flood, 7,659 landslide and 3,606 flash flood events with known location and time information and, in some cases, impact data. Compared to existing hazard datasets, HazMiner significantly improved hazard documentation, reducing the data gaps in many regions, especially in the Global South. The new versatile multilingual method and its dataset advances both text mining and natural hazard research.

papers.title: Review article: rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems through the lens of the early warnings for all framework – advances, gaps, and perspectives
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. This review is necessary at this time to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the rainfall-induced landslide early warning system (LEWS) through the lens of the United Nations ‘Early Warnings for All’ (EW4All) framework. This study integrates EW4All pillars, incorporates overlooked literature, examines information sharing in academic publications, and evaluates the global feasibility of implementing EW4All for LEWS. Of 61 rainfall-induced LEWS identified in the literature covering 23 countries, 14 are considered operational, meaning they are currently implemented and actively used for warning purposes, across only 10 countries. Among local, regional, and national systems, local LEWS is often less scalable and more resource-intensive. Most operational systems target debris flows and shallow landslides and rely mainly on rainfall thresholds. While some include susceptibility maps, risk maps are largely absent. Real-time sensor data are used in some systems; however, high maintenance costs limit scalability. Reliability is further constrained by data scarcity, limited forecast verification, suboptimal use of AI, and the lack of standardised forecasting approaches. Community engagement and multi-hazard integration remain limited. Although EW4All is transformative, implementing effective LEWS in rainfall-induced landslide-prone areas worldwide by 2027 remains impractical without localised approaches, sufficient funds, and resources.

papers.title: Reducing false alarms in crackmeter-based early warning of small-scale slope deformation via deep learning-driven asynchronous displacement–rainfall data fusion
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. Real-time crackmeter-based warning systems for rainfall-induced small-scale slope failures suffer from prohibitively high false alarm rates. Across diverse geological settings, existing approaches relying on fixed thresholds or isolated rainfall–displacement relationships are highly sensitive to noise, lacking the robustness to reliably distinguish genuine deformation signals from spurious measurements. To address this operational bottleneck, this study reframes the early warning paradigm from a traditional fixed-threshold alerting process reliant on manual discrimination to an automated alert truth verification problem, proposing a real-time binary classification framework to isolate true early warnings from sensor-triggered false alarms. Utilizing a multi-source dataset of crackmeter displacement and rainfall measurements from diverse monitored slopes in Fujian Province, China, all true early warning instances were rigorously calibrated via field investigations. A patch-based dual-branch temporally-aware Transformer model was developed to explicitly address asynchronous multi-rate data fusion, strict temporal causality between rainfall and displacement, and stringent real-time decision constraints. By simultaneously capturing long-term rainfall-displacement interactions and high-resolution displacement dynamics, the model outperforms competitive baselines, achieving a precision of 90.91 %, a recall of 93.53 %, and an F2-score of 92.99 % in identifying true early warnings. Interpretability analysis reveals the model’s decisions are primarily driven by localized displacement trends and relative rainfall intensity, aligning with expert judgment. The proposed framework significantly curtails false alarms without compromising reliability, acting as a robust decision-support layer to enhance automated slope hazard monitoring. Future work will fuse additional sensor types to suppress false alarms via cross-validation of multi-physical responses.

papers.title: GIS-Based Statistical Modelling for Landslide Susceptibility Zonation in Parts of Northwest Indian Himalayas
papers.source: Journal of the Indian Society of Remote Sensing

papers.title: Causal Geospatial Intelligence Framework for Identifying Environmental Drivers of Landslide Risk in Mountainous Regions
papers.source: International Journal of Engineering Science and Information Technology
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility models can effectively predict areas prone to landslides but generally provide limited evidence on whether specific environmental exposures causally influence landslide occurrence. This research proposes an integrated causal-geospatial framework combining predictive modeling with causal effect estimation and spatial heterogeneity analysis for landslide occurrence in Desa Wih Pase, Bener Meriah, Indonesia. An analytical dataset comprising 18,450 30 m × 30 m grid cells from observations in 2025 was analyzed using Random Forest and Logistic Regression for occurrence probability modeling, followed by Causal Forest to derive average treatment effect estimates together with grid-level Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). The Random Forest model reached a discrimination performance of 0.91 in AUC-ROC, exceeding the 0.79 achieved by the Logistic Regression baseline, demonstrating stronger predictive discrimination under the imbalanced landslide dataset. Causal analysis estimated a positive effect of cumulative rainfall, with a 100 mm increase associated with a 0.142 increase in landslide occurrence probability (95% CI: 0.089–0.195). A 10° increase in slope produced an estimated effect of 0.218 (95% CI: 0.161–0.275). Spatial CATE analysis revealed substantial heterogeneity, with rainfall effects ranging from ?0.039 to 0.302 and slope effects from ?0.024 to 0.490 across valid 30 m grid cells. Sensitivity analyses showed that the positive causal effects remained stable across alternative confounder sets, rainfall accumulation windows, and spatial resolutions. The framework distinguishes predictive susceptibility from causal environmental effects and provides a basis for spatially targeted landslide risk reduction and environmental engineering interventions

papers.title: Limit-state geometry of trailing-edge tensile cracks in soil slopes with a tensile strength threshold
papers.summary: Abstract Trailing-edge tensile cracks can contribute to tensile–shear slope failure. Many analytical models prescribe a vertical crack and solve only for depth, and tensile strength, σₜ , is also often neglected or treated indirectly. This study develops a limit-state formulation for an initially intact, homogeneous cemented soil slope under drained conditions. Shear resistance follows the Mohr–Coulomb criterion, while tensile failure is governed independently by \(\:{\sigma\:}_{t}\). The formulation treats the limit-state crack depth L and inclination δ as coupled unknowns of the tensile–shear limit-state problem rather than prescribing the crack inclination in advance. The solution satisfies tensile and shear failure conditions, equilibrium, and geometric constraints. The formulation is examined using theoretical benchmarks, a bounded loess field comparison, and simulations using MatDEM. The benchmarks reproduce established depth trends. The field measurement falls within the calculated range for the adopted tensile-strength ratio. The simulations preserve the crack/no-crack distinction and show closer correspondence in inclination than in depth, with mean absolute differences of 4.22° and 1.66 m, respectively. Increasing σₜ reduces L and δ and may suppress a positive-depth solution. The cohesion intercept generally increases both, while unit weight mainly reduces L . Global Sobol analysis ranks cohesion > tensile strength > friction angle > unit weight for the zero-including depth response.

papers.title: Enhancing soil creep index prediction accuracy using optimized XGBoost and LightGBM models with bio-inspired optimization algorithms: SHAP- and LIME-based explanation methods
papers.summary: Soil creep, as a form of long-term deformation, significantly influences the performance of foundations and earth structures. As this deformation develops over time, it can lead to major geotechnical issues such as slope failures, differential ground movement, and excessive settlement. Consequently, accurate estimation of the soil creep index is essential for informed geotechnical decision-making. To address this, the primary aim of this study is to develop precise models for estimating the soil creep index using modern machine learning methods. This study develops fourteen predictive models, including seven based on XGBoost and seven based on LightGBM. These include the standard XGBoost and LightGBM models, as well as their optimized variants enhanced using grey wolf optimizer (GWO), whale optimization algorithm (WOA), bat algorithm (BAT), dragonfly algorithm (DOA), crayfish optimization algorithm (COA), and grasshopper optimization algorithm (GOA). To assess the reliability of creep index prediction, the models were evaluated under four separate sets of input variables. In addition, SHAP, LIME, and SelectKBest methods were applied to explore the influence of individual input factors on the prediction outcomes. Each model’s effectiveness was assessed through four principal statistical indicators: the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), correlation coefficient (R), and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE). Based on the RMSE values, the top three hybrid XGBoost models were XGBoost-GOA (RMSE = 0.002259), XGBoost-GWO (RMSE = 0.002273), and XGBoost-COA (RMSE = 0.002316). Among the hybrid LightGBM models, the best performers were LightGBM-BAT (RMSE = 0.003813), LightGBM-GWO (RMSE = 0.003884), and LightGBM-COA (RMSE = 0.003885). For the standalone models, XGBoost (RMSE = 0.003084) outperformed CART (RMSE = 0.003398) and LightGBM (RMSE = 0.003972). The testing results indicate that XGBoost-based models provide a reliable and accurate approach for predictin

papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-4280
papers.summary: Abstract. The Marmara's Sea with its near-field tsunami complications in Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, is paradoxically surrounded by a densely urbanised, infrastructure-rich coastline and positioned above the North Anatolian Fault system with historical earthquake events, submarine slope processes and narrow-basin resonance that impact coastal water levels. This fact motivated the current study presenting a benchmark-consistent GeoClaw modelling roadmap on seven historical Marmara tsunami scenarios selected from 22-event source catalogue with numerical comparison through 20-lane. The lanes represent exclusively, different source-construction, turning strategy, comprising earthquake-only, earthquake-plus-landslide, adaptive sampling, hybrid site-blend, and close-loop correction variants. From the first lane to the final selected best lane of the simulations set, the benchmark error could be reduced from maximum 1.93 m to 0.019 m in MAE (Mean Absolute Error) and 2.26 m to 0.024 m in RMSE (Root Mean Square Error), with all seven events cases remaining below 10 % error and the largest absolute percent error is 2.4 %. After target-based scenario selection, the corresponding outputs such as gauge-history, travel-time, and bridge-ready hydrodynamic outputs, providing a reproducible chain from historical source interpretation to infrastructure demand inputs are extracted. The workflow is designed for regions where instrumental tsunami records are sparse, but historical runup constraints, bathymetry, mapped faults, and scenario logic can be combined transparently.

papers.title: Mitigasi dan Kesiapsiagaan Bencana di Indonesia: Telaah Literatur dan Implikasinya bagi Nusa Tenggara Timur
papers.source: Antigen Jurnal Kesehatan Masyarakat dan Ilmu Gizi
papers.summary: Indonesia and East Nusa Tenggara (NTT) face recurrent threats from earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, floods, and landslides, while the effectiveness of mitigation depends heavily on community preparedness and the reliability of early warning systems. This review aims to synthesize evidence on disaster risk reduction, community preparedness, and early warning systems, and to derive implications for NTT. A narrative-thematic literature review was conducted on 18 sources published between 2011 and 2026, selected using inclusion and exclusion criteria and supplemented with secondary disaster data for NTT from the regional disaster management agency and national media. The sources were analyzed using the LIPI-UNESCO/ISDR preparedness parameters. Three main patterns emerged. First, preparedness varies widely, from the not-ready category in a school near Mount Sinabung to the very-ready category in Pacitan Bay, with resource mobilization and drill frequency as the weakest components. Second, technology-based warning systems are often constrained by maintenance, budget, and communication chains, so they need to be combined with local wisdom such as smong. Third, discussions combined with drills, disaster literacy, and community institutions improve readiness. In NTT, 136 disaster events were recorded between January and April 2026, and the November 2024 eruption of Lewotobi Laki-laki killed 10 people. The implications are that mitigation in NTT should integrate contingency planning, regular drills, maintained early warning, and local knowledge, supported by preparedness surveys that remain scarce in this province.

papers.title: Machine learning-based landslide susceptibility assessment in the Uttarkashi District, Uttarakhand
papers.summary: Landslides are a major geological hazard that poses serious risks to infrastructure, transportation networks, and populations. This study develops a framework for evaluating landslide risk in the Uttarkashi District of Uttarakhand, India, using GIS and machine learning. With topographic, geological, hydrological, environmental, and anthropogenic characteristics, a landslide inventory comprising 1,994 landslide locations and the same number of non-landslide locations was prepared and evaluated using fourteen conditioning factors. Models like Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) were trained and evaluated using spatial five-fold cross-validation and an independent test dataset. Elevation, distance from roads, NDVI, aspect, lithology, and land-use/land-cover were found to be among the most significant predictors using feature-importance analysis, albeit their relative significance differed between models. The mean AUC values for RF, XGBoost and LightGBM were 0.8805, 0.8846, and 0.8840, respectively, based on the spatial cross-validation data. LightGBM obtained an AUC of 0.8950 on the independent test dataset, whereas RF and XGBoost obtained an AUC of 0.8988. High- and very-high-susceptibility zones were frequently identified on the resulting susceptibility maps along the Yamuna and Bhagirathi River systems as well as important transportation routes like the Yamunotri and Gangotri highways. Additionally, this study shows how machine learning combined with remote sensing and GIS can effectively assess the susceptibility of a region to landslides. In the Himalayan context, it offers spatial data to support infrastructure management, slope stabilization, land-use planning, and disaster risk reduction.

papers.title: Ein Erdrutsch in Mels, 1953
Three storms test a decade of multi-hazard warning in south-eastern Bangladesh
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides and flash floods in south-eastern Bangladesh share their storms but are warned for separately. This study compares the compound events of June 2017, August 2023 and July 2026 on the same slopes, using gauge-corrected rainfall, a date-checked landslide inventory, river records and situation reports. In 2017 the lower of two published rainfall thresholds for landslides was crossed 17 to 25 hours before the first failures and the higher one two to eight hours before, and gauges existed for both hazards but dedicated warnings for neither. By 2026 numbered landslide bulletins were issued for each sub-district under a draft national protocol and 38,422 people were sheltered. In Rangamati, where the district gauge recorded 343 mm in 24 hours in 2017 and 287 mm in 2026, deaths fell from 121 to one. A slope-stability model shows that the 2026 storm was no gentler on the slopes than that of 2017. The lower threshold is exceeded on 14 to 19 days of an average monsoon even at the region's two long-running gauges, while the higher one missed most dated landslides. The heaviest monsoon rain showed no detectable trend since 1950, but 3 °C of warming at about 7 % more rain per degree would make the higher threshold fire about 60 % more often. In 2026 the remaining landslide deaths concentrated in refugee camps on cut slopes despite warnings, suggesting that the missing part of the warning system lies between the warning and the people it reaches.

papers.title: Changes in root morphological and architectural traits are key factors influencing soil detachment capacity on shallow landslide scars during vegetation recovery on the Loess Plateau
papers.summary: The hypothesis of this study was that changes in root morphological and architectural traits are key factors influencing soil detachment capacity (Dc) on shallow landslide scars during vegetation recovery on the Loess Plateau. The dataset comprises the raw data used to generate Figs. 5–7. Figure 5 presents Dc at different slope positions and recovery times. Figure 6 shows root biomass and morphological traits, including root weight density, root length density, root surface area density, root volume density, root fractal dimension, and root fractal abundance. Figure 7 presents three-dimensional (3D) root architectural traits, including root topological index, root branching angle, and root link length, together with photographs of root systems at different recovery times. Data were collected from six shallow landslide scars representing 1, 3, and 5 years of vegetation recovery, and two newly formed scars used as controls (CK). Soil detachment capacity was measured using flume scour experiments at a slope gradient of 45° under five flow discharges (12–36 L min⁻¹). Root biomass and morphological traits were quantified through root scanning, while 3D architectural traits were characterized using root reconstruction. Measurements were obtained at different slope positions to capture spatial variations in Dc and root traits across recovery stages. The results identified root length density and topological index as key root traits influencing Dc during vegetation recovery. Changes in root morphological and architectural traits may also influence Dc partly through their effects on soil cohesion (c). The dataset provides a basis for examining how root morphological and 3D architectural traits vary with slope position and vegetation recovery time, and how these variations relate to changes in Dc. It can also support further investigation of the role of soil cohesion in mediating the effects of root traits on soil detachment.

papers.title: The Country and the City in the Himalayas
papers.summary: Kalimpong, a Himalayan foothill district in West Bengal, is facing an agrarian crisis as rice farming becomes increasingly unviable due to rising costs, water scarcity, and climate unpredictability. Sarah Besky analyzes how colonial “government estate” legacies, designed for rent extraction, now compound these challenges, pushing youth into service-sector migration. Meanwhile, homestay tourism—promoted as an alternative—commodifies local culture, relying on women’s unpaid care work and catering to Indian urban middle-class fantasies of a “Swiss-like” retreat. Yet, landslides, hydropower projects, and infrastructure strain worsen livability. This shift from farming to affective labor reveals how colonial and neoliberal logics converge, masking extraction behind nostalgia while deepening inequality and ecological precarity.

papers.title: MOVEMONT - Final Report
papers.summary: Landslides are common processes in mountain areas, forming an integral part of their long-term destruction. To society, such phenomena may mean risks and disasters on the one hand, having triggered a huge bulk of research. However, landslides may also represent significant natural and cultural heritage and offer services to society, aspects that are yet under-researched and may be included in the rather scarcely used concept of geosystem services. In this context, landslides also help us to learn how Earth surface systems are functioning. As landslides often represent spectacular phenomena creating remarkable landforms, they are suitable for generating enthusiasm for geo-scientific topics among people, and are therefore useful for demonstrating complex geomorphological processes. UNESCO Global Geoparks (UGGps) represent ideal environments of exploring and highlighting geosystem services related to landslides, particularly in Austria where the three existing UNESCO Global Geoparks (Karawanken/Karavanke, Erz der Alpen, Steirische Eisenwurzen) are characterized by the occurrence of a broad range of landslide types and magnitudes.

papers.title: Revisiting Crozier (2005)—Multiple-Occurrence Regional Landslide Events in New Zealand: Hazard Management Issues
papers.summary: Abstract This paper reviews the key contribution of Crozier (2005) on Multiple-Occurrence Regional Landslide Events (MORLE), a phenomenon with specific frequency, magnitude, and geomorphic impact, redefining regional-scale landslide hazard assessment. Using extensive landslide inventories and climatic datasets from New Zealand, the study correlates landslide distribution with rainfall intensity, antecedent moisture, terrain morphology, and lithology. The work highlights the limitations of site-specific hazard evaluation, advocates for regional, frequency/magnitude-based assessments integrating meteorological thresholds, and underscores the multi-hazard nature of MORLE. This new conceptual model has significantly influenced subsequent developments in susceptibility modelling, hazard evaluation, and early warning systems. The paper remains a milestone in landslide science, bridging geomorphology and risk governance while anticipating modern climate-driven hazard analysis and spatial modelling.

papers.title: Revisiting Guzzetti et al. (1999)—Landslide Hazard Evaluation: A Review of Current Techniques and Their Application in a Multiscale Study, Central Italy
papers.summary: Abstract This review analyses the article ‘Landslide hazard evaluation: a foundational insight to landslide hazard assessment’ by Guzzetti et al. (1999), who critically examined the concepts, assumptions and methods underpinning the field at the end of the twentieth century. The paper is rooted in the evolution of risk research and highlights its clear distinction between landslide hazard and landslide susceptibility. By exploring mapping units, modelling approaches and scale effects, and applying these to multiscale statistical analyses in Central Italy, the authors clarified both the potential and the limitations of Geographic Information System-based quantitative methods. The paper demonstrates how susceptibility modelling has consolidated as a legitimate planning tool. While it focuses on this specific aspect, the foundation it builds can pave the way for addressing broader questions of disaster risk, vulnerability and governance in subsequent research and applications. The analysis emphasises the paper’s conceptual rigour, methodological transparency and enduring relevance to modern research, situating its contributions within the hazard-centred paradigms that preceded later advances in integrated disaster risk studies.

papers.title: Compiled Data and Code for a Physics–Data Coupled Early-Warning Model for Rainfall-Induced Landslides
papers.summary: This repository contains compiled CSV data and code for “A Physics–Data Coupled Early-Warning Model for Rainfall-Induced Landslides.” The study focuses on landslides triggered by Typhoon Gaemi in Zixing City, China. The model combines a physics-informed neural network, rainfall infiltration, and infinite-slope stability analysis to estimate landslide occurrence probabilities. Data were compiled from published studies cited in the article. Please cite the associated article, this repository, and the original data sources when reusing these materials.

papers.title: A 3D Implementation of an Elastoviscoplastic Model and Application to Creep-Driven Slow-Moving Landslides
papers.summary: Abstract To analyze problems involving creep-driven slow-moving landslides interacting with structures and infrastructure and gain useful information for risk management, numerical modeling is the most comprehensive tool. When resorting to numerical simulations, appropriate constitutive modeling is key to capture the time-dependent behavior of geomaterials. However, a drawback of advanced constitutive models accounting for time dependency is the high number of parameters involved, which are commonly calibrated based on site-scale monitoring data, without accounting for the characteristic creep behavior of the material. This paper describes the implementation of an existing elastoviscoplastic model in a three-dimensional (3D) finite-difference software. The model, called SHELVIP (Stress Hardening Elastic Viscous Plastic), was derived from the classical theory of elastoplasticity by adding a viscoplastic component based on Perzyna’s overstress theory. After illustrating the model and the implementation procedure, the steps to tune the constitutive parameters, especially the viscoplastic ones, are described. First, the viscoplastic parameters are determined at the laboratory scale through an analytical calibration process based on laboratory creep tests. Then, tuning of some parameters at the site scale is performed, while other parameters are kept unchanged from their laboratory-scale value being representative of the intrinsic creep behavior. The final set of parameters can be used to run predictive analyses for problems of engineering relevance. The analytical calibration is exemplified with reference to triaxial creep tests on Palombini clays. Then, the implemented SHELVIP model is validated by comparing numerical, analytical, and experimental creep strains at different deviatoric stress levels. A three-dimensional numerical model of the interaction between a deep-seated landslide and an existing motorway tunnel is developed. The capability of the constitutive fram

papers.title: Spatiotemporal correlation of rainfall intensity and subsurface acoustic emission parameters for landslide initiation
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall-induced landslides pose severe geohazards in monsoon-dominated mountain regions. This study presents a coupled rainfall–acoustic emission (AE) monitoring system deployed at a landslide-prone slope near Narendra Nagar, Uttarakhand, India (Lesser Himalaya). AE signals were recorded from active hollow aluminium waveguides installed through mapped shear zones, synchronized with sub-minute rainfall data from an Automatic Weather Station. Analysis of 4,884 one-minute windows over the 2025 monsoon season revealed: (i) a site-specific critical rainfall intensity threshold of 2 mm/min (r = 0.70, p 4 mm/min, 60 min at < 1 mm/min); and (v) a dual-criterion (rainfall + AE) warning system that reduces false alarms by a factor of three compared to rain-only thresholds. A site-specific intensity–duration threshold (I = 0.088D^0.36) was derived from 51 AE-confirmed rainfall events. These results demonstrate the feasibility of physics-based, multi-criterion AE-driven landslide early warning in complex Himalayan terrain.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Statistical and Morphometric Models for Rainfall-Induced Shallow Landslide Susceptibility Mapping: A Case Study Along the Fujian–Guangdong Border
papers.summary: Extreme rainfall can trigger widespread shallow landslides, highlighting the need for reliable susceptibility assessment systems. This study compares an information value–logistic regression (IV-LR) model with a terrain-driven morphometric model in terms of their predictive performance for shallow landslides triggered by an extreme rainfall event along the Fujian–Guangdong border. The IV-LR model integrates 11 environmental predictors and was trained using 3633 landslide samples and an equal number of non-landslide samples, whereas the morphometric model relies on DEM-derived terrain attributes and required no landslide inventory for training. Both models were evaluated using a common spatially separated validation dataset comprising 2273 landslide and 2273 non-landslide samples. The IV-LR model achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.7537, an Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) of 0.2524, and a Brier score of 0.2336, compared with 0.5225, 0.0084, and 0.4172 for the morphometric model, respectively. Within the highest-ranked 20% of the common assessment area, the IV-LR model captured 53.06% of validation landslides, compared with 23.89% for the morphometric model. These findings support the feasibility of using an IV-LR model for detailed susceptibility assessment, while the morphometric model, which relies only on DEM-derived inputs, shows limited discriminatory performance.

papers.title: Revisiting Corominas et al. (2014)—Recommendations for the Quantitative Analysis of Landslide Risk
papers.summary: Abstract Corominas et al. (2014) synthesised recommended methodologies for quantitative landslide hazard, vulnerability and risk analysis across spatial scales and for verification/validation of outputs. This chapter revisits the paper as a technical benchmark for quantitative landslide risk analysis, highlighting its structured decomposition of hazard (spatial, temporal and intensity components), exposure characterisation and physical vulnerability assessment. Strengths include the explicit linkage from susceptibility to hazard, the treatment of different landslide types and a comprehensive toolbox for model testing. Remaining challenges concern the scarcity of temporal information, the limited representation of landslide intensity and runout at broader scales and the consistent propagation and communication of uncertainty in risk estimates.

papers.title: Knickpoint Database for the Indian Subcontinent
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Knickpoints, abrupt steepenings in river longitudinal profiles, record base-level change, differential rock uplift, lithological contrasts and valley blockage by landslides and glaciers, but no consistent, openly available inventory exists for the knickpoints at a regional scale or continental scale. Here we present a spatially continuous database of 70,420 knickpoints along 2.5 million km of channel in the Himalaya–Karakoram arc and Peninsular India, derived from the 90 m MERIT DEM with the TopoToolbox knickpointfinder algorithm (vertical tolerance 50 m; streams draining more than 0.81 km2). Each knickpoint carries coordinates, elevation, height, drainage area, channel slope, basin, lithology and distance to the nearest active fault. We compare the database with OpenStreetMap waterfalls (46 % lie within 500 m of a knickpoint, 4.9 times the random expectation) and test its sensitivity to the elevation model in two basins using SRTM, Copernicus, FABDEM and ALOS PALSAR. The data are archived on Zenodo and are intended as a ready-to-use variable for tectonic geomorphology, landslide susceptibility, hydropower and hazard studies.

papers.title: Regional covariation between climate-normalized storm rarity and landslide magnitude in Taiwan is sensitive to rainfall timing
papers.summary: Abstract Climate-normalized rainfall rarity may facilitate comparisons across climates, but pooled rainfall–landslide associations can obscure regional structure and rainfall timing. We examined 994 reported rainfall-induced landslides in Taiwan (1987–2018) using 2-km hourly precipitation and generalized extreme-value climatologies for 1980–2019. Rainfall rarity ( T max ) was defined as the maximum of 1–72-h duration-specific return periods, not the recurrence interval of an entire storm. Retrospective whole-storm T max was available for 912 records, including 708 with estimated volume. Within 18 selected spatial cells, 16 contained 393 volume-bearing records. Contextual decomposition yielded a positive between-cell rarity–volume coefficient ( β between = 0.945, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.642–1.248), but no detectable positive within-cell association ( β within = − 0.105, 95% CI = − 0.288–0.078). Cell-clustered inference was less decisive. The between-cell coefficient decreased to 0.279 after adjusting for absolute 24-h rainfall and to 0.317 after excluding Typhoon Morakot. When rarity was calculated using only rainfall preceding recorded failure, the positive between-cell association was not recovered ( β between = − 0.276, 95% CI = − 1.115–0.563; 361 volume-bearing records), although analytical populations differed. These findings identify a Morakot-anchored, inventory-specific association that is sensitive to absolute rainfall and exposure timing.

papers.title: Groundwater quality dynamics and hydrochemical indicators of water insecurity in the semi-arid Sokoto Basin, Northwestern Nigeria
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater is the surest water source in semi-arid regions, where surface water is seasonal and subject to climatic fluctuations. Growing climatic stress, along with anthropogenic pressures, in the Sokoto Basin of northwestern Nigeria poses a threat to groundwater quality and the region's water security. This paper has explored groundwater hydrochemistry and identified significant hydrochemical predictors of water insecurity across different geological environments in the Western Sokoto Basin. Fifty-four groundwater samples were collected from hand-dug wells and boreholes in the basement complex and sedimentary formations. The analysis of physicochemical and heavy-metal parameters was performed according to the standard APHA (2017) methods, and multivariate (PCA, HCA, correlation) and geostatistical (Ordinary Kriging, variogram modelling) analyses were used to demonstrate spatial patterns, controlling factors, and predictive accuracy. Findings indicate that groundwater quality differs considerably with lithology: basement complex aquifers are more mineralised and enriched in metals (Mn, Cr, Al, Zn, As) than sedimentary rocks, mainly due to extended water-rock interactions, weathering, and climatic concentration processes. Spatial interpolation revealed unique hot spots of contamination, especially in low-lying and high-evaporation areas, suggesting a magnifying effect of climate stress on solute buildup. High predictability (R 2 > 0.9 in most metals) of kriging models and uncertainty zones (as revealed by nRMSE mapping) was observed in areas of hydrochemical instability. Theoretically, the research will enhance geostatistical understanding of groundwater dynamics in data-limited, climate-sensitive basins by integrating climatic, geological, and geochemical factors into a single explanatory model. papers.title: Disaster management in Cameroon: Governance challenges, institutional gaps, and a proposed multi-level framework for landslide risk reduction
papers.summary: Abstract Effective disaster risk governance is the backbone of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (SFDRR) 2015–2030, yet many low- and middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa face persistent barriers to its implementation. Cameroon, a country with high multi-hazard exposure to floods, landslides, and drought, has experienced a series of escalating urban landslide disasters, culminating in the 2023 Mbankolo landslides in Yaoundé (≥30 fatalities). Using mixed-methods primary data from 250 household questionnaires, focus group discussions, and key informant interviews with officials from five ministries and two international organisations, combined with systematic review of Cameroon's disaster management legislation and institutional architecture, this study evaluates the country's contemporary disaster management system. Five systemic operational challenges are identified: gaps in legislative and policy frameworks; data scarcity and language barriers; weak institutional coordination; limited community and stakeholder participation; and insufficient resource allocation. A comprehensive, four-phase, multi-level disaster management framework tailored to Cameroon's specific governance context is proposed and subjected to a SWOT analysis. The framework integrates decentralised governance, multilingual communication, community-based disaster risk reduction, climate change adaptation, and alignment with SFDRR. The study provides a transferable model for comparable low-income tropical countries navigating the transition from reactive disaster response to proactive risk governance.

papers.title: Research on the Optimized 3D DEM‒SPH Algorithm and Impact Parameters of Surge Wave Amplitude for Granular Landslides
papers.source: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.summary: ObjectiveMesh-based and Eulerian-Lagrangian methods cannot adequately simulate large deformations, free-surface fragmentation, and fluid-solid interaction during granular landslide-induced surges. A three-dimensional meshless semi-resolved Discrete Element Method (DEM) and Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) coupling algorithm was developed, incorporating a multiphase flow model to optimize the volume fraction distribution at the coupling interface. The key parameters controlling the maximum surge wave amplitude were systematically investigated to support hazard prediction in reservoir areas.MethodsDEM with a nonlinear contact force model and rolling resistance simulated granular landslides. Each DEM particle obeyed Newton's second law. Normal and tangential contact forces were computed using a nonlinear model with damping. SPH solved the Navier-Stokes equations for the fluid phase using a Wendland C2 kernel with a compact support radius of 2h. A δ‒SPH density diffusion term (coefficient δ=0.1) was added to the continuity equation to reduce pressure noise. The multiphase flow model optimized the volume fraction calculation at the solid-liquid interface using a density-gradient-based control equation. Buoyancy, drag, and reaction forces between DEM and SPH particles were computed using a semi-resolved scheme. Buoyancy was calculated via pressure interpolation from surrounding fluid particles. Drag forces were computed using the Ergun correlation for void fractions below 0.8 and the Wen-Yu correlation for void fractions of 0.8 or above, based on local void fraction and relative velocity. Physical experiments were conducted in a three-dimensional wave tank. The granular landslide material was quartz sand with a mean diameter of 8 mm, density of 2 600 kg/m³, and porosity of 0.23. papers.title: Reply on RC1
papers.summary: Abstract. Landslide early warning remains challenging because many slopes evolve through intermittent, nonlinear, and non-monotonic deformation before catastrophic failure. Here, we develop an integrated early warning framework that combines three statistical physics-based diagnostics: velocity b-value tracking, dragon-king detection, and log-periodic power law singularity (LPPLS) time-to-failure analysis. The velocity b-value captures long-term changes in the distribution of slope displacement rates, dragon-king detection identifies statistically significant extreme velocity outliers, and LPPLS analysis describes the quasi-deterministic evolution towards a finite-time singularity yielding probabilistic estimates of the failure time and its uncertainty. Applied pseudo-prospectively to the Preonzo, Veslemannen, and Stampa landslides, the framework reveals a coherent sequence of precursory signals: b-value decline generally appears first, dragon-king outliers emerge later as failure becomes imminent, and LPPLS forecasts become increasingly constrained during the final acceleration stage. These complementary indicators are integrated into a traffic-light warning scheme that translates complex rupture dynamics into operationally interpretable warning levels. By combining precursory signals across multiple timescales, the proposed framework establishes a robust and physically grounded foundation for next-generation landslide early warning.

papers.summary: AI-Powered IoT Digital Twin for Multi-Hazard Prediction, Early Warning, Human Detection and Rescue Support.This project proposes an AI-Powered IoT Digital Twin for Multi-Hazard Prediction, Early Warning, Human Detection and Rescue Support, integrating IoT sensors, LoRa-based wireless communication, AI/ML, sensor fusion, cloud computing and Digital Twin technology. Distributed sensors monitor rainfall, water level, temperature, smoke/gas, soil moisture and ground movement. Sensor data is transmitted through LoRa to a gateway, where AI-based sensor fusion estimates hazard probability and predicts the progression of floods, fires and landslides. Cloud computing enables centralized data storage, historical analysis, remote monitoring and access to the Digital Twin from anywhere. A dynamic Digital Twin visualizes hazard intensity and spatial risk zones while generating risk scores and early warnings. mmWave/radar sensors support human-presence detection and approximate localization during emergencies. The system also incorporates what-if simulation, explainable AI, sensor-fault detection and rescue prioritization. Local processing can support essential monitoring and alerts during internet outages, improving system reliability and emergency response.

papers.title: An outlook on varied ecological engineering solutions for landslide prevention
papers.source: Journal of Environmental Science Health & Sustainability
papers.summary: This review assesses ecological engineering solutions for landslide prevention and slope stabilization by synthesizing evidence identified through scientific databases. The review encompasses the idea of applying vegetation-based techniques, including live stakes, brush layering, revegetation, grasses, herbaceous plants, bamboo plantations, and lithophytic life forms, together with conventional and structural measures such as natural geotextiles, live wooden crib walls, wattle fences, live silt fences, and live gully breaks. The reviewed evidence highlights the importance of species with strong root systems, which can influence the effectiveness of bioengineering interventions. Species such as Vetiver, Bermuda Grass, Ryegrass, Alder, selected Ficus species, and bamboo show deep-rooted control over soil reinforcement, erosion, and slope stabilization, while lithophytic life forms and pioneer colonizers may support the restoration of exposed rocky and landslide-affected surfaces. The review also examines the contribution of artificial intelligence, remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles, LiDAR, interferometric synthetic aperture radar, and machine learning models in landslide susceptibility assessment, monitoring, and advance warning. Overall, the findings revealed that integrated ecological engineering and data-driven monitoring may complement conventional stabilization measures, reduce landslide risk, restore degraded slopes, and inform sustainable land-management planning.

papers.title: NZ’s resource management rules have been rewritten. What happens after the election?
papers.summary: As each new environmental assessment shows, the impacts on New Zealand’s natural and urban areas are only compounding. The government’s most recent national snapshot describes polluted rivers and coastal waters, declining biodiversity, poor air quality in some communities and greenhouse gas emissions that remain high by international standards. Increasingly extreme weather is exposing the consequences of how we manage our land. Flooding and landslides have devastated communities, while damage caused by forestry slash during storms have brought heavy costs for people and property. Meanwhile, New Zealand faces ever-growing demands for housing, infrastructure and economic development. Yet the regulatory system meant to manage it remains unsettled. The previous Labour government passed legislation to replace the Resource Management Act (RMA), only for the National-led coalition to repeal it and introduce its own Planning Act and Natural Environment Act. The new system promises to make development easier, reduce costs and delays, and improve environmental management. But environment groups warn it could weaken protections for nature and leave communities facing even greater risks. Although the new legislation has passed, most of the changes will come into effect over the next four years. The outcome of this election, of course, may see the rulebook rewritten yet again

papers.title: GIS-Based Landslide Susceptibility Mapping Using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) in Batang Kali, Selangor, Malaysia
papers.summary: Landslides are a prevalent environmental risk in Malaysia, occurring mainly in hilly and tropical locations, often during the optimum time for heavy downpours. This study aims to assess the landslide susceptibility in Batang Kali, Selangor, Malaysia, utilizing the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) based on Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Based on historical records, aerial image interpretation, and remote sensing data, in combination with field verification, a landslide database of 46 identified landslide locations was produced. Sixteen influential factors, including various topographic, hydrological, environmental, and human factors, were selected for landslide susceptibility modeling. The landslide susceptibility map was created using weighted overlay analysis and classified into five levels of susceptibility, ranging from very low to very high. The resulting susceptibility map shows that 14.68% of the study area belongs to the very low susceptibility class, while 25.84%, 20.20%, 24.90%, and 14.38% belong to low, moderate, high, and very high susceptibility classes, respectively. The susceptibility map obtained from this study serves as a realistic decision-support tool for reducing landslide risk, designing infrastructure, and promoting sustainable land management in sensitive mountainous areas. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to measure the model's predictive performance, using the Area Under the Curve (AUC) as an overall measure of model discrimination. The ROC–AUC analysis showed an AUC value of 0.722 (72.2%), indicating acceptable model performance.

Comparison of GraphSAGE–Graph Attention Network and Best–Worst Method for Landslide Susceptibility Prediction Mapping
papers.summary: Landslides, as a natural hazard, pose a potential risk to human life and infrastructure. However, predicting and mitigating landslide susceptibility is challenging due to the complexity of contributing factors, such as slope, groundwater level, earthquakes, and vegetation. This study aims to develop a GraphSAGE–Graph Attention Network (GraphSAGE-GAT) and Best–Worst Method (BWM) for predicting landslides and generating landslide susceptibility maps (LSMs) in Savadkouh County (northern Iran). For this purpose, twelve conditioning factors relevant to LSMs were considered: slope, faults, precipitation, vegetation, soil, watercourses, roads, cities, villages, elevation, and temperature. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to evaluate model performance based on the number of events in the landslide susceptibility classes, as well as the Precision–Threshold curve, Recall, Precision, and Specificity across all possible thresholds. The most important factor in the BWM was slope, with 22.63%. By combining weights and layers in GIS, LSMs were generated using both BWM and GraphSAGE-GAT. The results show that 47% of the landslide points were classified as high susceptibility (high and very high) by BWM, whereas 67.33% were classified as high susceptibility by GraphSAGE-GAT. Furthermore, BWM achieved a maximum Precision of approximately 73%, while the Precision of GraphSAGE-GAT increased with the threshold and approached 100% at very high threshold values. The area under the ROC curve was 0.544 for BWM and 0.836 for GraphSAGE-GAT, demonstrating the substantially better discriminatory performance of GraphSAGE-GAT. papers.title: Landslide detection using deep learning models and remote sensing data
papers.summary: Landslide detection using remote sensing has advanced significantly with the rise of deep learning, yet the field remains fragmented in terms of methodological approaches, data sources, and geographic coverage. This paper presents a systematic review of 152 peer-reviewed studies published across 23 journals, with the aim of synthesizing methodological trends, identifying research gaps, and assessing the global representativeness of current work. We classify existing approaches into five categories—data type-based, model type-based, task-based, data fusion-based, and transfer learning/pre-trained models—and critically evaluate their applications. Our review highlights a strong reliance on optical and SAR datasets (for instance, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, PlanetScope, and UAV imagery). In terms of models, encoder–decoder segmentation architectures (particularly U-Net variants) dominate, alongside object detection frameworks (YOLO and RCNN), temporal models (LSTM), and unsupervised CNN-based change detection, yet comparative evaluations across these remain sparse. We also identify an uneven geographic distribution of study areas: research is heavily concentrated in Asia and South America, especially in regions affected by earthquake- and rainfall-induced landslides, while Europe, Africa, and North America are comparatively underrepresented. This imbalance reflects both data availability and hazard prevalence but also limits the generalizability of findings. By synthesizing these patterns, our review underscores the need for standardized evaluation practices, greater methodological diversity, and broader geographic representation to enhance the global applicability and robustness of deep learning in landslide hazard detection.

papers.summary: Abstract Long-term groundwater seepage promotes continuous water–rock interaction, resulting in progressive deterioration of weakly cemented soft rock and posing significant challenges to the long-term stability of underground excavations. To investigate the deformation and failure mechanisms and stability control of argillaceous weakly cemented soft-rock roadways under long-term water-seepage conditions, the 110803 working face in Qingshuiying coal mine was selected as the engineering background. Field investigation, theoretical analysis, numerical simulation, and in-situ monitoring were conducted. The results indicate that the surrounding rock is dominated by argillaceous weakly cemented soft rock and has undergone significant deterioration under long-term water seepage. The original support system is characterized by a weak anchoring foundation, low prestress, and insufficient bearing capacity, which limits effective deformation control. Based on the changes in the slope and deformation rate of the convergence curve, the roadway deformation process is divided into three stages: initial rapid deformation, intermediate accelerated deformation, and late slow deformation. A coupled progressive failure mechanism involving water seepage and three weak links is identified, including water-induced softening and swelling of the roof rock, a weak anchoring foundation, a weak prestress transmission layer, and low surrounding-rock bearing capacity. These factors drive deformation from local damage toward global instability, with water–rock interaction acting as the dominant driving factor. Accordingly, a control strategy of water isolation and threefold strengthening is proposed to isolate water from the surrounding rock and enhance anchoring capacity, prestress transmission, and overall rock-mass strength. Soil Texture Influences the Magnitude and Depth Persistence of Alfalfa Reinforcement and Its Contribution to Slope Stability
papers.summary: Vegetation-based slope stabilisation depends on coupled mechanical and hydraulic processes that vary with soil texture and depth. This study linked a five-month long, 0.5 m column experiment to annual two-dimensional transient seepage and analytical infinite-slope modelling to quantify how alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) and a mycorrhiza-containing formulation affect shallow root-zone stability in silty clay (SC) and silty sand (SS). Eighteen columns (n = 3 per soil–treatment combination) received unplanted control (C), alfalfa (A), or alfalfa plus mycorrhiza formulation (A + MF). Biomass, saturated hydraulic conductivity (ks), and saturated direct-shear response at six depths were measured. Relative to A, A + MF increased recovered root dry mass by 24.5% in SC and 53.2% in SS, and ks by 46.6% and 47.4%. Factorial ANOVA detected a soil × treatment interaction for ks (p = 0.00052), but not biomass. Exponential apparent-cohesion profiles separated reinforcement amplitude from depth persistence; fitted decay depths for A/A + MF were 0.167/0.176 m in SC and 0.064/0.22 m in SS. The measured mechanical and hydraulic parameters were applied to a 365-day model of a representative 1V:3H natural infinite slope. All planted cases retained higher annual minimum root-zone factors of safety than their controls, but retention, uptake and storm-timing sensitivities changed the A versus A + MF ranking. Reinforcement magnitude, depth persistence, and soil-specific hydrology should therefore be represented together when evaluating biologically treated shallow slopes.

papers.title: GeoFE-TH
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: GeoFE-TH is a simple program for the stress–deformation analysis of geotechnical structures inplane strain. It follows the approach of FLAC: the soil is divided into quadrilateral zones, theequations of motion are integrated explicitly with scaled masses and damping, and the model isstepped until the unbalanced forces vanish (static equilibrium) or keep growing (collapse).Because no global stiffness matrix is formed, strongly nonlinear behaviour — plastic flow, collapsemechanisms, excavation and fill sequences — is handled robustly. Typical applications: bearing capacity and settlement of shallow foundations slope stability by strength reduction (factor of safety plus failure mechanism) staged excavations with walls, anchors and struts embankments on soft clay: undrained loading and consolidation Buried box culvert and tunnel teaching of soil mechanics and numerical methods Disclaimer GeoFE-TH is only a tool to assist engineering analysis. papers.title: Identifying key controls on knickpoint dynamics in homogenous environments andimplications for the evolution of landscapes
papers.summary: Knickpoints are key landforms in geomorphology arising in many unique geomorphic environments, but most commonly, in fluvial settings. Characterised by areas of higher-than-average channel slopes, the most recognisable knickpoint is a waterfall. Knickpoints make up only a small proportion of the total length of river channels but have an important and disproportionate influence over channel dynamics. Since the banks of the channel act as the local base-level for adjoining hillslopes, knickpoints also influence the wider landscape. The impact of knickpoints, therefore, is wide ranging and acts across multiple scales. This suggests there is a need for a thorough, mechanistic understanding of knickpoints to truly understand landscape evolution in knickpoint environments. However, a fundamental knowledge of knickpoints is currently poorly developed. One of the most common settings where knickpoints form are bedrock rivers. Whilst known to form as a result of external perturbations such as fault-slip or lithological heterogeneity, more recent work focuses on knickpoints formed under constant forcing in the absence of external perturbations (namely, constant base- level fall and sediment flux in homogenous environments). This thesis aims to constrain channel evolution in incising bedrock rivers from local to landscape scale by understanding the knickpoint dynamics formed under constant forcing in homogenous environments. To assess the thesis aim, analogue, 'similarity of process' experiments were used to assess the impact of knickpoints across multiple scales. No direct scaling with any particular natural setting is sought. This experimental approach overcomes the issues of measuring knickpoints in-situ by allowing for the systematic exploration of the impact of key parameters (base-level fall rate, sediment flux and bedrock strength) on knickpoint dynamics at a reduced spatial and temporal scale. papers.title: Assessing Potential Rocky Mountain Pump Storage Sites for Fatal Flaws
papers.summary: Southwestern Colorado offers significant potential for the development of pumped storage hydropower (PSH) due to its favorable topography, existing water infrastructure, and alignment with regional renewable energy expansion. The area’s steep elevation gradients and numerous reservoirs create conditions well-suited for closed-loop and off-river storage systems that can balance intermittent wind and solar generation and baseload plants (such as coal, nuclear, or gas plants). As the demand for quick responding, reliable, long-duration energy storage increases, PSH in the Rocky Mountain region could play a pivotal role in enhancing grid stability and supporting decarbonization goals while stimulating local infrastructure investment. The region’s diverse geology, however, introduces notable geotechnical challenges that require site screening and detailed investigation to avoid potential fatal flaws when siting a project. Complex volcanic and intrusive formations, variable slope stability, historical mining disturbances, and heterogeneous groundwater systems necessitate comprehensive site characterization and potential risk mitigation strategies. Integrating advanced geotechnical methods, such as detailed subsurface mapping, rock mass classification, hydrogeologic modeling, remote sensing, and seismic assessment, will be key to ensuring safe, efficient, and sustainable design. With proper geotechnical planning and adaptive engineering, southwestern Colorado could become a model for resilient and responsible pumped storage development in mountainous terrain. This paper discusses the primary considerations when assessing the feasibility of future PSH projects.

papers.summary: Abstract To enhance the mechanical stability and resistance to plastic damage of Nickel-Titanium (NiTi) orthodontic archwires, this study employs numerical simulations to investigate the multiscale mechanical responses of three types of archwires with different diameters (0.014, 0.016, and 0.018 inch) coated with Titanium Nitride (TiN) of varying thicknesses (550–1550 nm) under uniaxial tension and cyclic loading. The study focuses on analyzing key parameters such as von Mises stress, elastic strain energy density, equivalent deviatoric strain, and axial displacement, and it explores the regulation mechanisms of TiN thickness variation in stiffness enhancement, stress sharing, energy storage, and deformation suppression. The results indicate that the TiN coating can enhance the overall stiffness, load-bearing capacity, and cyclic stability of the archwires; reduce plastic strain accumulation; and optimize energy distribution, among which the thickness range of 800–1300 nm yields the most balanced overall performance. When the coating thickness exceeds the critical value, the strengthening effect tends to saturate, and adverse boundary effects such as a local stress concentration may occur. In addition, archwires with smaller diameters are more sensitive to coating reinforcement, exhibiting higher performance gains. This study reveals the multiscale regulation mechanisms governing the mechanical properties of NiTi archwires as a function of TiN coating thickness, providing a theoretical basis and design guidance for their structural optimization and surface engineering.

Study on the performance of coal gangue and biomass ash cemented backfill under microbial induced calcium carbonate deposition
papers.summary: In this study, Microbially Induced Carbonate Precipitation (MICP) technology was applied to effectively consolidate closely spaced coal seams. The slurry and the entrained solid waste particles were stably cemented underground, thereby reducing pollutant migration and diffusion and preventing slurry inrush in the stope. A microbially cemented coal gangue filling material was developed. The mechanical properties and microstructural characteristics of microbially cemented coal gangue filling material with different biomass ash contents were investigated, and the effects of MICP modification on the mechanical properties of the materials were revealed. The results showed that MICP modification significantly improved the compressive strength and tensile strength of microbial-cemented coal gangue filling materials. The compressive strength and tensile strength of the coal gangue + 20% biomass ash + 10% cement + microorganism specimen reached 0.698 MPa and 0.0489 MPa respectively, which were 29.26% and 28.68% higher than those before microbial modification. The combined effects of MICP modification and the hydration reactions of cement and biomass ash generated substances containing flocculent structures, particle aggregation structures, and a small number of strip-like structures, which contributed to improving the pore structure of the specimens, enhancing interparticle cementation, increasing specimen compactness, and further improving the mechanical properties. The research results provide a new technical approach for grouting filling and coal gangue disposal in closely spaced coal seams and provide valuable insights for promoting green and efficient mining practices.

papers.title: Numerical simulation and monitoring experiment of liquid injection diffusion range in ionic rare earth ores
papers.summary: Abstract Currently, in-situ leaching is the predominant method for extracting ionic rare earth ores. However, this technique still faces persistent challenges such as low resource utilization efficiency and environmental issues including water and soil contamination. Clarifying the diffusion characteristics of the leach liquid is crucial for addressing these problems. Geophysical methods, particularly conductive electrical techniques, have been widely employed to monitor the diffusion range of the leach liquid. Nevertheless, these methods suffer from limitations such as operational complexity, high costs, and poor timeliness. To overcome these drawbacks, this study first utilizes numerical simulation to determine the influence range of liquid injection, and subsequently evaluates the effectiveness of the high-density resistivity method in delineating its diffusion extent. Based on the deep structural characteristics of a rare earth mine in Fujian, China, identified through high-density resistivity method, a suitable site was selected for a comparative experiment. The experiment compared time-lapse resistivity tomography monitoring with seepage numerical simulations of liquid injection faced actual geological model, and the results demonstrated good consistency in the diffusion ranges identified by both methods. Through theoretical analysis and comparative monitoring results, this study proposes that the integrated approach of “detailed deep structure investigation & seepage numerical simulation of liquid injection” can effectively characterize the diffusion behavior of the leach liquor. This provides theoretical support for the precise placement of injection wells and the design of anti-seepage systems in ionic rare earth mining. contributing to improved mineral recovery rates and reduced environmental pollution from liquid injection.

papers.title: Creep deformation until failure under constant water content in sandy model slope
papers.summary: The measurement of displacement on slopes under excavation or rainfall revealed that the displacement increased not only during excavation or rainfall but also afterward. The increase in displacement after stress loading can be identified as creep displacement under constant stress. However, the conditions for the generation of creep displacements are still unknown. To this end, inclined direct shear tests were conducted under constant stress and rainfall infiltration, and the measured data were analyzed to examine the conditions for creep displacement generation under rainfall infiltration. In some cases, shear displacement grew under constant volumetric water content (VWC) just prior to failure, but not in other cases. In the latter cases, shear displacement grew with increasing VWC. An accelerating increase in shear displacement just prior to failure—referred to as tertiary creep—could be observed in all cases in which shear displacement increased under constant VWC; meanwhile, a decelerating increase in shear displacement just after the start of the constant VWC duration—referred to as primary creep—could not be observed in some cases. The creep displacement normalized by all shear displacements until failure was larger when the increase in VWC corresponding to the shear displacement during soil absorption was greater. Thus, a larger increase in VWC corresponding to shear displacement during the absorption process is a condition for the generation of creep displacement under constant VWC. Primary creep displacement developed under the condition of no normal displacement, indicating a steady state in the shear zone. The primary creep displacement was greater for cases with a higher initial velocity at the start of the constant VWC duration. papers.summary: Introduction Groundwater is the primary dependable freshwater source in the arid coastal catchments of western Saudi Arabia, where natural recharge is limited and occurs mainly through episodic rainfall and flash‐flood infiltration along wadi systems. This study assesses groundwater potential in the Wadi Marwani basin (≈2,347 km 2 ), a major tributary of the Khulais system southeast of Rabigh, by integrating multi‐source remote sensing, GIS, and aeromagnetic data. Aeromagnetic data were reduced to the pole, upward continued, and enhanced using the modified Elliott function (MEF) filter and Center for Exploration Targeting (CET) grid analysis. The integrated groundwater potential map divides the basin into five classes; comparison with existing wells yields an AUC of 0.789, indicating acceptable to good predictive skill. For a 10-year 2-hour return period design storm of 39.7 mm, baseline simulation provided 0.79 runoff coefficient, 14.09 m³/s of peak runoff, and 11,693 m³ of system flooding. Scenarios MIX30 reduced 27.9%, 35.1%, and 59.5% of runoff volume, peak runoff, and flood volume, respectively. papers.title: Context-specific targeting of conservation agriculture reduces short-term yield penalty risk for maize and beans in Rwanda
papers.summary: Context and Objective Soil erosion is a major threat to smallholder farming systems in Rwanda. Terraces, while effective, are costly and reduce cultivable land area. Conservation agriculture (CA) offers a promising complementary practice if short-term yield penalties relative to current tillage (CT) remain acceptable to farmers. We assessed the seasonal and cumulative yield performance of a CA system relative to CT, farmers’ perceptions of soil erosion control under CA, and the site-level conditions under which CA yields remain within farmer-acceptable bounds. Methods A CA system combining reduced tillage, intercropped cover crops, and residue retention in a maize–bean rotation was evaluated over six cropping seasons (three years) across 473 farms in ten agroecological zones of Rwanda. A farmer-informed threshold for acceptable CA yield performance (CA:CT yield ratio ≥ 0.90) was derived from the empirical relationship between observed yield ratios and farmers' stated adoption intentions. Random forest models were used to identify site-level drivers of CA performance, and to inform a targeting approach based on observable field characteristics. Results and conclusions On average, CA yields were 19% lower than CT for maize and 24% lower for beans, yet farmers consistently perceived erosion reduction under CA, highlighting a trade-off between short-term yield penalties and longer-term soil protection. The amount of mulch cover at planting, accumulated rainfall, and weed pressure were the key drivers of CA performance. Site-level targeting increased the probability of achieving acceptable yield performance from 30% to 50%, though only ~20% of sites were initially identified as suitable for CA. Site-level targeting offers a realistic pathway to managing the trade-off between short-term yield penalties and longer-term soil protection benefits of CA. papers.summary: Abstract. Groundwater is the largest store of liquid fresh water, yet because it is hidden beneath the surface, it is primarily understood through models of porous-media flow. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. Consequently, operational models use reduced physics, either by assuming linearity or by using approximate solutions. Here, we introduce a scalable, open-source, three-dimensional solver for variably saturated groundwater flow implemented in G-ADOPT, an automated finite-element platform built on Firedrake. The implementation combines a locally conservative discontinuous Galerkin discretisation, Newton iteration with an exact Jacobian, implicit time integration through the Irksome library, used here with Backward Euler, and vertically lumped multigrid preconditioners designed for the extreme aspect ratios of production scenarios. We verify accuracy, convergence, and strict local mass conservation on two- and three-dimensional benchmarks, and apply the solver to the Lower Murrumbidgee floodplain in New South Wales, Australia. The model covers approximately 30 000 km², contains several hundred million degrees of freedom, and uses public stratigraphic, rainfall, and water-table data. Our scaling experiments show that the effectiveness of the preconditioner is controlled primarily by the physical regime in which the model is integrated. A single-level method (e.g., block-Jacobi ILU(0)) suffices at the short time steps of an infiltration study, but at seasonal time steps, the admissible time step decreases significantly under horizontal refinement. In a near-saturated profile without specific storage, such single-level methods do not converge at any tested step size. papers.title: Hydro-chemical Evolution and Groundwater Quality Dynamics under the Influence of Narmada Canal Irrigation in the Sanchore Region of Jalore District, Rajasthan, India
papers.source: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.summary: Groundwater is the main and last source of water for residential and agricultural use. The present paper deals with the influence of Narmada Canal irrigation system in the dry zone of low rainfall regions of the western Rajasthan namely the Sanchore area of Jalore district on ground water recharge, agricultural development and chemical features of the water. The present study deals with the assessment of hydro-chemical composition and groundwater quality in the command area of canal irrigation. Groundwater samples were collected from selected villages and analyzed for key physicochemical parameters like pH, Electrical Conductivity (EC), Total Dissolved Solids (TDS), Total Hardness (TH), Calcium, Magnesium, Bicarbonate, Chloride, Sulfate, Nitrate and Fluoride using standard analytical methods. The results showed that the Groundwater is generally neutral to slightly alkaline and the dissolved ion concentrations showed significant regional variation due to water-rock interactions, mineral dissolution, evaporation, canal seepage, irrigation return flow and agricultural activities. The results of the study show that the hydro-chemical character of groundwater in the area is controlled by natural geochemical processes and anthropogenic activities. The present study will be helpful in analyzing the groundwater quality, sustainable irrigation, water resource planning and long-term groundwater management in the Narmada Canal command region of western Rajasthan.
