papers.title: Impact of the spatial layout of effective impervious area increments on urban stormwater peak flow and runoff volume
papers.source: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.summary: To reveal the influence mechanism of the layout of effective impervious area (EIA) on urban stormwater processes，a refined stormwater model was constructed，and upstream and downstream sub-catchments were delineated. Taking the Shuangqiaobang runoff plot in Changzhou，Southern Jiangsu，China，as a typical study area，the impact on peak flow and runoff volume were systematically analyzed by setting different scenarios of EIA increments with different locations and scales. Results showed that the location of the EIA，infiltration capacity of the original pervious surface，and rainfall magnitude are key factors affecting the hydrological response. The spatial location effect of newly added EIA is significant，with the growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume in downstream areas being significantly higher than those in upstream areas，showing maximum difference of 18.48% and 7.70% under the moderate-infiltration scenario，respectively. Pervious areas with stronger original infiltration capacity exhibit a greater proportional increase in runoff after conversion to EIA. The growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume tend to decrease with increasing rainfall return period，exhibiting an amplification effect under low-return-period rainfall events. This study provides a scientific basis for optimizing the spatial patterns of underlying surfaces in urban settings and guiding the rational layout of stormwater facilities.

papers.title: Assessment of Fully Polarimetric Biomass Data for Soil Moisture Retrieval
papers.summary: Water management for irrigation is an essential activity especially in agricultural areas or where water is scarce. Water storage in the soil affects the vapour transpiration but also its heat storage capacity, its thermal conductivity and the energy separation between latent and sensible heat fluxes. From a hydrological perspective, soil moisture links the partitioning of rainfall into runoff and infiltration and therefore it has an important role in several ecological applications as flood forecasting, crop yield expectation, meteorological prediction, erosion and slope failure forecasting, water reservoir management, etc. Most of the soil moisture models describe only the bare soil response. In a real scenario, the presence of bare soil is not common as most of the time some kind of vegetation may be found on top. In order to reduce the amount of vegetation responses in addition to the soil moisture estimation longer wavelength can be used. In this study we like to explore the polarimetric and interferometric response of the BIOMASS mission, which operates in P band wavelength. Polarimetry can be used to define the scattering mechanisms and is able, when using decomposition methods to separate the ground and vegetation contribution. To perform this separation a physical model is employed and fully polarimetric data is needed in order to invert for the different involved parameters. It is worth mentioning that for extracting the ground response and the corresponding soil moisture, a significant degree of penetration into vegetation is required. For this reason, SAR soil moisture inversion has traditionally been investigated with L-band. In this study we use quad polarimetry in P band to investigate the sensitivity to bare soil and vegetated soil for soil moisture estimation [R1]. Differential SAR interferometry, a popular technique for measuring displacements of the Earth's surface, is potentially influenced by changes in soil moisture. Different mechanisms for th

papers.title: Urbanization-Induced Shifts in Hydrological Response of a Metropolitan Watershed
papers.source: Khazar Journal of Water and Environment
papers.summary: Rapid urban expansion in semi‑arid metropolitan areas alters hydrological response, yet the shift in the minimum rainfall depth required to initiate surface runoff—the runoff initiation threshold—has received limited quantitative attention. This study assesses this temporal shift in a part of Tehran metropolitan using Landsat‑based land‑use mapping, Random Forest classification in Google Earth Engine, and the SCS‑CN hydrological model. The novelty lies in three aspects: explicitly targeting the runoff initiation threshold as a primary response variable, isolating land‑cover change effects from interannual precipitation variability, and providing a replicable framework for data‑scarce semi‑arid catchments. Impervious surfaces expanded from 38.2% to 64.7% of the study area, while pervious cover declined from 56.8% to 31.2%. Consequently, the runoff initiation threshold decreased from approximately 10 mm to 8 mm, meaning that smaller and more frequent rainfall events now generate surface runoff. Direct runoff depth increased from 282 mm to 314 mm, although annual precipitation varied between 227 mm and 289 mm without a consistent upward trend. The Mann–Kendall test confirmed the statistical significance of these changes at the 95% confidence level. These findings demonstrate that urban expansion has measurably lowered the rainfall threshold for runoff generation, increasing flash flood risk under previously innocuous events. For District 22, low‑impact development interventions—permeable pavements, rain gardens, and infiltration trenches—are recommended, particularly in the intensively developed western and central sectors. The proposed framework can support evidence‑based stormwater management in rapidly growing cities with limited hydrological data.

papers.title: Deciphering morphometric and terrain-driven controls on groundwater recharge and agricultural suitability using geospatial and multivariate modeling
papers.summary: This study presents an integrated assessment of basin morphometry, groundwater recharge potential, and agricultural suitability in the Lower Thamirabarani River Basin, Tamil Nadu, using geospatial datasets and statistical analyses. The morphometric results indicate an elongated basin (Rf = 0.268; Re = 0.584) with a moderate drainage density (1.4 km/km 2 ), reflecting a balanced runoff response and a reduced tendency toward flash flooding. High relief (820 m), steep terrain (17.23%), and a high Melton Ruggedness Number (0.0333) signify strong erosional forces in the western highlands. Flow accumulation analysis shows that 18.7% of the basin experiences concentrated runoff, while curvature mapping identifies concave surfaces that enhance infiltration. Land-use and land-cover mapping indicates agricultural predominance (59.9%) and highlights the influence of expanding settlements on hydrological processes. The Recharge Potential Index (RPI) mapping reveals that moderate recharge zones cover 67.6% of the basin, with high recharge areas primarily located in the eastern floodplains. The Agricultural Suitability Index (ASI) indicates that over half of the basin is of low to moderate suitability, and unsuitable areas coincide with rocky, saline, or steep landscapes. A strong positive correlation exists between ASI and RPI ( R = 0.78, p < 0.001), indicating a close relationship between agricultural potential and groundwater recharge conditions. Principal Component Analysis and Hierarchical Cluster Analysis identify relief-related parameters as the major contributors to spatial variability. The novelty of this study lies in the development of an integrated framework that links basin morphometry, recharge potential, and agricultural suitability, supported by multivariate validation. The results support the prioritization of watersheds, erosion control, and sustainable land and water management practices.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of wicking nonwoven geotextiles embedded in unsaturated soil subgrade
papers.summary: Excess moisture in unsaturated subgrade layers is a primary cause of long-term deterioration in transportation embankments, leading to reduced soil stiffness and degraded performance under environmental and traffic loading. Conventional drainage systems, including traditional geotextiles, are ineffective in partially saturated soils governed by negative pore-water pressures. Recently developed wicking nonwoven geotextiles provide a promising alternative because they transmit water under both saturated and unsaturated conditions through capillary action. This study presents a numerical investigation of transportation embankments incorporating a wicking nonwoven geotextile. A finite element model based on Richards’ equation is developed to simulate unsaturated flow and is validated using laboratory column tests that reproduce soil capillary-rise behavior. The validated model is extended to full-scale embankment simulations to evaluate geotextile performance. The analyses consider two rainfall intensities, moderate and heavy, two soil types (sand with 23.4% silt and sand with 8.8% silt), and installation configurations including single- and multilayer applications. Water content and matric suction distributions are analyzed to quantify geotextile control of moisture migration. Changes in average resilient modulus are estimated using an empirical MEPDG relationship to assess the potential stiffness implications of moisture reduction. Results show that the wicking nonwoven geotextile reduces moisture under unsaturated conditions. The direct wicking depth of a single layer ranges from approximately 10 to 25 cm below its installation level, depending on soil type and embankment location, while the broader VWC influence zone can extend through the full 0.5 m embankment depth. Based on the MEPDG relationship, the estimated average resilient modulus increases by approximately 15% to 70%, indicating the potential benefit of wicking geotextiles for mitigating moisture-related d

papers.title: Data and Code for Delineating grey-green substitution thresholds for climate-resilient highway drainage
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This study defines a substitution index, the share of required grey drainage upsizing that a feasible green footprint can displace, and derives grey-mandatory, hybrid and green-only regimes from hydraulic reliability and life-cycle cost. A weighted 15-model CMIP6 ensemble with non-stationary extreme value fits, station-corrected satellite design rainfall, curve-number runoff and Green-Ampt infiltration were applied to 433 one-kilometer segments of two Chinese expressways. Existing drainage exceeded its reliability target on every segment under all three emissions scenarios.

papers.title: Progress in the Application of Distributed Fiber Optic Sensing Technology for Geohazard Monitoring and Early Warning: Principles, Applications and Development Trends
papers.summary: Driven by intensifying global climate change and anthropogenic engineering activities, geological hazards-such as landslides, rockfalls, debris flows, and land subsidence-exhibit characteristics of high incidence, wide distribution and complex evolutionary processes, thereby imposing more stringent requirements on monitoring and early warning technologies. Distributed Fiber Optic Sensing (DFOS) technology has emerged as a pivotal development direction in geohazard monitoring, owing to its distinct advantages, including long-distance continuous measurement, high spatial resolution, immunity to electromagnetic interference, and multi-physical-field collaborative sensing capabilities. This paper provides a systematic review of the fundamental principles and primary technical categories of DFOS, followed by an analysis of their respective characteristics and engineering applicability. Concurrently, research progress in DFOS is comprehensively summarized across three key dimensions: laboratory physical model testing, field engineering monitoring, and intelligent early warning systems. Furthermore, integrating current engineering practices, the inherent limitations and critical challenges confronting DFOS are discussed. An outlook is also presented on its deep integration with multi-source monitoring technologies (such as GNSS, InSAR, and LiDAR) alongside emerging technologies including artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and smart disaster prevention. Looking forward, DFOS is poised to gradually establish an integrated full-process monitoring and early warning framework encompassing “continuous sensing, intelligent analysis, risk prediction, and decision support,” ultimately providing more precise, efficient, and intelligent technical support for the hazard risk mitigation of major geological hazards.

papers.title: Climate-Informed Integrated Assessment of Flood and Landslide Susceptibility Using Spatially Validated Machine Learning in a Humid Mountainous Watershed
papers.summary: Future flood–landslide maps support engineering decisions by distinguishing persistent spatial priorities from changes sensitive to modelling assumptions. An integrated framework combines statistically downscaled precipitation with random forest (RF), boosted regression trees (BRT) and support vector machines (SVM) in the Tajan watershed, northern Iran. Nested spatial cross-validation is complemented by geomorphic assessment and historical evaluation of climatic inputs. Four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) cover 2024–2054 and 2055–2085, alongside four prescribed land-use experiments. Using mean annual maximum five-day precipitation ( Rx5day ), RF achieved mean outer-fold areas under the receiver operating characteristic ( ROC ) curve ( AUC ) of 0.928 for floods and 0.832 for landslides; an independently constructed geomorphic flood index (GFI) achieved AUC = 0.904. Across eight nominal futures, relative to 1985–2014, high/very-high flood susceptibility area increased by 4.38–4.96% and threshold-defined spatial overlap (Both) by 2.68–3.33%. High/very-high landslide area decreased by 6.31–15.39%, but this direction reversed when mean annual precipitation ( MAP ) replaced Rx5day , identifying descriptor dependence rather than established hazard reduction. Both area increased under all nine local threshold pairs and all eight tests transferring the full 2015–2023 simulated–observed discrepancy (full stress); combined land-use changes offset the nominal increase in two of four near-future cases. Road length in high/very-high flood classes increased by 23.84–24.67% nominally, but full-stress changes ranged from −3.85% to +15.30%. Settlement counts within Both increased in all eight full-stress cases. The Both category represents spatial co-susceptibility, not cascades or calibrated joint probability. The framework separates persistent screening priorities from input-dependent exposure changes, supporting targeted drainage, road-crossing and slope assessments.

papers.title: Displacement Increment Isosurface-Based Local Factor of Safety Method Considering Shear-Tensile Coupling for Slope Stability Analysis
papers.summary: Slope stability evaluation is essential for geotechnical hazard prevention and engineering safety design. Conventional factor of safety (FS) methods provide effective overall stability assessments but cannot adequately describe local progressive failure processes. This study developed a shear-tensile coupled local factor of safety (LFS) method based on displacement increment isosurfaces to address two limitations of existing LFS approaches: interference from cumulative displacement in sliding-zone identification and neglect of tensile failure. Potential sliding zones were identified by iteratively adjusting the maximum principal strain increment threshold until the extracted localization regions showed substantial spatial agreement with concentrated displacement increment isosurfaces. The shear local factor of safety (SLFS) and tensile local factor of safety (TLFS) were formulated using the Mohr-Coulomb criterion and the maximum principal stress criterion, respectively, and the smaller value was taken as the governing LFS. The global FS was then obtained through stress-weighted aggregation of elements within the identified potential sliding zone. The method was evaluated using the Extra11 benchmark slope, the Fengtongshan landslide, and the three-dimensional ZFDC engineering slope. The dual sliding-surface mechanism of the Baiyi landslide and the reinforcement performance of the ZFDC slope were further examined. The results showed that displacement increment isosurfaces reduced the influence of preceding deformation and boundary constraints on potential sliding-zone identification. The proposed LFS formulation captured both shear yielding and tensile cracking and described the progressive development of local instability. The calculated global FS agreed well with conventional limit equilibrium methods, with relative differences generally below 7%. The proposed method provides a unified framework for local and global stability evaluation of complex slopes.

papers.title: How Does Forest Litter Extraction Commonly Used in the Past Affect the Runoff Reaction to Heavy Rainfalls?
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Until the middle of the 20th century, organic material was removed from the forest floor in Central Europe and used as bedding in the stables. The mixture of excrements and organic material was finally spread as fertilizer on the fields. The presented study aims at quantifying the hydrological effect of this historical extraction practise, also called litter raking, at extreme rainfall events. We measured surface runoff before and after such an intervention at four experimental plots simulating a rainfall intensity of 100 mm/h. Additionally, soil moisture has been recorded continuously on the plots with litter extraction and nearby control plots. The results of the rainfall simulation campaigns were as follows: One of the four experimental plots, which already produced a high amount of surface runoff without litter extraction, reacted with an increase of the surface runoff coefficient from 0.49 to 0.63 following this intervention. Another plot showed a slight reaction after litter extraction, with an increase of the surface runoff coefficient from 0.01 to 0.16, and on two plots there was hardly any reaction. After almost a year, the surface runoff that occurred after the intervention had already decreased again. The removal of ground vegetation and reduction of organic layers' thickness by litter raking causes faster changes in soil moisture and a more pronounced short‐term response. Combining the different results of this study reveals a complex interplay of precipitation type, organic layers properties, its system status and the characteristics of the underlying mineral soil, which all together also controls the occurrence and intensity of surface runoff.

papers.title: Quantifying macroporosity and preferential flow variations in soil under rice and wheat cultivation
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract Soil macropores play a vital role in movement of water in agricultural fields, yet their spatial and structural dynamics under intensive crop rotation systems remain poorly quantified. This study investigates the contrasting effects of rice‐wheat cultivation on soil hydraulic properties, macropore function, and preferential flow dynamics. Field experiments were conducted post‐harvest of rice and wheat crops at an agricultural plot in IIT Kanpur. Dye‐tracer experiments were performed for visual confirmation of preferential flow. Tension disc and double ring infiltrometer measurements were taken at six different locations at 3 depths (10, 25, and 50 cm). The parameters for matrix ( and ) and macropore ( ) domains were estimated. Wheat soil exhibited significant difference depth‐wise in infiltration rate (). Critically, the steady‐state flux at 25 cm was 77.53% greater, indicating the sporadic activation of deep, high‐capacity macropores within a restrictive layer. No significant depth‐wise variation was observed in parameters under rice cropping (). Matrix parameters were significantly higher under wheat when compared to rice (mean: cm h −1 , cm −1 for rice; 24.26 cm h −1 , for wheat) and showed significant depth‐wise variation at 25 and 50 cm. This trend confirms the restorative and deep‐reaching effect of the wheat root system on pore continuity and subsoil structural stability. The findings emphasize that preferential flow under rice and wheat cultivation is dynamic and crop‐dependent, governed by alternating phases of structural degradation and recovery.

papers.title: Spatial and vertical variability of soil physico‐hydraulic properties and subsurface lithology in the Upper Indus Plain of Pakistan
papers.summary: Abstract Accurate characterization of soil physico‐hydraulic properties is critical for irrigation and drainage design, solute transport, soil–water–plant, and rainfall–runoff relationships. However, spatially representative datasets for these properties remain limited for the Indus Basin of Pakistan, where hydrological studies often rely on generalized parameters derived from other regions, introducing uncertainties in model‐based assessments. This study presents a basin‐scale integrated assessment of soil texture, bulk density, infiltration behavior, and soil moisture retention characteristics covering the Upper Indus Plain of Pakistan. Field‐based in situ measurements were conducted at 66 spatially distributed sites across four doabs (area between the two rivers) at surface, 0.5‐m, and 1.0‐m depths. An integrated methodological framework was employed, combining hydrometer analysis for soil texture, improved double‐ring infiltrometer tests for infiltration, pressure‐plate extractor for soil water retention, oven‐dried weight for bulk density, and resistivity survey for subsurface lithological assessment. Infiltration datasets were analyzed using the Horton and Philip cumulative infiltration models, while soil water retention behavior was quantified using hanging water column and pressure plate methods and parameterized using the van Genuchten model. Results indicate that the Horton infiltration model outperformed the Philip model for estimation of cumulative infiltration. Silty clay loam, sandy loam, and silt loam are the dominant texture classes. The soil with infiltration rates up to 30 mm/h remain predominant across the study area. This study provides robust and accurate baseline datasets along with an integrated methodological framework to support basin‐scale improved hydrological modeling, flood simulations, recharge estimation, and effective water resource management.

papers.title: GIS-Based Morphometric Analysis and Hydrological Assessment of the Hor Al-Shuwaicha Drainage Basins, Eastern Iraq
papers.summary: This study presents a comprehensive quantitative morphometric analysis of the five drainage basins of Hor Al-Shuwaicha in eastern Iraq, which cover a total area of 22,245.54 km². Previous morphometric studies have primarily focused on three basins (Torsaq, Shosharin, and Galal Badra), the morphometric characteristics of the entire drainage system insufficiently characterized. A 30 m Digital Elevation Model was processed using Geographic Information System techniques to delineate watershed boundaries and extract the drainage network, followed by the calculation of twenty-one linear, areal, and relief morphometric parameters using standard equations. The seventh-order stream represents the highest stream order. The Sayed Ghazal Basin exhibits the highest basin relief and a drainage intensity of 0.41, suggesting that rugged topography may enhance drainage. In contrast, the lowest drainage intensity (0.38) in the Galal Badra Basin suggests lower drainage response and potential temporary surface-water accumulation, which may contribute to localized flooding in some areas. Drainage density analysis reveals that the Shosharin Basin exhibits the highest drainage density (1.15 km/km²), indicating a potentially greater tendency for rapid surface runoff. Whereas the Mandaly Basin, with the lowest drainage density (1.09 km/km²), indicates relatively higher groundwater recharge potential. Furthermore, drainage texture ranges from very coarse to fine, while the form factor, circularity ratio, and elongation ratio consistently indicate predominantly elongated basin geometry, suggesting a potentially lower tendency for rapid concentration of runoff. These findings provide quantitative morphometric evidence that can support preliminary flood-hazard assessment and groundwater-recharge evaluation.

papers.title: Landslides: Challenges and Mitigation Strategies
papers.source: Journal of Mechanical Civil and Industrial Engineering
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards worldwide, causing extensive financial and human losses and destroying natural resources annually. Therefore, comprehensive investigation of these hazards is an unavoidable requirement for future human life. A landslide is a natural disaster that claims human and animal victims every year. In addition to loss of life, landslides cause millions of dollars in financial damage globally. According to NASA records, the highest numbers of landslides occurred in Brazil, India, China, Peru, Afghanistan, Nepal, Indonesia, and the Philippines between 1900 and 2011, resulting in heavy human and financial losses (USGS, 2014). A landslide is the movement of a portion of earth materials and is a general term for the downward movement of rock fragments and detached masses under the influence of gravity. This process operates on sloping lands and may cause the destruction of houses and facilities, blockage of roads and rivers, and in some cases, when its volume is enormous, it can create a disaster. Afghanistan, due to its high mountains, rugged relief, severe physical erosion, and its location in the Mediterranean–Indonesian seismic belt—especially in the central and northeastern regions—has a high potential for fall and landslide processes. The present study aims to identify the types of landslides, their triggering factors, control methods, and mitigation strategies. This research employs a library-based methodology, including descriptive and analytical approaches. The findings indicate that recognizing the type of landslide and its triggering factors is the first and most important step in reducing associated risks. Furthermore, the implementation of geotechnical, physical, and biotechnical measures can significantly mitigate landslide hazards. The study concludes with recommendations for relevant authorities to allocate specific budgets for landslide hazard assessment and mitigation across Afghanistan.

papers.title: Integrated Drought Vulnerability Assessment and Mapping of Bangalore City, India
papers.summary: Drought vulnerability mapping is essential for understanding the spatial distribution of water scarcity and its associated socio-environmental impacts. The present study assesses the overall drought vulnerability of Bangalore urban district, Karnataka, India, through an integrated approach combining the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Geographic Information System. Four thematic components: meteorological, agricultural, hydrological and socio-economic were selected, standardized and weighted using AHP to develop individual and composite vulnerability maps. The key meteorological parameters included land surface temperature (25.9-29.4°C), specific humidity (9.51-11.5 g/kg) and evaporation (1,490 -1,690 mm/year). Agricultural factors comprised of soil type, soil texture, NDVI (-0.18 to 0.50), curvature, land use/land cover and crop area (123-170 sq.km). Hydrological parameters included elevation (793- 1,003 m), slope, aspect and groundwater level (3.24- 16.0 m bgl). Socio-economic factors involved agricultural dependency (19.4-27.9%), groundwater use (33-50.5%), population density and poverty level (14.5-19.1%). The final Drought Vulnerability Index (DVI) ranged from 0.227 to 0.722, classified into five categories from very low to very high. ROC-AUC validation confirmed strong model reliability, with individual AUC values of 0.873 (meteorological), 0.856 (agricultural), 0.882 (hydrological), 0.842 (socio-economic) and an overall DVI AUC of 0.894, indicating an accuracy of about 89.4%. The results highlight that northern and northeastern zones exhibit high vulnerability due to elevated temperature, reduced vegetation and groundwater depletion, while southern and central regions show moderate to low risk. This integrated approach provides a comprehensive spatial framework for drought management and adaptive planning in rapidly urbanizing regions.

papers.title: An Integrated GIS and Machine Learning-based Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Wayanad District, Kerala, India
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in the Western Ghats, frequently causing substantial loss of life, infrastructure damage and environmental degradation. Wayanad District, Kerala, is particularly vulnerable because of its rugged topography, intense monsoon rainfall and complex geological conditions. This study presents an integrated Geographic Information System (GIS) and machine learning framework for landslide susceptibility mapping using Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) models. A total of 800 historical landslide inventory points and eleven landslide conditioning factors including elevation, slope, aspect, rainfall, Topographic Wetness Index (TWI), geology, geomorphology, land use/land cover (LULC), lineament density, distance to roads and NDVI, were employed to develop the predictive models. The dataset was divided into a 70:30 training-testing ratio and model performance was evaluated using fivefold cross-validation, confusion matrices, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Cohen's Kappa and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). Among the evaluated models, LightGBM achieved the highest predictive performance, with an Accuracy of 96.11%, Precision of 94.62%, Recall of 97.78%, F1-score of 96.17%, ROC-AUC of 0.961, Cohen's Kappa of 92.22% and MCC of 92.30%, outperforming XGBoost and Random Forest. Feature importance and SHAP analyses identified rainfall (23.5%), slope (20.8%) and TWI (15.4%) as the most influential conditioning factors governing landslide occurrence. The susceptibility outputs of the three models were integrated to generate a final landslide susceptibility map, classified into Very Low, Low, Moderate, High and Very High susceptibility zones. The integrated model effectively reduced prediction uncertainty and showed strong agreement with historical landslide locations. The proposed GIS-integrated ensemble

papers.title: Water stable isotopes reveal the ecohydrological importance of stemflow infiltration for mature and juvenile European beech
papers.summary: Stemflow of forest trees can contribute a significant fraction of water to forest's water fluxes; however, it is still unclear whether and to what extent trees and their neighbours use stemflow for water uptake and supply. We applied deuterium-enriched stemflow equivalent to a 23-mm throughfall event to adult Fagus sylvatica trees to trace stemflow through the soil and trees. We continuously measured in situ water stable isotopes in soil and xylem water and destructively sampled xylem water in the crowns of adult labelled, nonlabelled F. sylvatica and nonlabelled Picea abies, complemented by destructive xylem water sampling of neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica. Stemflow water supported up to 5.7 ± 2.1% of daily sap flux of adult F. sylvatica trees labelled at the stem base and was detectable in xylem water for several weeks. In the soil, deuterium-enriched stemflow was present at a maximum distance of 0.40 m from the labelled tree. Moreover, nonlabelled juvenile trees within a distance of 2 m showed uptake of labelled water, indicating rooting into soil compartments affected by stemflow. We demonstrate the importance of stemflow as a water source for both adult and neighbouring juvenile F. sylvatica, even when soil water is not limiting.

papers.title: AMFP-based probabilistic risk assessment of unsaturated slopes under stochastic rainfall
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall-induced landslides pose a significant threat to infrastructure and safety. Traditional deterministic approaches and many probabilistic methods are limited in their ability to evaluate the cumulative risk induced by multiple rainfall events over a specified time horizon. This study proposes a novel probabilistic framework to assess the average maximum failure probability (AMFP) of unsaturated soil slopes over a given exposure period ( T ) under multiple stochastic rainfall. The framework integrates rainfall randomness, geotechnical uncertainty, and unsaturated hydro–mechanical coupling, while addressing key challenges related to exposure-period aggregation and computational efficiency. The dependence structure between rainfall duration and intensity, including long-tail characteristics of extremes, is modeled using a Frank Copula based on historical rainfall data. Coupled seepage–stability simulations are implemented in FLAC3D through customized FISH scripting. To enable large-scale Monte Carlo analysis, a high-accuracy Support Vector Regression (SVR) surrogate model is constructed to replace computationally expensive numerical simulations. Application to a homogeneous slope in Baotou, China, indicates that the AMFP increases monotonically with exposure duration, rising from 2.52% ( T = 0.5 year) to 3.08% ( T = 5 years), demonstrating cumulative amplification of failure risk under stochastic rainfall. For T = 1 year (34 rainfall events), the AMFP is 2.69%, corresponding to a reliability index of 1.927. Sensitivity analysis shows that rainfall duration and intensity exert comparable influences on failure probability, while soil strength parameters remain the dominant controlling factors. By linking stochastic rainfall occurrence with exposure-period-based extreme response, the proposed framework provides a rigorous and computationally efficient tool for time-dependent slope reliability assessment and risk-informed engineering decision-making.

papers.title: Modelling the Impact of Initial Water Content on Sorptivity and β Parameters of the Cumulative Infiltration Curve
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Cumulative infiltration is a key factor for the accurate determination of the soil water balance. The 1D QEI model, which incorporates the hydraulic conductivity, K , for initial ( θ i ) and saturated ( θ s ) volumetric water contents the sorptivity, S , and the β parameter, has become a popular formulation to simulate the cumulative infiltration curve. However, given the complexity of estimating S and β for variable values of the hydrological studies tend to rely on infiltration measurements conducted under dry initial soil conditions, often overlooking how initial water content affects the shape of the infiltration curve. To address this issue, this work proposes two simple empirical functions (PTF) relating both S and β to Δ θ . These PTF, which were developed based on the corresponding analytical solutions for S and β , were applied to different values of Δ θ and six synthetic soils with textures ranging from loamy sand to clay. Keeping θ s constant, increasing values of θ i , from the residual water content, θ r , to θ s , were evaluated. The numerical consistency of the new models was evaluated by comparing the cumulative infiltration curves generated by applying the analytical solutions and the proposed PTFs to the QEI function for different soil textural characteristics and Δ θ values against the corresponding simulations performed with HYDRUS‐1D. The results demonstrated that θ i significantly influences the cumulative infiltration curve. While linear relationships passing through the origin ( R 2 = 0.99; p < 0.001) were observed between S 2 and Δ θ , asymptotic growth functions characterized the relationships between β and Δ θ ( R 2 = 0.99, p < 0.001). Excellent fits were also found between the HYDRUS‐1D simulations for increasing values of Δ θ and those generated with the QEI model using both the analytical solutions and the proposed PTF approaches. The results suggest that θ i must be considered in infiltration models to ensure the accuracy of h

papers.title: Physics-Informed Multimodal Graph-Temporal Network with Agentic Hydro-Mechanical Verification for Dynamic Slope Stability Prediction under Rainfall-Vegetation-Soil Coupling
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Overview Rainfall-induced shallow landslides on vegetated slopes are governed by nonlinear feedbacks among canopy interception, root water uptake, capillary hysteresis, and moisture-dependent root tensile reinforcement. Purely data-driven sequence models frequently violate water mass conservation and matric suction monotonicity during convective cloudbursts, whereas static soft-penalty physics-informed neural networks overlook drying-wetting retention loops, near-saturation root-soil slippage, and preferential macropore bypass. We present PIM-RVSNet, a physics-informed multimodal graph-temporal network coupled with an agentic hydro-mechanical equilibrium verifier for dynamic Factor of Safety (F_s(t)) and instability lead-time prediction. PIM-RVSNet integrates three irreducible mechanisms: a Multimodal Cross-Scale Eco-Hydrological Encoder (MC-EHE) using multi-head Depth-Directed Eco-Hydrological Cross-Attention (DEH-CA) and vertical soil-horizon graph-recurrent message passing to align atmospheric forcing, depth-specific canopy-root traits, and four-layer soil profiles; a Differentiable Richards-Wu-Mohr-Coulomb Coupled Operator (RWMC-Op) embedding scanning-curve van Genuchten hysteresis and saturation-attenuated root cohesion; and an Agentic Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Verifier (AHM-Verifier) that audits mass-balance drift, preferential bypass, and stress admissibility to iteratively recalibrate upper-boundary infiltration partitioning within at most three reflexion steps. Across 48 monitored slope units and 240 storm episodes (2,880 space-time states across four eco-geomorphic zones), PIM-RVSNet achieves a test coefficient of determination R^2 of 0.9514 ± 0.0028, RMSE_F_s of 0.1106 ± 0.0032, critical instability F1_crit of 0.8967 ± 0.0168, and a physical violation rate of 1.42 ± 0.41%, outperforming the strongest physics-informed baseline (R^2 = 0.9158 ± 0.0032, p_Holm = 1.24 × 10^-13) and extending mean pre-onset early-warning lead time from 2.15 h to 3.98 h. Cont

papers.title: Laboratory-scale LID infrastructure schemes for highly polluted urban stormwater runoff improvement: setup and initial testing
papers.summary: Urban stormwater runoff in highly polluted environments contains elevated concentrations of nutrients, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, as well as chemical oxygen demand (COD), posing significant challenges to environmental water quality. This study investigates the laboratory-scale setup and efficiency of three low-impact development (LID) systems, namely, rain gardens, filter strips, and vegetated swales, for treating synthetic stormwater mimicking highly polluted urban runoff. Experiments were conducted under controlled hydraulic loading rates (HLRs) and pollutant concentrations to evaluate pollutant removal efficiency. Rain gardens, constructed with layered engineered media, including sand, compost, and iron-enhanced biochar, achieved the highest pollutant removal, with average reductions of 70% for total phosphorus (TP), 65% for nitrate-N (NO₃⁻-N), and 85% for COD. Vegetated filter strips achieved moderate nutrient reductions of 45% for TP and 40% for NO₃⁻-N, and 60% for COD. Vegetated swales achieved average reductions of 60% for TP, 55% for NO₃⁻-N, and 65% for COD. The research compares the pollutant removal performance of three LID prototype types under controlled laboratory high-pollution conditions, while recognising that differences in media composition, vegetation, and hydraulic behaviour were not independently evaluated. The rain garden prototype demonstrated the highest overall pollutant removal efficiency, while the swale and filter strip showed comparatively lower performance under the tested conditions. These results suggest that combining different LID types in a treatment train may enhance overall system performance, particularly for pollutants such as dissolved organic nitrogen and COD in highly polluted runoff. The novelty of this study lies in the controlled laboratory comparison of multiple LID typologies under highly polluted conditions representative of poorly serviced urban environments, for which limited experimental data currently ex

papers.title: Reliability analysis of soil-rock composite slopes based on dimensionality reduction response surface method
papers.summary: To address the “curse of dimensionality” caused by high-dimensional parameters and the computational bottlenecks of 3D numerical simulations in the reliability evaluation of “overlying silty clay and underlying weathered mylonite” composite strata slopes, a reliability analysis framework combining 2D limit-equilibrium screening and a response-surface surrogate constructed from quasi-3D FLAC3D simulations is proposed. First, by combining the limit equilibrium method with an orthogonal experiment and multivariate analysis of variance (ANOVA), the 9-dimensional random variable space is reduced, identifying the cohesion, internal friction angle, and unit weight of the moderately weathered mylonite as the dominant parameters. Secondly, based on the equivalent continuum assumption for the fractured weathered rock mass, a quasi-3D finite-difference model implemented in FLAC3D is constructed, which demonstrates the progressive development of a deep-seated rotational failure mechanism in the composite slope. According to this, a second-order response surface surrogate model with a coefficient of determination R 2 = 0.9990 is developed using the Box–Behnken Design (BBD), which effectively captures the nonlinear coupling effects among the controlling parameters. Lastly, 100,000 Monte Carlo simulations using truncated-normal input distributions yield a baseline slope failure probability of 2.767% and an equivalent reliability index of 1.916. A Gaussian-Copula sensitivity analysis further shows that the estimated failure probability is influenced by the assumed dependence between cohesion and internal friction angle. The results demonstrate that probabilistic parameter variability can produce a non-negligible failure risk even when the deterministic mean - value condition gives F o S > 1.0 . This dimensionality-reduction response-surface framework provides an efficient approach for the probabilistic reliability assessment of heterogeneous Soil-Rock composite slopes.

papers.title: Soil erosion susceptibility modeling using stacking ensemble machine learning, Kangra District, north-western Himalaya, India
papers.summary: The present study aims to predict soil erosion-prone regions in Kangra District using ML algorithms; Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost and CatBoost and their stacking ensembles. Additionally, the study also utilizes the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) model to enhance the interpretability of the best-performing RF algorithm. For this, a comprehensive soil erosion point dataset was developed using empirical field survey integrated with visual interpretation of Google Earth historical images. The results show RF as the best-performing model, predicting 14.7% of the area into the very high susceptibility zone, followed by XGBoost (27.1%), SVM (24.4%) and CatBoost (16.4%), whereas the stacking ensemble predicted 25.2%. The SHAP analysis of the best-performing model (RF) indicates NDVI, slope and LULC as the primary governing factors influencing soil erosion in the region. This study also provides a scientific base for policy formulation and strategic planning to mitigate soil erosion in Kangra District.

papers.title: When anticipation fails: A forensic analysis of Tropical Cyclone Ditwah reveals whole-system performance limits in a small-island flood-risk system
papers.summary: Abstract. Tropical Cyclone (TC) Ditwah, which impacted Sri Lanka in November 2025, was one of the most damaging hydrometeorological disasters in the country's recent history, affecting more than two million people through widespread flooding and landslides. Early explanations attributed the disaster to failures in forecasting, reservoir operations, or institutional response. We argue instead that TC Ditwah revealed a breakdown in whole-system performance under extreme temporal stress. Using a forensic reconstruction spanning atmospheric evolution, hydrological response, reservoir operations, warning dissemination, institutional coordination, and community experience, we examine how multiple interconnected subsystems interacted during the event. Rapid cyclogenesis unusually close to Sri Lanka compressed forecast lead times, while the island's steep, rainfall-dominated catchments translated extreme rainfall into rapid flood responses across multiple basins. Reservoir preparedness, warning escalation, institutional decision processes, and community response operated on slower timescales, reducing the time available to convert anticipation into protective action. The resulting mismatch between fast physical processes and slower institutional and societal response generated an anticipation–action gap, despite the availability of hazard information. Rather than revealing isolated component failures, TC Ditwah exposed structural limitations in the design and operation of coupled flood-risk systems. We argue that improving forecasts alone is unlikely to substantially reduce future disaster risk unless forecasting, reservoir management, emergency governance, and community response are explicitly integrated into coordinated operational frameworks. More broadly, TC Ditwah illustrates the need to complement advances in prediction with simulation-based training, pre-defined decision protocols, and whole-system emergency operating modes capable of functioning under rapidly evolvi

papers.title: Forest and rangeland promote infiltration and minimize runoff: A water-balance-based approach using SWAT
Replication code for: Physics-Informed Multimodal Graph-Temporal Network with Agentic Hydro-Mechanical Verification for Dynamic Slope Stability Prediction under Rainfall-Vegetation-Soil Coupling
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Overview Reference implementation and evaluation pipeline for PIM-RVSNet, a physics-informed multimodal graph-temporal network with agentic hydro-mechanical verification for dynamic slope stability prediction under rainfall–vegetation–soil coupling. The package implements all three components described in the article: the Multimodal Cross-Scale Eco-Hydrological Encoder (MC-EHE, C1) with Depth-Directed Eco-Hydrological Cross-Attention and vertical soil-horizon graph-recurrent message passing; the Differentiable Richards–Wu–Mohr–Coulomb Coupled Operator (RWMC-Op, C2) with van Genuchten scanning hysteresis and moisture-attenuated Wu–Waldron root cohesion; and the Agentic Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Verifier (AHM-Verifier, C3) built from MassBalanceAudit, MacroporeBypassDetector, and SuctionEquilibriumCheck. Reference implementations of all competing baselines and the full metric suite (R², RMSEFs, MAEFs, RMSEψ, F1crit, AUROC, failure warning lead time, physical consistency violation rate, water mass-balance error, and Holm–Bonferroni paired tests) are included. Contents PathDescription pim_rvsnet/model.pyMC-EHE encoder (DEH-CA cross-attention, horizon graph-recurrent block) and the full PIMRVSNet architecture. pim_rvsnet/physics_operators.pyRWMC-Op differentiable coupled operator: conductivity-capped infiltration, root water uptake sink, scanning-curve hysteresis, saturation-attenuated root cohesion, infinite-slope Mohr–Coulomb equilibrium. pim_rvsnet/agent_verifier.pyAHM-Verifier and its three diagnostic tools, with bounded reflexion over upper-boundary partitioning. pim_rvsnet/baselines.pyReference implementations of the six competing baseline architectures and trainable-parameter accounting. pim_rvsnet/metrics.pyEvaluation metrics, failure warning lead time, physical violation accounting, and paired significance testing. reproduce.pyDeterministic evaluation entry point; regenerates every derived table from the deposited benchmark observations and prediction series.

papers.title: X‐Ray CT Analysis of Soil Pore Structure, Connectivity and Hydraulic Responses to Micro‐Nanobubble Aerated Drip Irrigation
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Soil pore network architecture is fundamental to rhizosphere functioning. This study employed high‐resolution X‐ray computed tomography (CT) to quantify rhizosphere pore structure, spatial distribution, connectivity and hydraulic function in greenhouse tomato across two consecutive growing seasons (S1 and S2) under five micro‐nanobubble (MNB) aeration scheduling treatments: nonaerated control (CK), early aeration (AE), reproductive aeration (AR), late aeration (AL) and continuous aeration (AC). CT‐derived parameters included void ratio, pore morphology, nearest neighbour index (NNI), fractal dimension, absolute permeability and pore‐throat characteristics. AC produced the greatest improvements in the void ratio and pore area across both seasons. AR recorded the highest pore count in Season 1 (1.45 × 10 5 ) and NNI in Season 2 (6.9), indicating concentrated root–bubble interactions during peak oxygen demand. At the end of S1 and S2, the absolute permeability under AC was 8.6 and 18.9 μm 2 , respectively, compared with 4.3 and 0.7 μm 2 under CK. Because CT sampling was destructive and different soil blocks were collected at the end of each season, these values represent season‐specific cross‐sectional contrasts rather than longitudinal changes in the same soil core. Overall, growth‐stage MNB aeration was associated with distinct end‐of‐season rhizosphere pore‐network characteristics, supporting precision oxygen management in greenhouse SDI systems.

papers.title: Machine Learning and GIS-Integrated Framework for Irrigation Water Quality Index (IWQI) Mapping and Hydrochemical Clustering in an Algerian Semi-Arid Watershed
papers.summary: Abstract In the Ain Temouchent region, surface water is severely limited, leaving groundwater as the primary source for both domestic supply and agricultural irrigation. This study evaluates the suitability of El Melah watershed groundwater for irrigation by computing the Irrigation Water Quality Index (IWQI) following the Meireles approach, mapping its spatial distribution through GIS, and complementing the analysis with two machine learning methods: (i) a Random Forest (RF) model with Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) and SHAP explainability analysis to identify the dominant drivers of IWQI degradation; and (ii) K-means and hierarchical clustering to delineate hydrochemical facies and provide a statistically grounded alternative to the conventional Wilcox diagram. Salinity is elevated throughout the study area (EC: 1,034–5,010 µS cm⁻¹). The RF model achieved LOOCV R² = 0.61, with Na⁺ and EC confirmed as the dominant IWQI degradation drivers by SHAP analysis. Hierarchical clustering resolved three hydrochemical facies: a Ca²⁺-HCO₃⁻ continental group, a Na⁺-Cl⁻ evaporite-influenced group, and a seawater-intrusion group, all confirmed as statistically distinct by one-way ANOVA (p < 0.05). Overall, groundwater quality in the watershed ranges from moderate to severe restriction for irrigation use, with the northern sector most critically affected by marine infiltration.

papers.title: Erosion-resistance mechanisms of biopolymer-vegetation reinforced slopes under rainfall using experimental and coupled CFD-DEM methods
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced surface erosion poses persistent threats to the stability of highway slopes, causing significant economic losses and ecological degradation worldwide. This study investigates the combined effects of biopolymer (Xanthan gum) and vegetation (Festuca arundinacea) on rainfall-induced surface erosion through rainfall simulation experiments and CFD-DEM numerical simulations. Nine treatment combinations of biopolymer dosage (0-0.5%) and vegetation density (0-60 g·m-2) were tested under three rainfall intensities. Biopolymer and vegetation exerted opposing hydrological effects, with biopolymer increasing surface runoff by up to 17% while vegetation reduced it by 19%-42% through root-enhanced infiltration. Their combination reduced cumulative erosion by 93.1% relative to bare soil, and the relative contribution of biopolymer-vegetation interaction to erosion resistance rose from 13.9% to 24.1% with increasing rainfall intensity. Numerical simulations revealed that untreated slopes developed a positive feedback between porosity growth (0.44 to 0.58) and flow velocity increase (0.37 to 0.52 m·s⁻¹), driving progressive erosion escalation. Biopolymer bonding sustained inter-particle contact forces five times greater than untreated counterparts at stabilization, and the coordination number of the combined treatment reached 2.48 at stabilization, 34% higher than bare soil, confirming superior preservation of contact network integrity. These findings provide mechanistic insight into biopolymer-vegetation synergistic slope protection for transportation infrastructure.

papers.title: Integrating geoinformatics and high-resolution soil water retention data for fine-scale desertification sensitivity mapping of the Oued-Sakni sub-catchment, Cheliff-Zahrez hydrographic Basin, Algeria
papers.summary: Introduction This study presents a large-scale, quantitative assessment of desertification sensitivity in the Oued-Sakni sub-catchment (SCOS), a representative unit of the steppe belt of central Algeria. Although the region’s vulnerability to land degradation has been noted in earlier national-scale surveys, its spatial pattern had not previously been mapped at a resolution fine enough to support local management decisions. Methods Geoinformatics and remote-sensing techniques were combined within the MEDALUS (Mediterranean Desertification and Land Use) framework to delineate Environmentally Sensitive Areas (ESAs). The Environmental Sensitivity Area Index (ESAI) was computed as the geometric mean of four thematic indices — the Soil Quality Index (SQI), Climate Quality Index (CQI), Vegetation Quality Index (VQI) and Management Quality Index (MQI) — each built from natural and anthropogenic layers that together describe the land’s susceptibility to degradation. To offset the scarcity of local, high-resolution soil survey data, a methodological adaptation was introduced: soil depth and texture were substituted with high-resolution Volumetric Water Retention (VWR) data drawn from the World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) database. Land cover, the most dynamic of the four inputs, was mapped independently through a Random Forest (RF) classifier trained on Sentinel-2 imagery within Google Earth Engine, achieving an overall accuracy of 86.2% and a Kappa coefficient of 0.823, which gives the vegetation and management layers an empirical grounding rarely available in comparable steppe studies. Results and discussion The results show that the SCOS sub-catchment is highly vulnerable to desertification: critical areas cover 43.6% of the total surface, fragile areas 49.2%, and only 7.2% is classed as potentially sensitive. These figures place the SCOS among the more severely affected steppe catchments reported in the recent regional literature. The resulting ESA maps constitute a

papers.title: Post‐Mining Conservation Measures for Erosion Control: A Global Assessment of Their Effectiveness on Runoff and Soil Erosion Reduction
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Mining activities severely disturb land surfaces and hydrological processes, intensifying hillslope erosion and soil loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of post‐mining restoration measures and identify the factors regulating their performance, we compiled a global dataset of runoff and soil erosion yield from 58 studies spanning multiple mine types, climatic zones, and restoration practices, and conducted a weighted meta‐analysis using random‐effects models. Overall, restoration measures reduced runoff by 49.0% and soil erosion yield by 67.6%, with consistently greater reductions in soil erosion. Combined measures were most effective, whereas soil amendment alone showed the weakest runoff reduction (21.1%). Runoff reduction increased with restoration duration, while soil erosion control was strong initially but showed a transient decline before recovering. Restoration effectiveness also varied substantially among mine types and environmental conditions. Soil erosion reduction was more sensitive than runoff to climatic and topographic factors, with higher rainfall intensity and steeper slopes generally weakening both runoff and soil erosion control. Slopes longer than 15 m sharply reduced soil erosion control (56.9% vs. > 70% on shorter slopes). Vegetation cover further revealed contrasting responses: runoff reduction plateaued at approximately 40% cover, whereas soil erosion reduction continued to increase up to 80%–100% cover. These findings demonstrate that post‐mining restoration effectiveness is jointly regulated by restoration strategy, recovery duration, and site conditions, highlighting the need for context‐specific combinations of restoration measures, vegetation targets, and landform configurations.

papers.title: Integrating soil erosion modelling and field verification for spatial assessment of critical land
papers.summary: Land degradation is a global environmental issue that affects the ecological functions and sustainability of land resources.In Indonesia, degraded land conditions are commonly addressed through the concept of critical land, particularly in watershed assessment, management, and rehabilitation.Spatial approaches have been widely applied to identify critical land over large areas; however, their representativeness is strongly influenced by input data quality and may not fully reflect site-level degradation conditions.This study assessed critical land using a spatial approach that integrated key biophysical parameters with field-based verification in part of the Serang Watershed.Critical land was identified using a multicriteria spatial approach based on P.3/PDASHL/SET/KUM.1/7/2018.Land cover was derived from Sentinel-2A imagery using Random Forest and quantitatively assessed using 45 field reference points.Soil erosion was estimated using USLE, with soil erodibility determined through laboratory analysis of 18 soil samples representing different land units.Five criticality classes were identified, with Slightly Critical land dominating 58.45% of the study area, while Critical and Highly Critical land accounted for 6.27%.Field-based verification of areas classified as Critical and Highly Critical revealed diverse degradation characteristics, including rill and gully erosion, topsoil loss, shallow soil, slope failure, and anthropogenic disturbances.These findings indicate that integrating spatial modelling with field-based verification can provide site-level information to support the interpretation of critical-land conditions and the development of site-specific soil conservation and land rehabilitation measures.

papers.title: Landslide identification and susceptibility assessment in high-consequence areas of the oilfield based on multi-band InSAR and machine learning
papers.summary: Loess landslides pose a serious threat to energy infrastructure on the Loess Plateau; however, studies on landslide identification and monitoring in high-consequence areas of oil and gas facilities remain limited. This study investigates landslide identification and susceptibility assessment in a high-consequence area of the Changqing Oilfield in Qingyang City, Gansu Province, China, using Lutan-1 and Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar data and machine learning. Combining optical remote sensing images and applying the Minimum Covariance Determinant method and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to the InSAR derived deformation results, 65 potential landslides are identified. A random forest model, incorporating 13 conditioning factors, is constructed to generate a susceptibility map, with Shapley Additive explanations (SHAP) analysis used to interpret factor contributions. The results indicate that high susceptibility zones are predominantly controlled by surface roughness, distance to streams, and land surface temperature, and contain the majority of identified landslide points. 21.7% of oilfield facilities fall within these high-risk zones, highlighting the urgent need for continuous monitoring. This integrated framework provides a practical approach for geological hazard prevention in loess areas with critical energy infrastructure.

papers.title: Enhancing Experimental Reliability Through Rainfall Simulator Calibration Under Intense Rainfall Rates
papers.summary: Acknowledging the benefit of Rainfall Simulators (RS) is continuously growing among researcher, mainly for laboratory-scale models where natural rainfall is either unavailable or inconsistent. RS put forward a reliable platform for replicating specific rainfall events under standardized set-up, making them invaluable for erosion, hydrology, and slope stability research needs. The present work offered a cost-effective Dripping Rainfall Simulator (DRS) for application on a 1.2 m² test plot area. After several standardizations, the DRS that produces replicable storms of rainfall (at 60 mm/hr and 120 mm/hr) demonstrated satisfactory spatial uniformity, with Christiansen’s uniformity coefficients (CUC) coverage ranging from 81.18–88.69% distribution across the monitoring plot. Additionally, the mean diameters (Dm ) and median volumetric drop diameters (D50), measured using a flour-pellet method, were found to extend from 3.8–4.4 mm and 2.7–3.1 mm independently which line up well with values reported in previous research. The relative terminal velocity (VT ) calculated was attained to range between 8.59–8.92 m/s with energy flux from 36.88 to 39.77 J/mm/m2 . These findings verify the RS capability to replicate natural rainfall with considerable accuracy let alone provide a strong foundation to be used in future applications in experimental modelling. From the basis of this study regarding RS, researchers will be able to create events-scale physical models in their relevant engineering areas.

papers.title: Effects of land‐use systems on macroaggregate pore structure, hydraulic conductivity, and physical protection capacity
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract Reclamation of saline–alkali land relies on salt leaching and restoring soil fertility. However, the micro‐scale pore‐architectural changes associated with different land‐use systems remain insufficiently characterized, particularly in relation to their potential implications for water transport and fertility retention. This study selected natural land‐use systems (wasteland [WL] and degraded grassland [GL]) and artificial land‐use systems (upland field [UF] and paddy field [PF]) in Jilin, China, and scanned 5–7 mm macroaggregates for computed tomography imaging. Results showed that WL had a dense structure with low porosity (12.74%), while GL contained many elongated pores (21.74%). Porosity increased in the cultivated soils of UF (27.8%) and PF (22.48%). Network analysis indicated that UF had the highest hydraulic conductivity, whereas PF exhibited a hydraulically restrictive network. Using topological metrics, we identified critical pores within the macroaggregates. In natural systems (WL: two critical pores; GL: three critical pores), these pores resembled root systems. In contrast, the critical pores in UF (two critical pores) and PF (eight critical pores) were morphologically more uniform. Our analysis suggests that the two reclaimed agricultural systems are associated with divergent intra‐macroaggregate pore‐network configurations: UF was characterized by low‐tortuosity vertical pathways, suggesting a higher potential for rapid water transmission, whereas the more compartmentalized pore network in PF may restrict flow and increase the potential for physical protection of soil organic matter. These findings show that land‐use choice can redirect macroaggregate structural development during saline–alkali land reclamation, with implications for balancing salt leaching, hydraulic transport, and fertility retention.

papers.title: Estimating soil water retention curves from co‐located in situ water content and matric potential sensors
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract The soil water retention curve (SWRC) governs water storage and redistribution in the vadose zone and is a key input for hydrologic and agroecosystem models. Laboratory evaporation methods provide high‐quality SWRCs but are destructive and represent static conditions that may not reflect in situ soil behavior under natural field conditions. Co‐located field sensors measuring volumetric water content ( θ ) and matric potential ( h ) offer a continuous, nondestructive alternative for estimating field‐based SWRCs. In this study, the extent to which SWRCs can be derived from field‐installed sensors by directly comparing in situ θ – h relationships with laboratory evaporation measurements was evaluated. Six parametric retention models (Brooks–Corey, Fredlund–Xing, Kosugi, van Genuchten‐mnvar, van Genuchten [ m = 1 − 1/ n ], and van Genuchten‐PDI) were fitted to laboratory and field datasets in silt‐loam soil. Model performance and parameter stability were assessed using root mean square error of water content (RMSE_ θ ), and corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc). Field capacity (FC), permanent wilting point (PWP), and plant‐available water (PAW) were also calculated. Field‐derived θ s was consistently lower than laboratory‐derived θ s , indicating effective saturation in field conditions than complete saturation in laboratory conditions. No single retention model consistently provided the best fit across all laboratory and field datasets. The FC was relatively consistent across models, but PWP and PAW were more sensitive to model structure and extrapolation for θ r . These results indicate that co‐located θ–h sensors can help field‐based SWRC estimation when model selection accounts for the limited suction domain. Additional high‐suction observations would improve constraint of dry‐end parameters and derived hydraulic indicators.

papers.title: Erosion Assessment of Slope Failure: A Case Study of UniMAP Pauh Campus
papers.summary: Erosional slope failures pose significant risks to infrastructure, ecosystems, and human safety, particularly in humid tropical regions where steep terrain and intense rainfall coincide. This study investigates erosion and its influence on slope stability at the UniMAP Pauh Campus through an integrated geotechnical and hydrological approach. Field surveys, soil sampling, and laboratory analyses were conducted to characterize soil profiles and evaluate erosion susceptibility using two established indicators, the ROM Scale for soil erodibility and the ROSE Index for rainfall erosivity. Key parameters, including slope gradient, soil texture, vegetation cover, drainage, rainfall intensity, and land-use patterns, were systematically examined across three representative slopes. Results indicate that Slope 1 exhibits very high erodibility (ROM = 10.1) due to its sandy texture and minimal clay content, while Slopes 2 and 3 show high erodibility (ROM = 4.4 and 7.9) under comparable rainfall conditions. The recorded ROSE values from 2021 to 2023 (6842.40, 5469.92, and 6475.05 tonne·m² ha?¹ hr?¹) reflect a persistently moderate erosive climate. These findings suggest that variations in soil composition and compaction, rather than rainfall intensity alone, are the primary drivers of erosion across the study area. Targeted mitigation measures are recommended, including vegetation reinforcement on Slope 1, enhanced drainage and contour realignment on Slope 2, and bio-geotextile stabilization on Slope 3. The study provides a site-specific framework for managing campus slope erosion and contributes to broader efforts toward sustainable, climate-resilient slope management in tropical institutional landscape.

papers.title: Curvature and confinement: robustness of dryland vegetation patterns on sloped, undulating terrain
papers.summary: We consider a topographic extension to the well known Klausmeier model describing vegetation on sloped undulating terrain with a primary uphill direction and perpendicular small amplitude undulation forming ridges and valleys. Previous studies of this system have shown that, like 1-dimensional sloped terrain, as rainfall levels decrease through a threshold, vegetation forms into patterned states consisting of bands or stripes which are transverse to the primary upslope direction and move slowly uphill. In this paper we investigate the links between undulation amplitude and pattern dynamics, with the goal of understanding how the terrain impacts the resilience of the vegetation. To do this we take advantage of features of the domain, the ridge and valley, to reduce the analysis to two related 1-dimensional problems. Using a combination of analysis and numerical simulations, we argue that a combination of the ridge and valley equations provide insight to the full 2-dimensional dynamics. In particular, we find that at small undulation, the ridge plays a critical role in determining the existence and stability of patterns. For undulation amplitudes smaller than a well-defined threshold, the added sensitivity of vegetation on the ridge to aridity stress causes vegetation to be less resilient than indicated by uniformly sloped models. For undulation amplitudes above this threshold, vegetation is able to survive longer by becoming localized in the valleys, but the amplitude must be increased further to mitigate the original detrimental effects.

Data‐Driven Discovery of Classical and Anomalous Transport Models From Sparse Breakthrough Curves in Heterogeneous Porous Media via Symbolic Regression
papers.source: Journal of Geophysical Research Machine Learning and Computation
papers.summary: Abstract Natural porous media are highly heterogeneous, with flow and transport controlled by pore‐space morphology and connectivity. Consequently, classical continuum models often fail to describe observed transport under strong heterogeneity. A key challenge is identifying physically interpretable transport models from sparse observational data. We address this using a physics‐informed, data‐driven machine‐learning framework combining symbolic regression with genetic programming system identification, a stochastic optimization approach that discovers candidate partial differential equations (PDEs) directly from data. We apply it to two classical experimental data sets of solute transport. For Scheidegger's (1959) breakthrough‐curve measurements in Berea sandstones, a long‐standing benchmark for anomalous transport, the framework identifies data‐consistent, physically interpretable models using only sparse outlet observations and physical constraints. These include fractional advection–dispersion equations with temporal and spatial fractional operators: the temporal derivative represents memory effects from solute trapping in dead‐end pores, whereas the spatial derivative captures nonlocal transport from preferential flow paths and conductivity heterogeneity. For the Levy and Berkowitz (2003, https://doi.org/10.1016/s0169‐7722(02)00204‐8 ) data, the framework recovers both classical and anomalous transport representations depending on medium heterogeneity, distinguishing Fickian from non‐Fickian regimes from sparse breakthrough curves alone. The identified models are validated against independent data at different injection rates. Both data sets are intentionally sparse (one and four breakthrough curves, respectively), so these results should be read as evidence of feasibility under severe data scarcity, not as a general demonstration across broad classes of porous media. papers.title: Humidity-Controlled Inverse Gas Chromatography for Characterizing the Adsorption-Relevant Surface State of Dehydration-Sensitive Pharmaceutical Hydrates
Climate-Driven Sink-to-Source Transitions for Microplastics in Terrestrial Systems
papers.summary: Abstract Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as pervasive contaminants in terrestrial environments, where soils act as major dynamic reservoirs that retain particles but can also release them through hydrological, erosional, and atmospheric pathways. Climate change is altering the physical, hydrological, and biogeochemical controls that govern the MP retention-release balance. This review develops a climate-driven sink-to-source transition framework in which terrestrial systems shift episodically from retention-dominated to export-active states. We synthesize evidence that changes in freeze–thaw regimes and drought-rewetting reorganize pore networks and preferential flow; extreme rainfall and runoff can exceed hydrological retention and redistribute MPs vertically and laterally; and warming and salinization reconfigure interfacial interactions, polymer aging, aggregation behavior, and microbially mediated transport processes. Atmospheric entrainment and snowpack-snowmelt pathways further connect terrestrial MP reservoirs with other environmental compartments. Across these climate drivers, MP mobility depends on the coupled evolution of pore architecture, water flux, particle properties, and biogeochemical conditions rather than on any single forcing factor. By integrating laboratory studies, field observations, and emerging modeling perspectives, this review provides a mechanistic foundation for predicting terrestrial MP redistribution and associated environmental risks under ongoing climate change.

Influence of Mine Geometry and Working Type on Geothermal Exploitation and Thermal Storage
papers.summary: Abstract Thermal plumes developed during two heat injection experiments in different flooded mine working levels at the UK Geoenergy Observatory in Glasgow recorded thermal breakthrough times (for 0.1 °C change) of 4.8 and 2.3 days under similar test conditions. Synthesis of the mine abandonment plan, borehole, and outcrop data was used to characterise differences in the mine geometry and working type. New insights on how backfilled, collapsed, and open voids affected groundwater flow and heat transport were obtained from the hydrogeological, wellhead, and downhole direct temperature sensor data measured during and after pumping of the open loop borehole doublets. Over 17 days, heat injection into the Glasgow Upper mine workings resulted in the gradual development of a thermal plume, within an area interpreted to have a greater percentage of backfill and more tortuous flow paths. After 3.9 days, temperatures at the abstraction borehole started to increase at ≈ 0.03 °C/day, with a ≈ 2.3 °C differential maintained 10 days after heat injection and pumping stopped. In the five-day Glasgow Main heat injection experiment, temperature increases after 1.4 days were ≈ 0.14 °C/d, which was interpreted to result from preferential flow and heat transport pathways with less surface area for heat transport through conduction to the rock mass, and quicker transit time to the abstraction borehole. This provides real-world, at-scale quantification for geothermal exploitation and mine thermal energy storage, and demonstrates how mine working type, which influences flow and heat transport, can affect system performance.

papers.title: Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. First, I built a model to predict how severely forests are likely to burn across the state. Next, I used simulated treatment scenarios to test how different fuel treatments changed wildfire severity in different forest types and under different weather conditions. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. The results showed that treatment effectiveness depends strongly on forest type. In some forests, especially ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and lodgepole pine, reducing fuels had a strong effect on lowering fire severity. In other forest types, weather played a larger role, which made treatments less effective. Across most forests, treatments that reduced both canopy fuels and surface fuels produced the greatest reductions in wildfire severity. At the watershed scale, treatment costs and benefits also varied. Prescribed burning was generally the most cost-effective treatment. In several watersheds, including Electric Lake, Big Cottonwood Canyon, Panguitch Lake, and Rockport, cost-effective treatments provided the greatest reduction in post-fire risk for the money invested, making them especially important areas for management.
