papers.title: The Role of Bank Failure in Postfire Debris-Flow Sediment Recruitment: A Field-Based Case Study from the Grizzly Creek Fire, Colorado
papers.summary: Postfire debris flows often exhibit abrupt downstream increases in volume growth rate. Although these sudden volume increases have been identified in the past, their cause remains incompletely understood. In the Grizzly Creek burn area of Glenwood Canyon, Colorado, we combined field observations, repeat LiDAR differencing, and post-event imagery to quantify the contribution of localized mass-wasting processes in debris-flow sediment recruitment. Our observations indicate that lateral erosion and episodic bank collapse along channel margins supply the majority of sediment for debris-flow growth. Bank failures contribute to local channel widening and rapid debris-flow volume growth, particularly where debris flows erode into weak lithologies near contacts or colluvial deposits at the base of cliffs. Field documentation and LiDAR-derived volume changes demonstrate that bank erosion is the primary control on debris-flow growth in this landscape. This case study underscores the importance of explicitly incorporating lateral instability, material strength contrasts, and threshold reach behavior into postfire debris-flow hazard assessments and predictive modeling frameworks.

papers.title: TellusPM: a GPU-accelerated material point method for large-deformation geomechanics driven by an AI agent, calibrated against analytical, numerical and experimental benchmarks
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: TellusPM is a material point method (MPM) program for geotechnical large deformation, written in Rust, whichruns one explicit algorithm in 2D and 3D on a CPU or, through a run-time compiled CUDA engine, on an NVIDIAGPU, and which an engineer, an embedded AI agent or any Model Context Protocol client can drive through thesame 28 tools. We verified it against closed-form solutions and calibrated it against other programs and experimentsin a campaign of about 120 runs on one RTX 4090. The code converges at second order on the vibrating bar, matchesthe logarithmic-strain oedometer within 0.6 % and Terzaghi consolidation within 3.9 % of the initial pore pressure,and gives a factor of safety of 1.34 to 1.40 for the Griffiths and Lane slope, against 1.35 to 1.40 from finite elements.The calibration showed that a per-step FLIP/PIC blend, local damping under displacement control and the absenceof volumetric averaging each changed answers by up to a third, and that the remaining errors in granular runout, a 25% short runout of aluminium rods and a 1.3 to 1.7 times long runout of tall columns, belong to the rate-independentMohr-Coulomb model. On the 2026 Patong debris flow, a single-source back-analysis matches a coupled DEM–SPH model on the deposition along Nanai Road, and releasing every cell whose saturated infinite-slope factor ofsafety is below 1, with the strength reduced by γ𝑠𝑎𝑡/γ’ = 1.96, reproduces the 99th-percentile travel of a finiteelement and DEM–SPH chain on the same release within 6 %, although the median travel is 38 % longer. The GPUengine reproduces the CPU engine at about 40 times its speed, and a whole-hillside scenario of 546,738 points on9.4 × 107 cells ran in 12 min.

papers.title: Erosion and sediment transfer by debris flows on Miocene intrashelf clinoforms, offshore New Jersey, USA
papers.summary: We integrate legacy 2-D and high-resolution 3-D seismic data with Integrated Ocean Drilling Program Expedition 313 cores and logs to investigate downslope sediment transport on the Miocene New Jersey shelf (offshore eastern United States). Medium- to coarse-grained glauconite and glauconitic quartz sands were recovered at the bases of Lower to Middle Miocene intrashelf clinoforms despite the apparent absence of canyons, channels, or other organized sediment conduits before ca. 13.5−12.7 Ma. 3-D seismic imaging, however, reveals closely spaced U- and V-shaped erosional features at the base of sequence m5.47 (ca. 18 Ma) and within sequence m5.3 (ca. 16.6−16.1 Ma). These morphologies, interpreted as grooves and irregular depressions, record erosion by debris flows transporting sand-rich sediment downslope. Their lengths (≤700 m) and low length-to-width ratios (∼3) suggest incision by substrate blocks locally entrained and rapidly abraded during transport. We propose that basal erosion reflects patchy coupling between the debris flow and the substrate, involving bulk entrainment of loose sands, localized stick-pluck detachment of semi-cohesive blocks that form irregular depressions, and short-lived dragging that produces grooves. Grooved and scarred basal surfaces overlain by debrites are restricted to sequences m5.47 and m5.3. Sequence m5.47 shows deeper incision that disrupts clinoform geometry and partially truncates underlying sequences, whereas m5.3 preserves normal progradation. Both sequences record similar erosional processes with an oblique transport direction (∼50°) relative to clinoform progradation direction, which we attribute to a regional trough to the south. These results demonstrate that debris flows can occur on low-angle intrashelf clinoforms and that both frequent smaller-volume and rare, large-volume mass-wasting events are important in shaping intrashelf stratigraphy.

papers.title: Pre- and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and elevation differences for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Trishuli/Rasuwa catastrophic flood
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal and Tibet. We provide here pre-event and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from Pléiades, SPOT6 and SPOT5 stereo-images. Date were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES. The collection includes three files: Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_pre-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_post-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_dh.tif =========================== Methods The post-event DEM is purely based on Pleiades stereo images. The pre-event DEM is based mostly Pléiades and SPOT6 stereopairs. A small fraction of the pre-event DEM was derived from 10 m SPOT5-HRS images. All DEMs were generated at a ground sampling distance of 4 m using the semiglobal matching algorithm of the Ames Stereo Pipeline (Beyer et al., 2018; Shean et al., 2016) and the processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). A ground sampling distance of 10 m was used for SPOT5-HRS. All individual DEMs were first co-registered and vertically adjusted to the Copernicus 30 (GLO-30) DEM, masking out glaciers using the Randolph Glacier Inventory v7 (RGI 7.0 consortium, 2023). Next, the individual pre- and post-event DEMs were co-registered in pairs to construct the most accurate DoD possible. Finally, those individual DoDs were mosaicked in a single map of elevation difference. The uncertainty on the mean elevation change was calculated using the patch method (Dussaillant et al., 2018). papers.title: Crack-free fused silica cooling mirror substrates via thermally matched sacrificial templating
Elemental Sulfur Deposition Downstream of Gas-Lift Flow Control Valves in Offshore Gas Lift Operations: Field Evidence, Root-Cause Analysis, and Mitigation
papers.source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
papers.summary: Abstract Elemental sulfur deposition (ESD) constitutes a principal constraint on flow assurance and production availability in the gas-lift systems of offshore sites. Following the commissioning of gas-lift operations, bright-yellow solids accumulated within the gas-lift flow-control valves (FCVs), downstream flanges and Modular surface-actuated safety (M-SAS) valves, resulting in flow restriction and enforced gas lift shutdowns to the Production wells. This work characterizes the composition, provenance and formation mechanisms of these deposits in order to define appropriate mitigation measures. The investigation is based on field data acquired at Sites A, B, C and D facilities, together with compositional analyses of the reservoir fluids, the gas streams and the recovered solids. Laboratory characterization established that the deposits consist predominantly of elemental sulfur, at concentrations up to 98.5 wt%. Iron corrosion products, comprising FeS, Fe2O3 and FeSO4, were additionally identified in pipeline pigging debris and at compressor suction strainers. Although the lift gas contains no more than 2 ppm hydrogen sulfide and the crude contains no free elemental sulfur, near-pure sulfur is formed at any location subject to a substantial pressure reduction, such as that imposed across the FCV. These observations are consistent with vapor-phase transport followed by desublimation. An extensive root-cause analysis and an independent review by Third party Consultant were undertaken to evaluate the elemental Sulfur formation routes. Both identify oxygen-driven oxidation of trace H2S on metal surfaces (H2S + 1/2 O2 -> H2O + 1/8 S8) as the governing mechanism. The oxygen is attributable to start-up procedures, sub-specification purge nitrogen and recycled compressor seal-gas vents. A phased mitigation program is accordingly proposed, comprising oxygen exclusion, thermal-hydraulic control and interim corrosion product deposit removal.

papers.title: Redirecting gypsum scaling in pervaporation desalination via activated alumina granules
papers.summary: Membrane scaling, particularly CaSO4 (gypsum) crystallisation, severely limits the practical application of pervaporation (PV) desalination for high-salinity wastewater treatment. Herein, an online interception strategy using nitric acid-activated alumina granules (AAG) is proposed to redirect gypsum scaling from the membrane surface to a sacrificial medium. By tuning nitric acid activation, the physicochemical properties of AAG were optimised. AAG activated with 7.5% nitric acid exhibits an optimal pore structure (specific surface area of 295.4 m2/g, pore volume of 0.361 cm3/g) and surface positive charge, significantly reducing the heterogeneous nucleation energy barrier for gypsum crystallisation. This enables the transfer of scaling from the membrane surface to AAG, reducing the membrane surface scaling amount by approximately 45%. Combined with the extended XDLVO theory analysis, the dominant mechanism of surface-induced heterogeneous nucleation by AAG was elucidated. Moreover, ultrasonic–EDTA cleaning enables efficient regeneration of AAG, and the strategy is validated using real reverse osmosis concentrate. This work establishes a scaling control paradigm based on crystallisation relocation rather than inhibition, providing mechanistic insight and a scalable approach for fouling mitigation in PV desalination.

papers.title: Thermo-hydraulic behaviour of energy pile in chalk: First experimental characterisation and field-scale performance assessment under unsaturated conditions
papers.summary: Energy piles—foundation elements that simultaneously provide structural support and exchange heat with the ground—offer a direct response to the growing heating and cooling demands of north-western Europe, where chalk is the primary bearing stratum for pile foundations. Despite the widespread occurrence of chalk and its frequently unsaturated state, its coupled thermo-hydraulic behaviour has not yet been characterised as a host medium for energy piles: existing estimates of chalk thermal conductivity correspond to discrete saturation states rather than to a continuous conductivity–saturation relationship established experimentally, representing a gap in geothermal foundation design. This study addresses that gap by delivering the first chalk-specific experimental dataset, constitutive framework, and validated numerical model for energy pile performance in unsaturated chalk. Thermal conductivity was measured on intact chalk specimens using a transient needle-probe across controlled degrees of saturation, and the data were used to calibrate a thermal conductivity function. A fully coupled thermo-hydraulic formulation was implemented in the finite-element framework COMSOL Multiphysics and verified against two independent benchmarks: a field thermal response test on an energy pile in saturated clayey sand and a laboratory model energy-pile test in unsaturated sand. The validated model was then applied to a three-dimensional field-scale energy pile in three chalk formations, and compared with representative sand, silt and clay, to examine the effect of saturation on thermal performance under a seasonal heating–cooling cycle. For the investigated configuration, increasing GWT depth from 0 to 29 m reduces the end-of-extraction heat rate by 6.1%, 8.8% and 11.9% for Estreux, Château-Landon and Seaford chalk, respectively, compared with 3.6% for clay, 8.6% for silt and 26.0% for sand. At 29 m, the chalk cases retain 159.4–169.9 W m − 1 , compared with 135.5 W m − 1 for sand.

papers.title: A Modified Quirk-Millington Equation for Partially Saturated Reactive Porous Media
papers.summary: Diffusion-induced mineral precipitation in partially saturated porous media is observed in various subsurface applications for future energy needs, such as CO 2 sequestration, deep geothermal reservoirs, and deep geological disposal of nuclear waste. The presence of gas might promote mineralization, which can significantly alter the pore space (e.g., geometry, connectivity, diffusivity), possibly causing porosity clogging, and leading to pressure build up and fracturing. Assessing the safety and stability of such systems requires understanding of the effects of mineral precipitation on porosity and effective diffusivity and quantifying the resulting reductions in these properties. Here, we developed a 3D column-diffusion experiment monitored with time resolved micro computed tomography (micro-CT) to evaluate celestine precipitation patterns within partially saturated porous media. In the scans, we can observe enhanced precipitation at the gas-liquid interface and a decrease in porosity with time. The 3D pore structures are used for tracer injection simulation with lattice Boltzmann to determine effective diffusivity. Results from three different experiments with increasing gas content show a decrease in effective diffusivity with time and are used to determine a modified porosity-diffusivity relationship in an evolving pore space as function of water saturation. A comparison with the established power law function of Quirk-Millington (QM) for sandy porous media shows that it overestimates effective diffusivity by several orders of magnitude for some cases. We propose a revised relationship of QM for describing mineralization in partially saturated porous media.

papers.title: Using soil moisture and seed germination timing to understand annual grass invasion post-fire and restoration implications
papers.summary: Abstract In semiarid ecosystems, precipitation and soil-water storage in shallow soils contribute to differences in seed germination of native perennial species and invasive annuals grasses. Invasive annual grasses contribute to wildfire, which displaces native vegetation and changes surface soils through post-fire erosion and loss of organic matter, decreasing surface soil moisture storage, impacting seed-based restoration, and the prevalence of invasive grasses. To understand how soils, precipitation, and fire contribute to surface soil moisture and seed germination, we used the Soil Heat and Water model (SHAW) and seed germination models to estimate shallow soil moisture and seed responses of three native species relative to Bromus tectorum. Across the semiarid regions of the Great Basin, USA, we found variation in sand content produced differences in surface soil moisture duration comparable to those generated by the wettest and driest years on record. The shallow soil environment and precipitation regimes impacted seeds differently, with greater reductions of germination probabilities in sandier soils and during years with lower-than-average spring precipitation. On average, germination probability decreased by 4% for every 10% increase in sand content. The negative effects of sand content on germination were reduced when soils had higher water content following a wetter-than-average winter. Using a literature review, we also estimated an average fire-effect on soil texture and bulk density. Based on the average fire-effects on soils, the modeled number of days of plant-available soil moisture decreased by four days, and germination probability decreased by 6% across species, soils, and precipitation regimes. Because resource availability, contributes to differences in post-wildfire recovery and annual grass invasion, soil plays a critical role during restoration. papers.title: Theoretical and Applied Framework of River Geophysics
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract: Rivers and their adjoining catchments form interconnected physical systems comprising river water, groundwater, soils, rock formations, and riverbanks. Stage fluctuations, bank erosion, unsaturated infiltration, and flood propagation occur across different spatial scales, making it difficult to distinguish underlying mechanisms using a single observation type or parameter set. This review examines representative processes, measurable quantities, and observational approaches at three terrestrial scales: the channel-riverbank, hillslope-vadose zone, and catchment-river network. It compares the contributions and limitations of studies on river-groundwater exchange, near-surface geophysical monitoring, conceptual hydrological modelling, and uncertainty analysis, and distinguishes measured properties from effective model parameters. Ancient Martian channels and water-/ice-related landforms are also considered as potential comparative targets, not as evidence that terrestrial hydrological mechanisms can be transferred directly to other planets. A framework linking phenomenon identification, joint observation, mechanism-based modelling, uncertainty assessment, and independent validation is then summarized. This perspective supports testable cross-scale interpretation and may inform bank protection, flood-risk assessment, and monitoring design; practical benefits require independent field and cross-event evaluation. papers.title: A Simplified CPT-Based Method for Estimating the Friction Angle of Partially Saturated Compacted Soils
papers.summary: Embankments and other compacted earth structures are widely used in civil engineering, and their mechanical behaviour depends on the properties of compacted soils, which are often affected by unsaturated conditions and matric suction. This study presents an empirical methodology aimed at the preliminary estimation of the peak friction angle of compacted unsaturated soils from cone penetration test (CPT) data, intended to support engineering assessments when laboratory testing and site investigation are limited. The approach was developed using CPT measurements collected at three levee test sites in northeastern Italy (Grizzaga, Panaro, and Tagliamento Rivers), combined with laboratory shear test results on undisturbed samples and supplemented by selected data from the literature. Three empirical equations were proposed and compared using different normalization schemes of cone tip resistance with respect to in situ stress conditions, while considering the influence of matric suction. For the soils examined in this study, the estimated peak friction angles were generally consistent with laboratory results, suggesting that the proposed relationships may provide a reasonable first approximation under similar soil conditions. The proposed procedure is intended as a preliminary engineering tool to complement, rather than replace, detailed laboratory testing in the geotechnical characterization of levees, embankments, and other compacted earth structures.

papers.title: Pollutant Concentration Reconstruction in Porous Media from Localized Measurements
papers.summary: Reliable environmental monitoring and groundwater protection heavily rely on the ability to reconstruct full pollutant concentration fields from sparse, partial field measurements. In porous media, dissolved contaminants are transported by groundwater flow while undergoing hydrodynamic dispersion and complex chemical or biological reactions. To address practical contamination challenges, this work investigates the reconstruction of pollutant distributions using water samples collected at discrete locations in unsaturated or saturated soils via sampling tubes equipped with ceramic tips. While these suction samplers provide critical local data, they inherently capture only a fraction of the subsurface environment, leaving wide areas unmonitored. Motivated by this real-world monitoring procedure, we propose steady and time-dependent advection-diffusion-reaction models to simulate contaminant transport. Our main contribution is a generalized unique continuation result demonstrating that, under appropriate physical and mathematical assumptions, two concentration fields coinciding on a non-empty observation region must match throughout the entire space-time domain, even when originating from different source configurations. We investigate this problem from both theoretical and numerical perspectives, backing our mathematical uniqueness results with numerical simulations that validate the efficiency and practical utility of our approach. The theoretical proofs combine regularity properties away from source singularities with unique-continuation principles for parabolic and elliptic partial differential equations, providing a robust framework for environmental risk assessment and site remediation.

papers.title: A Medium-Entropy Alloy PdRuCuNi/TiO2 Catalyst for Efficient Photothermal Conversion of Castor Oil into Liquid Hydrocarbon Fuel
Characterization of physical and chemical properties controlling the transport of 129I and 99Tc in ultra-high-performance grout
papers.summary: Ultra-high-performance grout (UHPG) was evaluated as an engineered barrier for encapsulating solid waste generated during nuclear waste processing. The objective of this study was to measure geochemical, hydrological, and physical properties related to 129 I and 99 Tc transport through UHPG. 99 Tc and 129 I are key health-risk drivers associated with near-subsurface nuclear disposal facilities. To provide context, a second flowable Baseline grout currently used in nuclear waste disposal facilities was also characterized. Compressive strength and bulk density were appreciably greater in the UHPG (120.5 MPa and 2.2 g/cm 3 , respectively) than the Baseline grout (8.4 MPa and 1.5 g/cm 3 ). UHPG had appreciably lower porosity (0.15 cm 3 /cm 3 ) and hydraulic conductivity ( K = 5.8 ×10 −14 cm/sec) than the Baseline grout (porosity = 0.32 cm 3 /cm 3 ; K = 9.4 ×10 −7 cm/sec). Desorption partitioning experiments indicated that both grouts had similar 129 I partitioning coefficients (C Solid /C Liquid ; K d ), of ∼100 (moles/g)/(moles/mL) and had similar aqueous iodine speciation: I - > > IO 3 - > organo-I. 99 Tc aqueous concentrations appeared to be controlled by solubility (7 ×10 −8 mol/L) in the UHPG, likely because slag in the UHPG formulation produced a reducing environment that converted the highly mobile aqueous TcO 4 - to a much less mobile Tc(IV) solid species, TcO 4 · n H 2 O. 129 I and 99 Tc observed diffusivity ( D obs ) were 6 and 7 orders of magnitude less, respectively, in the UHPG than in the Baseline grout. These tests provide multiple lines of evidence indicating that UHPG possesses excellent characteristics for encapsulating 99 Tc and 129 I waste.

papers.title: Incorporating physical guidance into deep learning through hard constraints for water transport modeling in unsaturated zone
Sustainable silty sand reinforcement using stipa tenacissima Fibers: insights from triaxial testing
papers.source: European Journal of Environmental and Civil engineering
papers.summary: As a sustainable alternative, natural plant fibre reinforcements offer an economical and environmentally friendly solution for enhancing the mechanical performance of earthen construction materials. This study investigates the use of Stipa Tenacissima (Alfa) plant as inclusions to improve silty sand’s mechanical properties. Initially, unsaturated triaxial tests at a constant water content were conducted on, compacted silty sand soil reinforced with 2% Alfa fibres, enabling the evaluation of the complete stress-strain behaviour while controlling confinement and suction. Alfa fibres, which were either cut into 10 mm stems or milled, were blended with natural silty sand, and specimens were compacted under optimum proctor conditions prior to triaxial shear testing. The results indicate an increase in shear strength of 8-15% and an improvement in stiffness modulus exceeding 50%, together with a notable increase in friction angle. Microstructural interactions analysed using scanning electron microscopy reveal smooth fibre surface morphologies that facilitate physical adhesion and interlocking at the fibre-soil interface. While cut fibres primarily enhance the apparent cohesion, milled fibres are shown to modify the mechanical interlocking with the soil particles and to increase the frictional interaction. These findings present novel perspectives and analysis using Alfa fibres-reinforced soil as a sustainable natural reinforcement material.

papers.title: Interpreting changes in soil pore-size distribution following vegetation establishment in a salt marsh: an exploratory case study in the Yellow River Delta, China
Integrated Geotechnical and Seismic Stability Assessment of Tropical Residual Slopes in Sitinjau Lauik, West Sumatra, Indonesia
papers.summary: Sitinjau Lauik, a national road corridor in West Sumatra, Indonesia, is one of the most landslide-prone segments of the Bukit Barisan volcanic belt. This study assesses the geotechnical and seismic stability of three tropical residual soil slopes at this location by combining cone penetration testing (CPT), laboratory index testing, consolidated-drained direct shear testing (DST), and Morgenstern–Price limit-equilibrium analysis under static and pseudo-static seismic loading. CPT profiles revealed a weak layer (qc = 0.4–0.6 MPa) at 1.2–2.8 m depth in Slope 1. This slope also has a high plasticity index (PI = 39.7%), a high void ratio (e = 1.50), and a low dry density (γd = 10.06 kN/m³), resulting in lower shear-strength parameters (c' = 17.8 kPa, φ' = 19.2°) than Slopes 2 and 3 (PI < 10%). Static factors of safety (FS) were 1.08, 1.54, and 1.49 for Slopes 1, 2, and 3, respectively. A pseudo-static coefficient of kh = 0.15, consistent with regional peak ground acceleration zoning, reduced the FS values to 0.77, 1.23, and 1.17, making Slope 1 unstable during earthquakes. At kh = 0.20, none of the slopes met the minimum FS of 1.1 required by the Indonesian National Standard (SNI) 8460:2017. High plasticity, a high void ratio, and low CPT resistance distinguished the critical Slope 1 from the other slopes. Because only three slopes were examined, these findings are site-specific; nevertheless, they provide a basis for prioritizing slope remediation and early warning along this corridor.

papers.title: Embedding Probabilistic Pore Occupancy into Soil Hydraulic Models
papers.summary: Conventional soil hydraulic models describe unsaturated water retention and conductivity by assuming that water occupies the smallest pores, i.e., lower-energy pores. The author introduces a statistical pore occupancy framework to quantify the pore states by a pore distribution, retrieved from the retention function, allowing statistical inference of pore state conditions. The framework introduces a parameter b, which represents the water pore occupancy distribution, impacting the behavior of the retention and conductivity functions. The approach uses an effective energy formulation to facilitate the calculations, allowing direct integration into traditional soil-water dynamic simulators. As a second step, a back transformation is introduced for a direct physical interpretation of the pore-filling condition, leading to the probability of pores being filled or not filled with water. The framework introduces a modified closed-form formulation of the Van Genuchten-Mualem model. The new model can quantify hysteretic behavior of the retention function and simultaneously predict the hydraulic conductivity behavior. Root mean square differences (RMSD) ranged from 0.007 to 0.021 m3 m-3, for the retention data, predicting both drying and wetting experiment scenarios; and from 0.117 to 0.216 for the conductivity, expressed as log10⁡(K). The embedded statistical mechanic can also assist in quantifying the solute transport. The respective shapes of the solute breakthrough curves (BTC) were reproduced, leading to a calibration RMSD of 0.018 and 0.016 [–]. A discussion regarding the back-transformation showed how the framework can be used to infer the configuration of pores filled with water in the soil, considering the model assumptions.

papers.title: A review of partial saturation in liquefaction assessment: theory, laboratory studies, and field case histories
papers.summary: Abstract Liquefaction triggering analyses commonly assume that soils below the groundwater table (GWT) are fully saturated. In loose, granular soil deposits, this assumption suggests an increased potential for liquefaction. However, soil deposits below the GWT may be only partially saturated due to the presence of entrapped air in the pore water, which can significantly alter liquefaction resistance. Laboratory studies have shown that liquefaction resistance increases as the degree of saturation (S r ) decreases. P-wave velocity (V P ) is a reliable parameter for assessing saturation conditions in both laboratory and field settings. In fully saturated soils, compression waves propagate at velocities comparable to that of water, (~ 1500 m/s), whereas V P values below this threshold indicate partial saturation. Laboratory results show a strong, nearly exponential empirical relationship between V P and liquefaction resistance, with resistance increasing significantly as V P decreases. This relationship enables the development of partial saturation correction factors that can be applied to the factor of safety against liquefaction triggering, thereby improving prediction accuracy by accounting for the additional liquefaction resistance associated with partial saturation. This paper provides researchers and practitioners with a consolidated basis for understanding and accounting for partial saturation in liquefaction assessment, progressing from its theoretical and experimental basis to field identification and application. The review consolidates findings dispersed across individual studies and provides a new synthesis of field case histories within a common framework, enabling consistent comparison and a unified interpretation of the influence of partial saturation on liquefaction response. The findings highlight how accounting for partial saturation can support more representative liquefaction hazard and risk assessment.

papers.title: Wetting-Drying Cycles and Cone Penetration Tests in Clay - How Does Seasonal Drought and Vegetation-Induced Suction Affect Clay Strength?
papers.summary: The increasing frequency and duration of droughts over the last decade raise concerns about the behaviour of clay soils that support shallow foundations. This study investigates the response of clay strength to repeated wetting–drying cycles using mini‑cone penetration tests (mini-CPTs). A laboratory procedure was developed to subject clay samples to controlled and reproducible realistic wetting-drying cycles. Tests were conducted on two clay types: a homogeneous, artificially prepared Vingerling clay, and a natural clay obtained from the eastern Netherlands. The resulting mini-CPT results show a clear relationship between water content and cone penetration force. For the Vingerling clay, this relationship follows an almost perfect logarithmic trend. The natural clay, which is considerably stronger, shows the same logarithmic trend, although with greater scatter, likely due to the clay’s heterogeneity. No systematic trend was observed between the number of wetting–drying cycles and the cone penetration force..

papers.title: A calculation method for the ultimate support pressure of a shield tunnel excavation face accounting for fault dip angle
papers.summary: Abstract This study investigated the influence of fault dip angle on tunnel excavation-face stability. Starting from the conventional wedge instability model for homogeneous strata, an associated flow rule was introduced to improve the wedge model, and a modified wedge calculation model that accounts for the fault dip angle is proposed. Then, by establishing the compatibility relationship between the rupture angles of the upper and lower strata, an analytical formula for the ultimate support pressure of the excavation face under inclined fault conditions is derived using the limit equilibrium method, along with the corresponding calculation procedure. Three-dimensional numerical simulations are performed to evaluate the theoretical model, and the results reveal that the trends in the theoretical predictions and numerical simulations are consistent, with relative errors ranging from 3.2% to 15% across all working conditions, indicating good agreement between the theoretical and numerical results. The calculation results reveal that stratum strength parameters and fault dip angle are the key factors controlling ultimate support pressure. The proposed calculation method for the ultimate support force of the excavation face considering fault dip angle can quantitatively estimate ultimate support pressure in faulted strata, providing a theoretical basis for assessing support parameters and evaluating excavation-face stability during slurry-shield tunneling through fault fracture zones.

papers.title: Hydrodeoxygenation of pyrolysis oil from retired wind turbine blades over Ru-NbOPO4 for the synthesis of cycloalkane fuels
Characterizing gas diffusivity, air permeability, and extracellular enzyme activity in an early‐stage comparison of conventional and regenerative pasture
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract Regenerative pasture is an emerging agricultural framework characterized by high forage diversity, adaptive grazing, and reduced external inputs. However, early‐stage soil structural transitions and associated microbial activities remain unclear, particularly given the higher spatial variability expected in these systems. We compared regenerative and conventional pastures after 3 years of management at an experimental site in Canterbury, New Zealand, evaluating soil‐water retention, diffusion‐controlled aeration, and macropore‐dependent properties, alongside extracellular enzyme activities as an early biological indicator. Twenty undisturbed cores were analyzed for soil‐water retention (−1 to −1500 kPa), soil‐gas diffusivity ( D p / D o ) and air permeability ( k a ) (−1 to −10 kPa), bulk density ( ρ b), and saturated hydraulic conductivity ( K s ). Additional cores were used to measure eight hydrolytic and oxidative enzyme activities and compare spatial heterogeneity. Regenerative soils showed modestly lower ρ b (1.29 g cm − 3 ) than conventional soils (1.33 g cm − 3 ) and consistently higher water retention, giving 9.8% more plant‐available water. Derived pore‐size distributions indicated emerging micropore connectivity despite minimal change in total porosity. The D p / D o slope coefficient ( A ) was ∼30% higher in regenerative soils, allowing well‐aerated conditions ( D p / D o > 0.01) at field capacity, whereas conventional soils remained largely hypoxic. In contrast, macropore‐sensitive indicators ( k a and K s ) were highly variable and lower in regenerative soils, suggesting early reorganization favors functional macropore connectivity rather than increased pore volume. Mean enzyme activities did not differ between systems, but within‐plot variability was higher in regenerative plots. Functionally meaningful responses are therefore not yet clearly evident, and longer term monitoring is required to detect statistically distinguishable outcomes.

From Rainfall to Absolute Landslide Probability: A Machine Learning–Based Approach
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are prevalent geological hazards in mountainous and hilly regions, posing significant threats to human lives, property, and infrastructure, especially when external factors such as heavy rainfall elevate the risk of occurrence. In recent years, the rapid development of remote sensing technology, geographic information system, and big data analytics has enabled the establishment of landslide databases and the refinement of landslide hazard assessment methodologies, opening new avenues for disaster prediction and prevention research. This study focuses on the probabilistic hazard assessment of rainfall-induced landslides, using the heavy rainfall event in Nanping City, Fujian, in 2019 as a case study. The absolute probability of landslide occurrence was quantified by integrating machine learning models with Bayesian probability theory. To analyze their contributions to landslide hazard, the study comprehensively considered nine key factors: elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, topographic wetness index, fault distance, rainfall amount, topographic position index, land cover, and stratum. The findings reveal that rainfall intensity is the primary trigger for landslides. However, the occurrence of landslides also depends on the combined influence of topography, geology, and human activities rather than rainfall alone. Building on these insights, this study extends the established landslide probability assessment model to a wider region. And simulating landslide occurrence probabilities under various rainfall scenarios. This approach confirms the strong correlation between rainfall and landslides while offering scientific support for emergency management and disaster warning systems. The research provides a robust foundation for disaster prevention and control in mountainous areas, infrastructure planning, and the development of emergency response systems, particularly by refining landslide prediction models that account for multiple factors. A real-time visual monitoring method for landslide creep using platform attitude self-calibration
papers.summary: High-frequency, high-precision, real-time displacement monitoring is essential for early warning of landslide creep, a key precursor to slope failure. However, platform attitude disturbances, such as wind-induced vibration and foundation settlement, can introduce spurious displacement into image sequences and reduce the accuracy of conventional vision-based monitoring. This study proposes a real-time visual monitoring technique for landslide creep based on platform attitude self-calibration. An optical tracker and an inertial measurement unit were integrated to acquire target images and attitude data simultaneously. A displacement decomposition model incorporating attitude fluctuations was developed to separate true slope movement from attitude-induced spurious displacement. Subpixel target localization used gradient-direction voting and weighted elliptical fitting, and real-time attitude estimation used an error-state Kalman filter. Indoor vibration tests at 40 m achieved an RMSE below 0.7 mm, with reductions of 0.955 and 0.846 compared with vision-only and vision-plus-reference-point correction approaches, respectively. During a 93-day field campaign at the Dayangshan landslide, Suzhou, the approach achieved a data capture rate of 0.986, an RMSE of 0.28–0.36 mm, and a correlation coefficient above 0.91 versus GNSS data. The approach provides a practical option for early warning of slope failure by accurately and continuously monitoring landslide creep under unstable platform conditions and unfavorable weather.

Factors Affecting Machine Learning-Based Landslide Detection for the 2015 Lefkada Earthquake
A GeoAI framework for landslide susceptibility mapping using Google Earth Engine, ensemble machine learning, and SHAP explainable AI
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in mountainous regions, yet susceptibility mapping in data-scarce areas remains challenging. This study proposes a reproducible Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) framework that integrates Google Earth Engine (GEE), ensemble machine learning, and explainable AI (XAI) for landslide susceptibility mapping in central Nepal. Using a balanced dataset of 9,479 observations from 4,743 landslide and 4,736 non-landslide locations, extracted seven conditioning factors: topographic (elevation, slope, aspect), climatic (rainfall), ecological (NDVI, land cover), and anthropogenic (population density) within the GEE cloud computing environment. Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models using stratified train-test splitting and 10-fold cross-validation. Both models showed strong predictive performance, with XGBoost achieving superior results (Accuracy: 88.3%, ROC-AUC: 0.952) compared to RF (Accuracy: 87.9%, ROC-AUC: 0.945). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified slope as the most influential predictor associated with model predictions followed by rainfall (16%) and elevation (15%), while lower NDVI values consistently correlated with higher susceptibility. The susceptibility map identified high-risk zones concentrated in Sindhupalchok, Dolakha, Dhading, Rasuwa, Gorkha, and Nuwakot districts. This framework reveals that freely available satellite data, cloud computing, and explainable machine learning can be effectively integrated for susceptibility mapping and community resilience initiatives.

papers.source: Journal on Applied and Chemical Physics
papers.summary: Climate Change Impact on Landslides Rising global temperatures contribute to more extreme weather patterns, including intense rainfall events that increase soil saturation and slope instability. Additionally, the melting of permafrost in colder regions due to warming temperatures weakens mountain slopes, heightening the risk of landslides. Deforestation and land-use changes further exacerbate these conditions by reducing natural vegetation that stabilizes soil. Research significance Researching climate change’s impact on landslides is critical as rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and extreme weather events intensify landslide risks globally. Increased rainfall and rapid snowmelt contribute to soil saturation and instability on slopes, while droughts can dry soils, leading to heightened erosion and landslide susceptibility. Methodology Climate models project changes in temperature, precipitation, and extreme weather, which can trigger landslides. Landslide susceptibility maps, created using GIS tools and machine learning algorithms, help identify high-risk zones based on topography, soil type, and vegetation. Historical landslide records are analyzed alongside climate data to detect trends and correlations. GIS-AHP-Based Landslide Susceptibility Assessment of the Bradost Anticline, Northern Iraq
papers.summary: The use of landslide susceptibility assessment is a vital step for sustainable land-use planning and risk mitigation, especially in mountainous areas and in complex tectonic and geomorphological environments. The present study aims to assess the landslide susceptibility in the Bradost Anticline through an integrated Geographic Information System (GIS) and Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) approach. The following 10 conditioning factors were considered: geology, lineament density, slope, elevation, stream density, gully density, slope curvature, topographic wetness index, normalized difference vegetation index, land use/land cover. All the factors were treated, standardized and visualised as thematic GIS layers. The AHP was then applied to normalize the weights and weighted layers were combined to create a landslide susceptibility map. Very high, high and moderate stability zones cover 11.36%, 25.05% and 29.87% of the area, respectively. The low and very-low-stability areas constitute 23.05% and 10.67%, respectively, showing high or very high landslide susceptibility (33.72%) in the study area. The highest weights were recalculated for geology, lineament density, and slope (0.190, 0.188, and 0.179, respectively). An overall accuracy of 83.06%, a kappa coefficient of 0.787, and an area under the ROC curve of 0.894 were used to validate the model. These outcomes show high level of agreement with the observations in the field and high level of discriminatory performance. The framework can be used as a regional screening basis for landslide mitigation, land-use planning and infrastructure protection in vulnerable mountainous terrain.

Stability Assessment of Landslides under Coupling Action of Rainfall and Earthquake
papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

Dual-Geometry Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR for Landslide-Related Deformation Mapping and InSAR-Informed Susceptibility Assessment in Tizi Ouzou, Northern Algeria
papers.summary: This study presents a regional-scale, process-oriented assessment of active landslide-related deformation in TiziOuzou, northernAlgeria, over approximately 2429 km2, using dual-geometry Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR time-series analysis. Ascending and descending Sentinel-1 datasets acquired between January 2023 and December 2025 were processed to derive line-of-sight (LOS) deformation products and dual-geometry deformation indicators. A multi-criteria hotspot detection framework was developed by combining absolute LOS velocity, cumulative displacement, temporal coherence, C-index-based geometric visibility, spatial velocity gradients, and approximate two-dimensional deformation amplitude. The final hotspot layer identified 260 deformation polygons, grouped into 190 unique hotspot identifiers, covering approximately 47.9 km2. Of these 190 hotspots, 64 met the size and score criteria for temporal analysis. These hotspots were interpreted as InSAR-derived active deformation candidates rather than confirmed landslide boundaries. Their relevance was assessed through benchmarking against velocity-threshold, Sobel-gradient, and Getis–Ord Gi* strategies, comparison with a compiled bibliographic landslide inventory, temporal rainfall–deformation screening, targeted field verification, and first-order infrastructure exposure analysis. At HS_119, a sustained ascending LOS displacement trend contrasted with predominantly oscillatory descending behaviour. Descending absolute displacement rates showed similar correlations with 60-day antecedent rainfall at the hotspot and a nearby terrain-matched comparison area (r = 0.240 and 0.241, respectively). Targeted field verification at the Boubroun hotspot in the Azazga area provided qualitative support for the InSAR-based interpretation by documenting landslide-related deformation indicators within the inspected sector. To quantitatively integrate environmental conditioning factors, a Random Forest model was trained using hotspot-derived posit

Multiobjective Optimization of Landslide Rheological Parameters Based on Random Forest and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II
papers.summary: Abstract Rheological parameters (e.g., pore pressure coefficient r u and dynamic friction angle ϕ ) are necessary input for landslide runout evaluation. However, due to high randomness of initiation, propagation, and accumulation, it is impossible to directly measure rheological properties. This study proposes an optimization method for calibrating landslide rheological parameters based on random forest (RF) and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). Firstly, a dynamic numerical model of landslide is established using three-dimensional model DAN (DAN3D). Then, the lateral accumulation width and the longitudinal runout distance at different spatial locations across the deposit are integrated to calibrate the rheological parameters. Next, the NSGA-II algorithm is employed to obtain the Pareto solutions of rheological parameters by minimizing the prediction errors of lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at each location. To avoid extensive repetitive DAN3D simulations within NSGA-II, RF-based surrogate models are established to estimate the lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at different spatial locations. The final optimal rheological parameters are objectively selected from Pareto solutions by the entropy weight method (EWM). Finally, the proposed approaches are illustrated and validated using two landslides that occurred in Gansu Province, China. Results indicated that rheological parameters optimized by the proposed approaches not only can accurately characterize the endangered area of historical events, but also provide reasonable forward prediction of runout behavior of similar landslide events with desired accuracy. RF surrogate models can remove the computational burden within NSGA-II. Integrating both the lateral accumulation width and longitudinal runout distance into the calibration of rheological parameters can improve the prediction accuracy of landslide endangered area.

Kalman filter seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average with exogenous variables for forecasting Burundi rainfall
Numerical Simulation of Landslide-Generated Waves in Reservoirs Using a Coupled SPH-DCDEM Method
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

papers.title: Recurrent Landslide Hazards in Ramban District, NW Himalaya, India: An Interplay of Geology, Climate Change, and Anthropogenic Factors
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide hazards along the Banihal–Ramban corridor of the Jammu–Srinagar National Highway (NH-44) represent a critical geoenvironmental challenge in Northwestern Himalaya, where active tectonics, fragile lithology, steep terrain, and increasing extreme precipitation interact with intensive infrastructure development. This technical note presents a focused analysis of flash floods and landslides of April 20, 2025, examining their triggering mechanisms, cascading geomorphic processes, and impacts on transportation infrastructure and settlements. Historical landslide records (1990–2025) and regional hydroclimatic observations are incorporated to contextualize the event within evolving patterns of hazard frequency and anthropogenic slope modification along the NH-44 corridor. The April 2025 disaster resulted from the localized high-intensity precipitation, which elevated pore-water pressures, reduced slope stability, and triggered multiple failures in structurally weakened rock formations. Results highlight a transition from isolated slope failures toward compound and cascading hazard scenarios involving flash floods, debris flows, and infrastructure disruption. The study underscores the increasing vulnerability of this strategic Himalayan lifeline. It emphasizes the need for geologically informed engineering design, improved drainage management, and integrated early warning strategies to enhance long-term resilience.

papers.summary: Climate change has led to more frequent occurrences of extreme weather conditions and irregular rainfall patterns, making accurate prediction of rainfall amounts essential. In this paper, the performance of a Hybrid Temporal-Spatial Attention Network (HTSAN) model in predicting rainfall for the next day is evaluated using 12 meteorological predictors from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset. The geographical area covered by this research spans a 17 × 17 grid with 0.25° × 0.25° nominal resolution around Bangalore. HTSAN’s architecture involved a convolutional feature extractor, recurrent temporal representation, a transformer encoder, and a regression layer. HTSAN's performance was benchmarked against recurrent, convolutional-recurrent, and attention-based approaches using chronological test data. In this, benchmarking, the TFT approach resulted in the best RMSE value of 7.1474, while HTSAN had an RMSE of 7.5911, an MAE of 3.6779, and an R² of 0.4259. Extreme-rainfall benchmarking also revealed that HTSAN’s critical success index values were lower than those of the comparison approaches at the selected grid-cell rainfall thresholds. Thus, it can be inferred that the current version of HTSAN did not perform better than the selected benchmarks.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.summary: Disturbed granite residual soil slopes are highly susceptible to rainfall-induced erosion because loose surface particles can be rapidly detached and transported by runoff. Polymer-film treatment and vegetation establishment are both used for surface protection, but the sediment-delivery behavior of a polymer–vegetation system during the establishment stage remains insufficiently clarified. This study examined the erosion-control response of granite residual soil slopes treated with modified hydrophilic polyurethane (W-OH), Cynodon dactylon seeding, and their combined application under simulated rainfall. Seed germination tests were first conducted to identify a suitable W-OH application range for vegetation establishment. Then, 60-min rainfall erosion tests were performed under three slope angles (33°, 45°, and 53°) and three rainfall intensities (90, 180, and 270 mm·24 h−1). Sediment-yield ratios, sediment transmission ratios, interaction indices, and within-event temporal slopes were used to evaluate the relationship between the W-OH film and vegetation establishment. The results showed that high W-OH concentration strongly inhibited seed emergence, while the 1–4% concentration range at 1.5 L·m−2 provided a more suitable basis for evaluating W-OH-assisted vegetation protection. Untreated slopes exhibited increasing sediment yield with slope angle and rainfall intensity, confirming the high erosion sensitivity of granite residual soil. Cynodon dactylon seeding reduced sediment delivery, but its protective effect remained dependent on rainfall and terrain conditions. In the combined treatment, sediment yield decreased as W-OH concentration increased, indicating improved surface stabilization relative to vegetation-only slopes. These findings provide experimental support for optimizing W-OH-assisted vegetation measures for early-stage sediment control on rainfall-eroded granite residual soil slopes.

Extreme Rainfall-Induced Landslides on 1 June 2025 in Southern Assam, Northeast India
papers.source: Journal Of The Geological Society Of India
papers.summary: ABSTRACT In the early hours of 1 June 2025, a series of landslides occurred in the Rajpur Village of southern Assam, Northeast India, following incessant rainfall due to early onset of the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM). The landslides occurred almost simultaneously along the partially weathered hillslopes composed primarily of matrix supported gravels, between 03:00 and 03:30 IST. These were preceded by an extreme rainfall pulse of 230 mm recorded at 02:30 IST which is part of a cumulative total of 458.8 mm over the previous three days in the area. The landsides caused grievous injuries to a few people and damaged number of dwelling units with consequent displacements. Post disaster site investigation and first-hand accounts suggest an extreme rainfall triggered shallow landslide mechanism in play when saturation in the porous rock and soil mass exceeded threshold. In this report we present a preliminary assessment of the rainfall event and physical site factors leading to the landslides on this particular date. The good correlation observed here between rainfall record and occurrence of landslides provides an important case study to work out a regional threshold for rainfall triggered landslides in the foreland fold belt region of Northeast India. This will further contribute towards developing a region-specific landslide early warning system in a scenario of changing monsoonal regime.

papers.summary: Cross-sensor landslide mapping is limited by differences in image resolution and unreliable target pseudo-labels. We present SCALAR (Scale Anchoring and Label-Free Recalibration), an unsupervised adaptation workflow built on an exponential-moving-average teacher and ClassMix. GSD Anchoring (GSA) uses ground sampling distance metadata for bounded resampling. Logit-Otsu Calibration (LOC) jointly adjusts the pseudo-label boundary and relative retention margins. Ratio-Signed Regularization (RSR) makes these margins asymmetric according to the target-to-anchor GSD ratio. It is exploratory; GSA + LOC with symmetric margins is the recommended configuration. These modules introduce no trainable parameters. In the primary CAS region-held-out evaluation across five seeds, GSA + LOC increased the landslide intersection over union (IoU) by 17.9±4.5 points beyond scale anchoring when transferring satellite/aerial imagery (SAT) to unmanned aerial vehicle imagery (UAV), with no resolved additional gain in UAV-to-SAT. At seed 0, SAT-to-UAV threshold-independent average precision (AP) increased from 0.3484 for the anchored source to 0.4809 with GSA + LOC on held-out regions, compared with an increase from 0.6371 to 0.6495 under the original transductive protocol. Under that protocol, fixed-checkpoint region-cluster bootstrap supported GSA gains in both directions and LOC gains only in SAT-to-UAV; RSR’s 95% intervals included zero in both directions. UAV-to-SAT benefits varied across backbones, and negative transfer occurred in some tested settings. The findings support coordinating scale and pseudo-label decisions within CAS while identifying teacher reliability and target resolution as conditions to examine before broader deployment.

papers.summary: Abstract The soil layer up to a certain depth below the ground surface exists in an unsaturated state, where factors such as precipitation, evaporation, and prolonged subsurface heat waves control the state and material properties of soil. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

Vertical Acceleration Effect on Slope Stability: A Simplified Coupled Insight
papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.title: Slope stability and critical thresholds of red clay under rainfall and slope‐cutting effects: A case study of Hunan Province, Central China
papers.summary: Abstract Assessing the stability and critical thresholds of red clay slopes in Central China under rainfall and excavation is crucial for effective risk mitigation. Through field investigations and laboratory tests, a representative red clay slope was characterized at both macro‐ and micro‐scales. A finite element model was developed, and three scenarios were considered: rainfall (continuous and short‐duration), slope cutting (varying height and angle) and their combined effects. The factor of safety (FoS) for each scenario was calculated using the Morgenstern–Price method to determine critical thresholds. Results show that: (1) Although the slope currently exhibits favourable stability, the high illite content presents a significant risk for softening and shallow instability under prolonged rainfall. (2) Short‐duration rainfall had minimal impact, whereas continuous rainfall reduced the FoS below 1.0, highlighting a critical sensitivity to prolonged rainfall. The FoS decreased with increasing cut height and angle, directly reducing stability, though it did not change the slope's response to rainfall. (3) The failure thresholds for the three investigated scenarios were identified as 40 mm/day for rainfall, 10 m/60° for excavation and 20 mm/day of rainfall under critical excavation conditions, demonstrating their synergistic weakening effect. This research provides practical guidance for safe excavation and rainfall early warning in red clay regions.

papers.title: Slope Stability Classification with XGBoost Optimized by an Improved Remora Optimization Algorithm
papers.summary: Rapid and accurate slope-stability prediction is important for engineering safety. However, non-linear interactions among multiple influencing factors complicate slope-stability prediction, limiting the effectiveness of conventional methods under complex slope conditions. To address these issues, an Improved Remora Optimization Algorithm (IROA) is developed and used to optimize XGBoost hyperparameters for slope-stability classification. IROA integrates hybrid Latin hypercube–random initialization, probabilistic multistrategy search, and stagnation-triggered recovery. A 23 full-factorial ablation study on CEC2017 F16 showed that complete IROA and the recovery-only variant reduced the mean objective value by 24.03% and 22.91%, respectively, relative to standard ROA. At D = 50, IROA achieved the lowest mean objective value on all 12 selected CEC2017 functions, with an average rank of 1.000 compared with 2.500 for the next-best algorithm, BWO. Using 256 slope cases and six input variables—unit weight, cohesion, internal friction angle, slope angle, slope height, and pore-pressure ratio—XGBoost hyperparameters were selected through five-fold cross-validation within the training set. On the held-out test set, IROA–XGBoost achieved an accuracy of 0.9608, an F1 score of 0.9697, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.9411. Based on the reported accuracy values, observed test accuracy was 11.77 and 3.92 percentage points higher than that of baseline XGBoost and ROA–XGBoost, respectively. Gain-based feature-importance analysis was used to interpret the relative contributions of the inputs within the fitted model. Predictions for all ten supplementary engineering cases agreed with their source-reported stability states. These results suggest that IROA–XGBoost is a promising approach to slope-stability classification and may support engineering assessment under the evaluated conditions.

papers.summary: Climate change intensifies rainfall-induced landslides, necessitating sustainable ground improvement alternatives to carbon-intensive cement. This study innovatively employs the biopolymer xanthan gum to stabilize soil from a vulnerable slope in Lohaghat, India. A comprehensive evaluation of mechanical, durability and microstructural properties was conducted. Xanthan gum was added at dosages from 0.25% to 2.5% by soil weight, with 1% xanthan gum selected as the engineering optimum because it provided the most balanced overall engineering performance. Durability testing through six wetting–drying cycles showed moderate mass loss but maintained a substantial proportion of its initial strength and remained stronger than the untreated soil. Scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses confirmed a physical stabilization mechanism. To further enhance the performance, a novel composite was created by adding low cement content (2–6%) to the optimal biopolymer mix. This xanthan-cement combined effect increased unconfined compressive strength and cohesion. The findings demonstrate that xanthan gum and its hybrid composite provide an effective, eco-friendly slope stabilization solution. The proposed xanthan gum–cement composite demonstrated enhanced mechanical performance under the investigated laboratory conditions and contributes to the growing body of research on biopolymer-based stabilization for more sustainable geotechnical applications.

Rapid Assessment of Seismic Slope Stability Considering the Increase of Excess Pore-Water Pressure
papers.summary: Abstract For soil slopes, excess pore-water pressure (EPWP) buildup in soil elements is a major cause of slope failure during seismic loading. In this study, an EPWP coefficient was proposed and integrated into the simplified Bishop method to rapidly assess the influence of EPWP buildup on seismic slope stability and to calculate the slope factor of safety. To determine the value of the EPWP coefficient, numerical simulations of soil slopes with different inclinations were performed. During seismic loading, the decrease in the factor of safety for the slope can be clearly observed with the increase in EPWP. It was found that the value of the EPWP coefficient was negatively correlated with the slope angle. A linear function was employed to fit the correlation between the EPWP coefficient and the slope angle. It enables easy prediction of the EPWP coefficient based on the slope geometry and further facilitates seismic slope stability analysis that considers the EPWP buildup.

Analytical Solutions for Water Infiltration in an Infinite Vegetated Slope under Heavy Rainfall and Its Shallow Stability
papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

The SEEP/W and SLOPE/W modules of GeoStudio were employed to perform coupled numerical simulations of unsaturated seepage and slope stability. The reservoir water level was set to rise from 90 m to 120 m at a rate of 1.2 m/d, combined with six continuous rainfall intensities (duration: 25 days) of 20, 40, 80, 120, 160, and 200 mm/d. Reference scenarios involving only reservoir water level rise and only rainfall infiltration were additionally considered. The zoning response characteristics of pore water pressure at the slope front and rear were analyzed, and the individual contributions and coupled effect of rainfall and reservoir water level were quantitatively distinguished using a contribution decomposition method. The results indicate that the pore water pressure at the slope front is mainly governed by reservoir water level rise, whereas the pore water pressure at the slope rear is highly sensitive to rainfall infiltration. As the rainfall intensity increases from 20 mm/d to 200 mm/d, the factor of safety under the coupled condition decreases from 1.611 to 0.969. Furthermore, the dominant factor of instability evolves with rainfall intensity: the contribution decomposition results show that under higher rainfall intensities (80–200 mm/d), the rainfall-only contribution rate ranges from 43.6% to 57.0%, while, under lower rainfall intensities (20–40 mm/d), reservoir water level rise becomes the dominant factor. Throughout all coupled scenarios, the additional coupling contribution rate ranges from 18.2% to 52.9%, indicating a significant non-additive coupled hazard effect between the two factors. papers.title: Hydraulic-Mechanical Coupled Model of Unsaturated Soil Considering Time Effect
papers.summary: Abstract In this study, a hydraulic-mechanical coupled model of unsaturated soil considering the effect of time was established based on unsaturated elastic-plastic theory. The model considers not only the influence of the degree of saturation and viscoplastic strain on soil hardening but also that of viscous volumetric strain on the soil-water characteristic curve. The model could completely describe creep, soil-water characteristics, and mechanical properties of unsaturated soil. The elastic-viscoplastic uniform tangent modulus of the coupled model was derived using an implicit integration algorithm. The user material ( U mat ) subroutine was written using the algorithm so that the tangent stiffness matrix could be exported for finite-element calculations. To validate the correctness of the algorithm and program, the model parameters were obtained from wetting-drying cycles and isotropic compression tests. The program was used to predict creep, mechanical, and hydraulic properties under shearing creep and triaxial compression tests. Comparison of the predictions with the experimental results indicated that the coupled model was able to capture the main features of time-dependent hydraulic-mechanical coupled behavior, including hydraulic and mechanical behavior.

papers.summary: The present study is aimed at mitigating the detrimental effects of vehicle induced surface blast on the upward slope. The role of pile foundations as a mitigation measure to reduce blast effects is not yet well understood and is therefore investigated in the present study. The lower portion of the pile can act as an anchor, providing stiffness to the upper half. The presence of a pile at a particular location increases the stiffness of that sub-domain. This may result in fewer surface deformations than in the no-pile condition. But at the same time, it can cause substantial movement and deformation of the piles. Pile should be appropriately designed to minimize the pile deformation at the top and flexural stresses. This study presents a quantitative analysis of a sloping domain incorporating piles as a mitigation measure. The pile length, out-of-plane spacing (s), relative soil density, and ground slope are identified as critical parameters governing the system response. A parametric study was conducted to demonstrate their influence. Lateral displacement and PPV of surface points and the pile head are considered response parameters. With an increase in the slope angle, overburden on the right side increases, offering greater passive resistance and resulting in a drop in surface displacements at the toe. At smaller pile spacing, the equivalent pile stiffness increases, leading to a decrease in surface displacement.
