papers.summary: Agricultural water management plays a key role in sustainable crop production. Controlled drainage has been proposed as a method for mitigating the environmental impacts of drained agricultural lands and adapting to meteorological variability and climate change. However, there remains a lack of quantitative understanding of how controlled drainage influences field-scale hydrology across different soil types and climatic conditions. A process-based hydrological model was used to simulate the field-scale hydrological effects of controlled drainage in comparison to conventional free drainage in Finland. The main objective was to quantify the effects on groundwater table depths and field water balance and analyze how the effects change during the 21st century due to climate change. The simulations applied both mineral soil and peatland parameterizations. Furthermore, the dissertation addressed the following objectives: 1) to analyze the hydrology and performance of controlled drainage on a peatland field with a strong groundwater connection to an upslope forest area, 2) to couple hydrological simulations with peat subsidence under controlled drainage, and 3) to simulate the combination of controlled drainage and open ditch damming and assess the spatial distribution of the effects on groundwater table depths. The simulation results showed controlled drainage to be a viable method to reduce groundwater table depth, with even growing season groundwater table depths being reduced by 0.06–0.26 m. Especially when storing water in the field during earlier months, controlled drainage has potential to reduce growing season drought risk and the environmental impacts of deep groundwater levels. Drain discharge was reduced by 7–23%. This was reflected in increased lateral groundwater outflow, which may be beneficial in reducing substance load, but the peatland simulations showed also a strong increase in surface layer runoff. papers.title: Infiltration in a novel unsaturated multi-layered cover system for use in tailings storage facilities
papers.summary: Conventional barrier systems in tailings storage facilities often rely on thick monolithic geomaterials (1.5 m-2.5 m) or geosynthetics that fail under ex-treme precipitation or snowmelt events typical in Nordic climates. This study proposes and evaluates a novel, fully unsaturated multi-layered cover system (MLCS) constructed majorly from on-site sourced tailings and waste rock. The tailings are modified through either mixing with biochar and clay or by altering surface polarity to make them functional components of a newly conceptual-ized MLCS. The MLCS design integrates capillary barrier mechanisms with a water-entry-head-controlled hydrophobic interface to act as a final hydraulic buffer during extreme ponding conditions. Laboratory characterization of soil-water retention curves (SWRCs), unsaturated hydraulic conductivity functions (SHCFs), and hydrophobicity confirmed the enhanced water-buffering capaci-ty of the modified tailings mixtures. Especially, the threshold-based break-through resistance of the hydrophobic layer (WEH ≈ 4.71 kPa) allowed the construction of an overall thin MLCS (≤0.5-m-thick). This MLCS was physically modelled in an instrumented 1-D column subjected to a ponding head equivalent to a 500-year rainfall event. Results showed complete suppression of percolation below the MLCS for 61 days of testing period, with the hydro-phobic layer preventing breakthrough even after upper layers neared saturation. Complementary two-stage finite element simulations, incorporating WEH-triggered hydraulic switching, accurately reproduced observed suction, water-content, and percolation behaviour. The findings demonstrate that the proposed MLCS provides a climate-resilient, all-weather hydraulic barrier, reduces dependence on imported materials, and offers a feasible, low-cost closure strategy for Nordic TSFs. Further work should assess performance under field-scale slopes including lateral drainage conditions.

papers.title: Groundwater Flow and Age Tracer Modeling in the Montérégie Est Bedrock Aquifer using MODFLOW, MODPATH, and MT3D-USGS
papers.summary: Groundwater residence times and flow pathways are difficult to constrain in regional fractured bedrock aquifers because groundwater movement is controlled by heterogeneous fracture networks, variable recharge conditions, and mixing between local and regional flow systems. This study developed a numerical coupled groundwater flow, particle-tracking, and age-tracer transport model for the 9,218 km² Montérégie Est fractured bedrock aquifer system in southern Québec, Canada. The model was constructed using MODFLOW-NWT to simulate steady-state regional groundwater flow, and hydraulic head, MODPATH-7 to evaluate advective flow pathways, and MT3D-USGS to simulate the infiltration, transport and decay of tritium (³H) and radiocarbon (¹⁴C) from major recharge zones in the region. The model was developed and calibrated using hydrogeological and geochemical datasets from the 2010 PACES field campaign and was subsequently independently evaluated using groundwater samples collected during a 2025 field campaign. The 2025 sampling targeted wells located near model-derived regional flowpaths and included analyses of ³H, ¹⁴C, dissolved inorganic carbon, δ²H, δ¹⁸O, and major ions. Surface-water samples were also collected from the region's major watersheds to assess potential river influence. Simulated hydraulic heads reproduced the regional groundwater gradient well, with strong agreement between measured and modelled heads. The model also captured the main spatial patterns in groundwater age-tracer distributions. ³H simulations reproduced the overall measured–predicted relationship across the 2010 and 2025 datasets, although local deviations indicate unresolved variability in recharge, mixing, and flowpath geometry. ¹⁴C simulations showed strong agreement with measured values from 2025, supporting the model's ability to reproduce first-order regional residence-time patterns, while also highlighting the presence of water-rock interactions. papers.title: Direction-Dependent Skin Friction of Snakeskin-Inspired Surfaces, Piles, and Suction Caissons in Clay and Sand
papers.summary: The installation and performance of geotechnical structures such as piles, anchors, and suction caissons are governed by the skin friction mobilized at soil–structure interfaces. Conventional surfaces typically mobilize slightly greater skin friction in compression than tension, leading to a fundamental trade-off: a high skin friction translates to greater capacity but also leads to greater installation forces, while a low skin friction is beneficial for installation but can result in a limited ultimate capacity and excessive movements. Inspired by the ventral scales of snakes, which generate smaller friction when moving in the caudal direction (along the scales) than in the cranial direction (against the scales), this dissertation investigates the direction-dependent shear behavior of snakeskin-inspired surfaces across a broad range of soils, drainage conditions, and structural applications through interface element testing and centrifuge physical modeling.Interfaces between snakeskin-inspired surfaces and normally consolidated kaolin clay were characterized through direct interface shear tests performed under drained and undrained conditions, together with centrifuge load tests on axially loaded piles. Cranial shearing consistently mobilized greater strength than caudal shearing, and the interface strength increased as the asperity height (H) was increased and the asperity length (L) was decreased, with the L/H ratio unifying the effects of asperity geometry. Piles installed caudally and pulled cranially mobilized skin friction up to 60% greater during pullout than installation, and tensile skin friction 2.8 to 4.1 times greater than an untextured reference pile.Characterization of the interface response was also performed with compacted, unsaturated silty clay through interface shear tests that examined the coupled effects of asperity geometry, normal stress, and water content. papers.title: Application of the Material Point Method to the Stability and Runout Analysis of Vegetated Slopes
papers.summary: Slope failures cause severe human and economic losses worldwide, yet conventional stability methods describe them only up to the onset of failure. Limit equilibrium methods treat the failing mass as rigid and perfectly plastic, and the finite element method is restricted to small deformations, so neither follows the slide once it forms. The Material Point Method (MPM) avoids this limitation by discretizing soil into Lagrangian material points that move through a fixed background mesh, so no mesh distortion develops under large deformation. This dissertation applies MPM to the analysis of slope failures in two parts, the assessment of slope stability and the influence of vegetation on rainfall-induced failures. The one-phase and coupled two-phase formulations are first derived and verified against classical benchmark problems in poromechanics. Next, MPM is applied to evaluate the stability of slopes using the strength reduction technique. For dry and unsaturated slopes, slip surfaces agree with finite element solutions and factors of safety differ by less than about 10%, reflecting the different criteria by which each method identifies failure. Unlike mesh-based methods, MPM continues past the onset of failure and captures the post-failure runout. The effect of root reinforcement is then investigated. A multiple-hardening constitutive model for root-reinforced soil is implemented within the coupled formulation and validated against triaxial tests. Comparative analyses of bare and vegetated slopes under rainfall show that roots delay the initiation of failure, roughly halve the displacement, and change a retrogressive slide into the movement of a single block, although they do not prevent failure under continued rainfall. Finally, the method is validated against a documented centrifuge slope test. papers.title: Managing the effect of infiltration variability on the performance of surface irrigation
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: Infiltration variability is a major issue during the design phase and management for all types of irrigation systems. Infiltration is of particular significance for furrow irrigation and other forms of surface irrigation as the soil intake rate at any given position not only determines the depth applied but also governs the distribution of water to other locations in the field. Despite this, existing measurement and evaluation procedures generally assume homogeneous soil infiltration rates across the field to simplify data collection and computational requirements. This study was conducted to (a) determine whether spatial and temporal variations in soil infiltration characteristics have a significant impact on the performance of surface irrigation and (b) identify more appropriate management strategies that account for this variability and substantially improve irrigation performance. The soil infiltration rate is typically expressed as an empirical function of opportunity time. The infiltration function parameters cannot be directly measured but are commonly estimated from field hydraulic measurements using an appropriate simulation model. The volume balance model as used in the inverse solution for infiltration (e.g. Two Point Method) was modified to enable runoff data collected during the inflow period to be used in the estimation of the infiltration parameters. The resulting model, IPARM also accommodates the full (variable) inflow hydrograph rather than relying on a constant inflow assumption. Inclusion of runoff data in the inverse solution improved the accuracy of the infiltration curve during the runoff phase and hence offered the greatest benefit where the irrigation time exceeded the completion of advance. papers.title: Toward real-time control of surface irrigation
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: The performance of surface irrigation is a function of the field design, infiltration characteristic of the soil, and the irrigation management practice. However, the complexity of the interactions makes it difficult for irrigators to identify optimal design or management practices. The infiltration characteristic of the soil is the most crucial of all the factors affecting the performance of surface irrigation and both spatial and temporal variations in the infiltration characteristic are a major physical constraint to achieving higher irrigation application efficiencies. Real-time optimisation and control has the potential to overcome these spatial and temporal variations and return highly significant improvements in performance. Calculation of the infiltration parameters from irrigation advance data is now the preferred method. If the process is to be included in a real time control system it must be done accurately, reliably and rapidly, and with a minimum of field data. Substantial work has been directed towards developing methods to estimate the infiltration characteristics of soil from irrigation advance data. However, none of the existing methods are entirely suitable for use in real time control. The greatest limitation is that they are data intensive and or unreliable and provide soil infiltration properties after an irrigation event. A simple real-time control system for furrow irrigation is proposed that: predicts the infiltration characteristics of the soil in real-time using data measured during an irrigation event, simulates the irrigation, and determines the optimum time to cut-off for that irrigation. The basis of the system is a new method for the Real-time Estimation of the Infiltration Parameters (REIP) under furrow irrigation, developed during this research study, and that uses a model infiltration curve, and a scaling process to predict the infiltration characteristics for each furrow and each irrigation event. papers.title: STUDI PERENCANAAN JALAN DAN PENGAMANAN LERENG PADA TRASE JALAN UJAN MAS PADA STA 0+050 SAMPAI STA 2+550
papers.source: UMM Institutional Repository (University of Maine at Machias)
papers.summary: The development of safe and efficient road infrastructure is a crucial element in regional development. This study aims to conduct technical planning for new roads and slope protection systems on the Ujan Mas Road Trace (STA 0+050 to STA 2+550). Given the location's topography, which is dominated by steep slopes, this planning integrates geometric design of the road, pavement structure, drainage system, and retaining wall design. The study methodology includes primary and secondary data collection, hydrological analysis for the design flood discharge calculation, and soil mechanics investigation to ensure the stability of the retaining wall structure against overturning, shearing, and dynamic earthquake loads (Mononobe-Okabe method). In addition to technical aspects, this study also includes the preparation of a Cost Budget Plan (RAB) to accurately estimate construction funding requirements based on the calculated work volume. The geometric design of the road refers to the Bina Marga standard, while the pavement analysis uses the Bina Marga method. The final results of this study are expected to provide a comprehensive and economical technical solution for road infrastructure development in the area, while prioritizing safety aspects and sustainable slope stability

papers.title: Boundary Influence in Truncated Groundwater Models: Reconstructing a Local-Scale MODFLOW Model from a Consultant-Developed Regional Model in the Monterey Subbasin
papers.summary: Regional groundwater models built by consultants contain valuable calibrated frameworks but are often too large and complex for repeated local-scale analysis. Rather than rebuilding an entirely new smaller model, this study truncates the existing consultant-built regional model of the Monterey Subbasin, preserving the original grid structure and parameter framework while reducing the active domain to a manageable size for planning-level use. A key finding is that boundary-condition representation exerted a dominant influence on simulated groundwater behavior within the truncated domain, highlighting that truncation is a structural decision that meaningfully affects how the model responds. Model performance was evaluated two ways. Alternative hydraulic conductivity fields derived from AEM resistivity data were used to assess how sensitive the reconstructed model was to changes in internal parameter structure. Transient injection simulations produced cumulative groundwater mounding that grew progressively over repeated seasonal cycles, confirming realistic aquifer behavior and demonstrating the model's value as a practical and transparent planning-level tool.

papers.title: CAPILLARY-DRIVEN TRANSPORT IN POROUS MEDIA: UNSATURATED FLOW, THERMAL EFFECTS, AND VADOSE-ZONE CYCLING
papers.summary: Capillary-driven transport in porous media plays a fundamental role in a wide range of natural and engineered systems, including heat pipes, fibrous and ceramic materials, soils, contaminant transport in the vadose zone, and moisture-management technologies. Although substantial progress has been made in modeling and characterizing wicking under simplified conditions, important gaps remain in understanding how thermal gradients, partial saturation, and evaporation-driven solute cycling influence liquid transport in porous media. This dissertation addresses these gaps through a combined experimental, analytical, and numerical investigation of capillary-driven flow in porous materials across thermal, engineered, and environmental settings.The first part of this dissertation develops a Richards equation-based numerical framework to model moisture infusion in porous ceramics and other engineered materials by incorporating capillary pressure–saturation and relative permeability relationships. The model was validated against high-resolution neutron microscope imaging experiments and two independent analytical solutions. Extended simulations were then performed to investigate the role of engineered wettability — including hydrophilic surface coatings and hydrophobic inclusions — on two-dimensional moisture migration patterns. These results demonstrate how material design and local wettability modification can be used to control liquid transport pathways in porous systems. The second part of this work investigates non-isothermal wicking in porous media. Experiments were conducted using sintered polymer-bead wicks and hydrocarbon liquids under imposed temperature differences between the liquid and the wick. A sharp-front Darcy-based framework was developed to model the transient rise of liquid while accounting for temperature-dependent viscosity, surface tension, and density. papers.title: Impacts of Cover Crops, No-Tillage and Cotton-Sorghum Rotation on Soil-Water Dynamics: Environmental and Economic Implications
papers.summary: Water scarcity associated with declining groundwater levels in the Ogallala Aquifer threatens the long-term sustainability of irrigated agriculture in the semi-arid Texas High Plains. As irrigation capacity decreases, management strategies that improve soil-mediated water capture and enhance production resilience are increasingly important. This thesis integrates a regional literature synthesis with field-based evaluation of conservation practices aimed at improving water-use efficiency in cotton-based cropping systems. The literature identifies irrigation technology improvements, precision agriculture technologies, and soil health management as key pathways for reducing water demand and enhancing precipitation capture, while also emphasizing economic constraints and site-specific performance of conservation practices. A two-year field study assessed the short-term effects of cover crops and cotton–sorghum rotation under no-tillage on soil physical properties, crop productivity, and economic indicators. Soil measurements included saturated hydraulic conductivity, aggregate stability, compaction, and total organic carbon, alongside cotton and sorghum yield and fiber quality. Results showed limited short-term changes in most soil properties, although aggregate stability increased under rotational systems with cover crops. Cotton yield remained consistent across treatments, but fiber quality and associated economic returns declined in rotation-based systems. Sorghum performance was largely influenced by interannual climatic variability rather than management effects. Overall, findings suggest that while conservation practices hold potential to improve soil function and water-use efficiency, measurable agronomic and economic benefits may require long-term adoption. Extended evaluation is necessary to determine whether gradual soil health improvements can enhance system resilience and profitability under increasing water limitations.

papers.title: Mechanistic Investigation Of Arsenic Removal From Drinking Water Using Metal–organic Frameworks And Granular Activated Carbon
papers.source: UND Scholarly Commons (University of North Dakota)
papers.summary: Arsenic contamination in groundwater represents a critical environmental and public health challenge due to its high toxicity and widespread occurrence in natural aquifers. Chronic exposure to arsenic, even at trace levels, is associated with severe health effects, including skin lesions and increased cancer risk. Conventional treatment technologies, such as adsorption using activated carbon or metal oxides, often suffer from limited selectivity, regeneration difficulty, and reduced efficiency under varying pH conditions. Therefore, developing advanced sorbent materials with high capacity, selectivity, and structural stability is essential for addressing arsenic pollution in decentralized water systems.Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have recently emerged as promising materials for water purification owing to their tunable pore structures, high surface areas, and functional versatility. Among them, zirconium-based MOFs such as UiO-66 are particularly attractive because of their excellent water stability and Zr–OH active sites favorable for arsenate binding. However, the powdered nature of most MOFs presents significant challenges for practical filtration applications, including clogging, high pressure drop, and regeneration difficulties. To overcome these limitations, this work first focused on integrating UiO-66 and UiO-66-NH₂ with granular activated carbon (GAC) to develop hybrid point-of-use filtration materials. The composite exhibited uniform MOF attachment on GAC surfaces, mitigating issues related to powder handling and mobility. Batch adsorption tests revealed that UiO-66–GAC outperformed UiO-66-NH₂–GAC under near-neutral pH, highlighting the influence of surface chemistry on arsenic affinity.
